#552. Alpine Linux Users Urged to Patch OpenSSH Authentication Flaw

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (821 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Infoq

Alpine Linux Users Urged to Patch OpenSSH Authentication Flaw

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (821 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Alpine Linux Users Urged to Patch OpenSSH Authentication Flaw.
  • Nov 16, 2026 4 min read.
  • In a recent development, the flaw comes from the way OpenSSH checks passwords when musl handles the underlying crypt() call.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Alpine Linux Users Urged to Patch OpenSSH Authentication Flaw.

Nov 16, 2026 4 min read.

In a recent development, the flaw comes from the way OpenSSH checks passwords when musl handles the underlying crypt() call. On an affected system, a password longer than 256 bytes causes musl to return an error value. That value is an asterisk, the same character Linux uses in /etc/shadow to mark an account as having no password. OpenSSH then treats the returned asterisk as a match and permits the login.

In a recent development, the conditions to exploit the vulnerability are however quite narrow. The server must run OpenSSH before version 10.6p2, be built against the musl library rather than glibc, and operate without PAM. It must also have at least one account with a SHA-256 or SHA-512 password hash and another account marked with an asterisk in its shadow entry. When those conditions are met, any password between 257 and 1,024 characters can authenticate against the passwordless account.

Sources indicate that alpine Linux is the most prominent distribution affected, as it uses musl and its default OpenSSH configuration does not enable PAM. Other musl-based environments, including OpenWrt, Buildroot and Yocto, may also be affected where the same configuration applies. Systems using glibc, PAM, Dropbear or OpenBSD are not affected.

Ozgun Kultekin, a security researcher at Wakefield, published the technical explanation on the *sshole site. Kultekin traces the problem to two musl changes made in 2012: the first replaced the NULL error return from crypt() with an asterisk, and the second added a 256-byte limit to SHA-512 password hashing, so longer inputs caused an error. Together, the changes produced a value that could be mistaken for a password hash.

In a recent development, the OpenSSH side of the problem dates from a 2016 fix for CVE-2016-6210, which was a timing attack that could reveal whether a username existed. To make responses take a similar amount of time for valid and invalid people, OpenSSH borrowed the salt from another account and hashed the supplied password anyway. That workaround also applied to real accounts whose shadow entry contained an asterisk.

Kultekin writes that the matter remained unnoticed for roughly a decade because the vulnerable combination was uncommon in testing. OpenSSH is tested on OpenBSD and glibc-based systems, while many Linux distributions route authentication through PAM, which does not call crypt() for asterisk entries in the same way. Kultekin says the bug was found after building OpenSSH in several configurations and testing about 17,600 unusual login attempts.

It has been revealed that on Alpine's official AWS and Azure images, the default alpine user is marked as passwordless and can use doas without a password. This means that an attacker who reaches that account can therefore obtain root privileges. Dan Goodin reports for Ars Technica that the matter can give unauthenticated access to high-privilege accounts within seconds on affected systems.

Sources indicate that openSSH 10.6p2 contains a fix. Operators who cannot revision immediately can disable password authentication by setting PasswordAuthentication no in the SSH server configuration and restarting sshd. Kultekin also advises checking authentication logs for evidence that an account with no password accepted a password. The project has published a detection and background repository.

The vulnerability is being actively exploited. Goodin notes that GreyNoise reported that honeypots in Southeast Asia had been attacked by a group it is tracking known as GT10, which reportedly deploys a backdoor which supports shell commands, reconnaissance and persistence. Goodin reports that watchTowr linked the activity to botnets and cryptocurrency operations, while Previdian recorded 20 exploitation attempts from 13 IP addresses in nine countries. The United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency added CVE-2026-123158 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 9 November, according to Hackread.

Sources indicate that red Hat has remarked that its products are not affected because they do not meet the required combination of musl and no PAM. Amazon has likewise marked Amazon Linux 2 and Amazon Linux 2023 as not affected. That does not remove the risk for teams running Alpine-based containers, embedded devices or custom musl builds. Administrators should look for SSH servers built against musl, check whether PAM is disabled, review shadow entries for asterisk-locked accounts, apply OpenSSH 10.6p2 and restart the service.

Recent findings suggest that the vulnerability was publicly disclosed on 5 November and exploitation reports followed within days. For organisations with internet-facing SSH services, the immediate action to take is fairly straightforward: upgrade OpenSSH, restart it, and remove password authentication where it is not needed.

  • Nov 16, 2026 3 min read.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Uno Platform 7.0 Adds WebGPU Backend, Apple TV and Reactor Support, and Retires Native Rendering.

Nov 16, 2026 3 min read.

Recent findings suggest that the Uno Platform team released Uno Platform 7.0, which unifies rendering on SkiaSharp 4 with an experimental WebGPU backend, adds Apple TV as a target platform and supports .NET 11 from day zero. The release also brings third-party .NET MAUI controls and Microsoft.UI.Reactor library to every target, and removes native rendering and Mac Catalyst.

Recent findings suggest that uno Platform is an open-source framework for building .NET applications with C# and WinUI XAML for Windows, Android, iOS, macOS, Linux and WebAssembly. The team describes 7.0 as its largest release, with 5,219 commits and 704 closed complications since 6.7. According to the team’s benchmarks, 7.0 is about 2x faster at the median and 5x smaller than 6.7, with some operations, such as brush creation, up to 38x faster. These figures come from the vendor and the workloads were not published in detail.

All targets now render through one pluggable pipeline. SkiaSharp 4 is the default, and Uno Platform is a co-maintainer of the library alongside the .NET team at Microsoft. On Android, Windows and Linux, Skia now renders through Vulkan by default. The WebGPU backend, available on all desktop, mobile and WebAssembly targets, is enabled by adding WebGpu to UnoFeatures and registering the backend on the host builder. It uses wgpu-native outside the browser and the browser’s own WebGPU support on WebAssembly. The team measured up to a 50% frame-rate improvement depending on the scene, and states a WebGPU-only app drops about 6 MB of uncompressed native code from WebAssembly builds. A new WebGpuCanvasElement lets applications problem their own WebGPU commands inside the UI.

Through .NET MAUI Embedding, controls from vendors such as Syncfusion, Telerik, Infragistics, DevExpress and Esri previously ran only on iOS, Android, macOS and Windows. They now work on every Uno Platform target, including the web and Linux. In the other direction, existing .NET MAUI apps can reach the browser and Linux through Uno Platform’s .NET MAUI handlers.

Industry observers note that microsoft.UI.Reactor, Microsoft’s declarative C# framework for WinUI with hooks such as UseState and no XAML, now runs on desktop, browser, Android and iOS. It is enabled with the Reactor UnoFeature, is in preview, and can coexist with existing XAML pages in the same visual tree. Apple TV support is added through the net10.0-tvos target framework, targets tvOS 15 and later, renders through Metal and uses the Siri Remote for focus navigation. .NET 11 is supported on every head, for example through dotnet new unoapp -tfm net11.0, while .NET 10 remains the long-term support option.

Industry observers note that richTextBlock and RichEditBox are now available on every platform, closing an issue opened in 2018. WinUI alignment continues with ItemsRepeater and ItemsView ported from current WinUI sources, LinedFlowLayout, the TitleBar control, multiple windows on iPad and Lottie rendering through Composition. Smaller additions include built-in input validation through INotifyDataErrorInfo, TalkBack, VoiceOver and AT-SPI screen-reader support, and the uno-devserver app command for launching and inspecting running apps from scripts and CI.

Sources indicate that most apps upgrade by changing the Uno.Sdk version in global.json, following the migration guide. The team released Uno Platform Studio 3.3 alongside it.

The release follows Uno Platform 6.7 in September, which added Android TV, Android Auto and Wear OS targets, semantic styles shared by the Material and Simple themes, and damage-region repainting on Skia renderers. It also removed the WPF targets.

In a recent development, roadzen confirmed on November 16, 2026 a common-equity financing of approximately $10 million for its India subsidiary, Roadzen AI Limited, at a standalone post-money valuation of approximately $300 million. The transaction has not yet closed and would leave the parent with approximately 89% of the unit.

It has been revealed that the securities are common equity only, with no warrants or preferred rights, and rank equally with Roadzen’s existing shareholding. The company noted issuing them at the subsidiary creates no direct dilution at the Nasdaq-listed parent.

Roadzen said subsequent closes could increase the total capital raised, citing strong investor demand.

The valuation applies to Roadzen AI Limited on a standalone basis, not to the listed parent. The offering therefore concerns the holding firm for Roadzen’s operating businesses, rather than an issuance of parent-company shares.

It has been revealed that the financing accompanies a consolidation of Roadzen’s global operating businesses under Roadzen AI Limited, formerly Roadzen Technologies Limited. Roadzen Inc. remains the Nasdaq-listed parent, while the subsidiary serves as the holding tech giant for those operations.

Roadzen noted the structure gives the business direct access to a deeper pool of fundamental investors in India and could accommodate a potential future listing in the country. No listing decision or timetable was announced.

Prime Securities Limited is acting as the exclusive investment bank for the offering. N. Jayakumar, its managing director and group CEO, said: “The Indian market continues to offer superior valuations for high-growth AI businesses.”.

Roadzen prepares to use the proceeds for growth priorities across its insurance and mobility businesses and to strengthen its balance sheet. Management is targeting a $100 million annual revenue run-rate for the current fiscal year.

In the United States, the manufacturer is expanding sales capacity to pursue near-term growth opportunities. In India, Roadzen projects that VehicleCare, its AI-enabled claims-to-repair business, will grow revenue more than tenfold in 2026.

Roadzen describes DrivebuddyAI as India’s only AIS-184-validated driver-safety platform, with new safety mandates covering more than one million new commercial vehicles annually forming the market backdrop for its expansion. The two businesses show how the India subsidiary spans both claims automation and vehicle safety.

The financing is expected to close over the two weeks following the announcement, subject to customary closing conditions.

According to recent reports, roadzen was also scheduled to release its second-quarter fiscal 2027 results after the market close that day. Those results offer a near-term check on reported performance against the run-rate objective, giving the financing announcement an immediate financial context beyond the subsidiary’s valuation.

#549. AWS Nitro Sandboxes Put Each EKS Pod in Its Own MicroVM with One RuntimeClass Field

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (916 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Infoq

AWS Nitro Sandboxes Put Each EKS Pod in Its Own MicroVM with One RuntimeClass Field

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (916 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News AWS Nitro Sandboxes Put Each EKS Pod in Its Own MicroVM with One RuntimeClass Field.
  • Nov 16, 2026 4 min read.
  • It has been revealed that AWS has released Nitro Sandboxes, which run an opted-in Kubernetes pod, ECS task, or EC2 workload inside its own lightweight virtual machine with a separate guest kernel, carved out of a running EC2 instance by the Nitro hypervisor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News AWS Nitro Sandboxes Put Each EKS Pod in Its Own MicroVM with One RuntimeClass Field.

Nov 16, 2026 4 min read.

It has been revealed that AWS has released Nitro Sandboxes, which run an opted-in Kubernetes pod, ECS task, or EC2 workload inside its own lightweight virtual machine with a separate guest kernel, carved out of a running EC2 instance by the Nitro hypervisor. On Amazon EKS, the whole change is one pod field: runtimeClassName: isolated-sandbox or confidential-sandbox.

According to recent reports, the feature is available in all commercial regions at no additional charge, and AWS positions it for workloads where the tenant or the code cannot be trusted, with coding agents named first. In an AWS blog post, Carlos Santana and Trishi Mehta write:.

Each pod gets its own operating system, completely separate from the host and from every neighbor.

According to the EKS documentation, a containerd-shim-nitro-sandbox-v2 process on the parent instance debuts a Firecracker microVM as a first-level guest with hardware-assisted virtualization, after which an agent inside the VM runs the pod’s containers through its own containerd and the two sides communicate over virtio and vsock. The result is a sandbox that shares neither kernel nor memory mappings with the parent instance or any other sandbox, while the containers themselves start unchanged. How the nodes get there depends on the cluster type: on EKS Auto Mode the two RuntimeClasses ship with every cluster and sandbox-capable nodes are provisioned on demand, whereas on standard EKS a team builds a sandbox-enabled AMI for its node groups or Karpenter.

(Source: Amazon EKS User Guide).

What separates the two modes is which side of the boundary is trusted. Isolated mode trusts the parent instance and not the guest, which is why kubectl exec, logs, and process listing keep working, whereas confidential mode treats the parent as untrusted and moves enforcement inside the VM: a Cedar policy generated from the pod spec pins image digests, arguments, environment, mounts and capabilities, exec and stdin are denied, the Nitro Secure Module measures the image and policy into PCRs, and a KMS key policy can release secrets only to a sandbox whose measurements match. Image layers can be encrypted as well, so the parent moves ciphertext it never reads.

That chain only holds if something checks the measurements, and the documentation says so: without a KMS policy or external verifier checking the PCR values, "the attestation measurement is recorded but never verified, and the confidentiality guarantees of confidential mode are incomplete." Separately from either mode, a network-isolated annotation boots the sandbox with no network device at all, which also removes DNS, NTP, IMDS and Pod Identity and breaks HTTP and TCP probes.

Sandip Das, an AWS Container Hero, read the documentation the same way and drew out what isolated mode leaves to the operator: the protection "only runs in one direction," so a compromised parent can still observe or tamper with unencrypted traffic and DNS, writes the pod's /etc/hosts, and can mint Pod Identity credentials for any pod on the node. He also lists prerequisites the blog post does not, among them Kubernetes 1.36 or later, a launch template with Nitro Enclaves enabled on managed node groups, without which "sandboxed pods sit in Pending," and Pod Identity rather than IRSA for credentials. On AWS's description of performance as near-native, he advises treating it "as a vendor claim" and benchmarking startup latency, I/O throughput and tail latency.

Beyond agents, AWS lists multi-tenant SaaS, regulated workloads, CI builds and remote IDEs, and points to the open-source agent-sandbox project for warm pools that hand out a pre-booted VM in about two seconds.

It has been revealed that the constraints are on the considerations page, and the largest is GPU and device passthrough, which is not supported at launch because Firecracker cannot pass host devices into a guest, so GPU pods run without the sandbox class. Density is capped twice over: total sandbox vCPUs may not exceed five times the node's vCPU count, and neither may the number of sandboxes, halved on CPU-overcommit types, which gives a 4-vCPU node room for twenty 1-vCPU sandboxes or five 4-vCPU ones. Simultaneous multithreading costs more than the arithmetic suggests, because core scheduling stops two sandboxes sharing the sibling threads of one core and leaves roughly half the advertised vCPUs usable; Graviton, with one thread per core, is unaffected.

The nearest comparison is GKE Sandbox, which has offered a gvisor RuntimeClass since 2019 and more recently a microvm class built on Kata Containers and Cloud Hypervisor. gVisor intercepts syscalls in a user-space kernel, starts in under 200 milliseconds and supports CUDA on a subset of GPUs; Google's microVM option carries a fixed 250 mCPU and 130 MiB per pod, starts in one to two seconds and does not support GPUs. AWS has taken the VM side of that split and expressed its overhead as density and threads rather than per-pod resources.

On EC2, Amazon Linux and Firecracker are supported natively and patches are available for other virtual machine monitors. The EC2 User Guide carries the supported instance list and notes that snapshot, restore and live migration are not available.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenAI revealed on November 16, 2026 that it is donating £1 million to The King’s Trust for a UK program intended to give up to 25,000 young people practical AI skills over 18 months, prioritizing those not in education, employment or training.

The program is designed to build confidence and help participants progress into education or work. Its learning model mixes AI skills, recognized qualifications and practical experience, with OpenAI contributing AI expertise alongside the donation. The King’s Trust is asking employers, AI specialists and young people which capabilities will be needed as AI becomes part of everyday work.

It has been revealed that the Open University’s Business Barometer 2026 is based on a survey of 1,500 UK organization leaders and 1,000 people aged 16–24 who were not in education, employment or training. Among those young respondents, 68% mentioned they would train or upskill to improve their job prospects. At the same time, 42% agreed that AI threatens their future job prospects and 49% were wary about its effect on their careers.

In a recent development, the employer responses add another dimension to that picture. The survey reported that 57% of employers were experiencing a skills shortage and 51% saw AI affecting hiring or recruitment. While 80% stated they were prepared to train young people entering the workforce, only 43% offered work-experience placements and 11% ran initiatives specifically for young people not in education, employment or training.

According to recent reports, the partnership forms part of a wider program of nationally recognized AI qualifications that The King’s Trust plans to launch in the coming months. The charity is also examining how these skills can complement the employability training already embedded across its programs, tying the AI initiative to its existing youth-support work.

The announcement comes during The King’s Trust’s 50th year, and the charity says it has supported more than 1.3 million young people over that period. It also precedes the final report of the independent Young People and Work review. Alan Milburn welcomed the partnership, saying: “AI will bring disruption as well as opportunity, so it is vital that young people get a fair share of the opportunity and don’t bear the cost of the disruption.”.

In a recent development, openAI described the partnership as part of its broader effort to make practical AI learning more accessible. The company launched the OpenAI Academy’s free public resource hub on March 25, 2025, providing online materials, workshops and other content for students, job-seekers, educators and other learners. The King’s Trust program gives that effort a specific UK youth focus and connects AI learning with employability support.

Recent findings suggest that the practical-experience component is therefore consequential. The survey indicates strong interest in training alongside limited employer-provided routes into work; the partnership’s central task is to connect that interest to recognized learning and tangible routes into education or employment.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that zoox confirmed on November 16, 2026, that its robotaxis had begun serving Uber riders in Las Vegas, adding the ride-hailing app as a second distribution channel for its autonomous service. Uber customers on eligible trips can now be matched with a Zoox vehicle, while rides remain available through the Zoox app.

Riders using either app can travel to popular resorts and venues on and around the Las Vegas Strip, along with destinations in Downtown and the Arts District. Zoox intends to add more destinations and is starting the Uber rollout with a small fleet, with expansion possible as it refines operations, technology and the customer experience. For Zoox, the addition provides a way to introduce its vehicle to riders who have not used its standalone app.

Zoox and Uber are the official robotaxi and rideshare partners, respectively, of MGM Resorts’ Las Vegas properties. The companies are working with MGM to improve on-property wayfinding, provide in-app guidance and make infrastructure changes intended to simplify pickups and drop-offs and support smoother traffic flow.

It has been revealed that those arrangements address the physical handoff between passenger and vehicle. A rider still has to reach the correct pickup area, and a driverless vehicle still has to enter and leave busy resort properties efficiently; the launch includes those operating details alongside autonomous driving.

In a recent development, the launch implements a strategic partnership revealed on March 11, 2026. Uber’s release at the time described it as Zoox’s first partnership with a third-party platform and targeted a summer 2026 debut in Las Vegas, followed by Los Angeles by mid-2027. The actual Las Vegas start came after that initial summer window.

Zoox’s vehicle was designed as a robotaxi rather than retrofitted from a passenger car. It is fully autonomous, all-electric and bidirectional. The four-passenger cabin uses carriage-style seating, with riders facing one another.

It has been revealed that the Uber option builds on an existing Las Vegas operation. Zoox launched rides through its own app on and around the Strip on September 10, 2025. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News GitHub Rebuilds the Copilot App's Diff Surface to Open Million-Line Pull Requests Without Jank.

Nov 16, 2026 2 min read.

GitHub engineering has published a detailed account of how it rebuilt the diff surface in the GitHub Copilot app to open a pull request with 2,200 files, over a million changed lines and more than 400 inline review comments without turning the review into a waiting exercise.

The post, by Principal Design Engineer Alberto Gimeno, lands at a moment when AI coding agents are producing far more pull requests than reviewers can digest, and the bottleneck has moved from writing code to reading it.

Industry observers note that at the heart of the rebuild is a decision to stop pretending a pull request is a single uniform list. Code rows have a known height at a known font size, so their geometry can be computed up front and never rebuilt. Comments do not. A markdown body wraps differently at different widths, sections can be toggled in place, reply composers grow as a user types, and images change height when they load. Rather than force one variable-height virtualizer to absorb both, the team split the document into two independent domains:.

It has been revealed that dynamic blocks are keyed by identity (file, line, side) rather than pixel position, with a fingerprint tracking content, open state and measurement width. A single idle-gated measurement pass reads mounted blocks in one batch, scoped to roughly 2,400 pixels around the viewport, and corrections are anchored to whatever the reader is looking at so the surface never fights an active scroll.

It has been revealed that gimeno is open about an early mistake, the team's first instinct was one ResizeObserver per block writing heights back into the layout, a classic feedback loop whose cost grows with every mounted block. The shipped design keeps the observer but defaults it to flagging rather than writing, with a deliberate frame-synchronous exception when the user toggles a or expands a reply composer, so the code below moves in the same frame.

The work builds on an April 2026 post from the main github.com files-changed team, who reported that unified-view diff lines previously rendered as roughly eight React components and ten DOM elements each, and cut both roughly in half.

GitHub's own stacked pull requests went into public preview on 30 July 2026 as an explicit answer to AI-generated monsters, and a DEV Community piece cited Microsoft research finding review quality degrades sharply once a pull request exceeds roughly 200 lines, a rounding error against the Copilot app's million-line test case.

Third-party tools have filled the gap from the review side. Graphite, Pullfrog and CodeRabbit each take different runs at agent-era review, with Codegen CEO Jay Hack arguing that the winners in this upcoming era will be the teams that redesign their workflows around the fact that review, not code, is now the bottleneck.

Industry observers note that the team also describes the measurement loop built around the rebuild. The surface carries permanent structured probes for its own invariants, which run as CI budgets against a synthetic huge-pull-request fixture, and an autopilot drives the real desktop app through a scripted flow, cold and warm, so an agent can read the on-disk log and spot regressions without anyone at the keyboard. Gimeno's closing line is addressed to anyone who reviews code for a living: open the worst pull request you have got.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog.

Scale also said it spent the year before the launch working inside hospitals, including a U.S. health system it described as top-ranked but did not name, on work aimed at helping clinicians identify safety events sooner. The five applications form the first part of a broader portfolio, with additional applications and agents planned for the months after launch.

Industry observers note that the Scheduling Intelligence Agent is designed to triage referrals by clinical urgency and match visits to slots based on room and equipment requirements and physician preferences. It can rearrange existing schedules for urgent patients and coordinate visits across specialties. The Order Guidance Agent reviews patient history, flags missing tests, and recommends laboratory work, imaging, and prescriptions with cited evidence for clinician review.

For information-heavy work, the Medical Record Review & Summarization Agent assembles a patient history from scattered records and links each extracted finding to its source for checking. The Safety & Incident Investigation Agent prioritizes safety events and searches for recurring patterns, so teams can investigate higher-risk incidents first instead of processing reports only in arrival order. The Clinical Documentation & Quality Review Agent drafts reports for clinician review and sign-off, checks documentation against hospital guidelines, and requires auditors to confirm each finding.

The announcement connects the portfolio to three Scale Labs healthcare benchmarks. CliniCARE-Bench uses real, de-identified longitudinal electronic health records, with 25 clinician-validated scenarios instantiated across 750 cases spanning 14 specialties and ten reasoning skills. It separates cases lacking data from those that remain medically ambiguous, logs retrieval and citations, and scores evidence grounding, policy grounding, process adherence, and calibrated abstention, meaning appropriate deferral when a record cannot support a definitive answer.

Scale Labs reports that the 16 agentic systems it tested achieved raw accuracy of 65.3% to 76.1%, but defect-free accuracy fell by 4.8 to 14.8 percentage points when prohibited reasoning shortcuts were penalized. Every system under-abstained, committing to definitive answers more often than deferring on cases the record could not settle. Those are benchmark findings for the tested systems, not reported validation results for the five hospital applications.

Sources indicate that two related benchmarks extend that approach. PSEBench contains 5,074 patient-safety triage cases built around Minnesota’s 29 Reportable Adverse Health Events, including complete, missing-information, and uncertain variants, and was used to evaluate 15 language models. DistressBench contains 718 clinician-authored conversations across 23 suicide and self-harm subcategories. Scale Labs reports that in 35.3% of conversations where a model fully recognized a crisis, it still did not direct the user toward human help.

In a recent development, scale claims this research underpins custom evaluations built around each health system’s workflows while also providing a common way to compare models. That emphasis on ambiguity and process connects with the review controls described for order guidance, record checking, report sign-off, and audit findings.

A 2025 JAMA Network Open study cited by Scale examined 263 ambulatory clinicians across six U.S. health systems using the same Abridge ambient AI scribe for 30 days; it did not evaluate Scale’s products. In its adjusted analysis, estimated burnout prevalence decreased from 51.9% to 38.8%. Participants also reported improvements in note-related cognitive load, after-hours documentation, and focused attention on patients.

The results support the administrative-burden rationale for AI documentation tools, but they concern outpatient use of a different product rather than the fresh hospital-operations portfolio. The researchers listed vital qualifications: participation was voluntary, surveys were not anonymous, outcomes were self-reported, and there was no control group to account for temporal trends. Those constraints limit what the 30-day before-and-after results establish, particularly as Scale extends the administrative-burden argument from outpatient documentation to scheduling, orders, and safety triage.

Sources indicate that for health systems, the launch’s central question is whether evaluations built around their own workflows can verify evidence retrieval, policy compliance, and appropriate deferral alongside answer accuracy. Scale’s benchmarks show how correct answers can conceal flawed processes; the new applications’ source links, cited recommendations, clinician sign-off, and auditor confirmation are the mechanisms intended to expose those problems to human review.

The partnership packages functions that organizations would otherwise have to assemble themselves: inference serving, vector databases, access control, accelerator management and observability. In a recent development, from a self-service portal, customers can deploy open-source large language models, retrieval-augmented generation pipelines and agents. Average system power use is 8–10 kW, with a 12 kW maximum that can be configured up to 14.5 kW.

For expansion, the system offers up to 56 800-GbE QSFP-DD ports for cluster scale-out. Customers can run one server or build a supercluster in their own data center, while Tenstorrent’s listed configurations extend to 36 or more Galaxy systems for large-scale language-model inference and private AI infrastructure.

Sources indicate that standalone Galaxy Blackhole hardware has a $160,000 list price, while a four-system Blackhole supercluster starts at $640,000. The published prices establish the hardware entry cost for the two deployment patterns.

Sources indicate that tenstorrent claims its full software stack, from compiler to kernel, is open source. Owners can compile and run supported models or tune kernels directly, providing a customization path beneath ConfidentialMind’s deployment and management software.

Sources indicate that confidentialMind brings existing European deployments at the University of Helsinki, LUT University, Centria University of Applied Sciences and Elastx. I started by making a single eight-ounce cup of coffee. I pulled out the platform and set my mug upon it. I measured out the amount of coffee suggested in the user guide into the plastic reusable filter. I selected the 'bold' setting and started the brew. In just about three minutes, I had a hot cup of delicious coffee in my hand.

Recent findings suggest that the night before I wanted a pot of coffee, I set up the Auto-On function and measured out the appropriate amount of coffee for a half carafe. The Keep Warm function turns on automatically when you're using the carafe; the is no heater in the smaller mug platform. Sources indicate that I brewed a single espresso with ease. I chose the smaller filter basket and inserted it into the portafilter. The user guide recommends running a warm-up cycle with just water so I did that first. Then I used the included measuring scoop and put the grounds into the filter basket. The other end of the measuring scoop is a tamper, so I used that to tamp down my grounds. Brewing time was less than a minute. The espresso was very strong and had a generous crema.

I made an espresso as directed. As the user guide suggested, I started with 3.5 ounces of milk in a container that can hold a lot more than that. I used a full-fat oat milk. I set the steam wand to the Cappuccino setting and started frothing. It frothed up to about 12 ounces, so it more than tripled in volume. The froth had big bubbles which were quite sturdy and held up well to stirring. This was quite tasty.

A latte is similar to a cappuccino, only instead of added steamed milk plus lots of froth, you just add steamed milk. At least, that's a latte according to the user guide. Of course you can adjust the recipes as you like. Again, I made an espresso and poured 3.5 ounces of oat milk into a measuring cup. This time, I set the steam wand on the Latte setting. The milk did more than double in volume due to the steam, but there was almost no foam. I poured what I wanted into the espresso and it was delicious.

Sources indicate that in general coffee terms, a cold brew is brewed in the refrigerator for eight or more hours for a strong but smooth brew. Technically, a coffee machine can't make cold brew like that, but it does have a Cold Brew setting so I tested that out. I set up the coffee using a paper filter as recommended in the user guide. Brewing was slow, it took about 12 minutes to brew eight ounces of lukewarm coffee. This wasn't my favorite setting to be honest. Once I added ice, the coffee went pretty weak.

According to recent reports, this special setting brews a small amount of coffee very strongly, intended to be brewed over ice. I measured the recommended amount of coffee into the reusable coffee filter. I put a container half-filled with ice on the coffee platform, as the user guide suggested. I used the eight-ounce Over Ice setting and it took only three minutes to brew. This is a quarter of the time it took to brew the same size serving of cold brew. I preferred this method for making iced coffee, it tasted better to my palette. The coffee strength held up better to the ice using this setting.

The frother whisk is different from the steam wand. It foams but doesn't add any steam to your milk. It also doesn't change the temperature. So, it's perfect if you want cold foam for your favorite iced coffee beverage. It can also make hot foam, you just have to heat your milk before using this. I decided to make an iced coffee with cold foam using some of the iced coffee I had made previously. I put a few ounces of oat milk into a small glass jar and frothed it. It quickly tripled or quadrupled in volume, though for some reason it wasn't as airy-looking as my steamed foam was. I poured what I wanted into my mug. The foam held up well to stirring.

It's certainly not cheap, but it might be cheaper than buying a separate espresso machine, coffee machine, and milk frother.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Nov 16, 2026 2 min read.
  • It has been revealed that AWS has released AWS Emulator, a local program that serves an HTTPS endpoint for the public APIs of more than 200 AWS services.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News AWS Open-Sources Emulator for Local Testing of 200+ Services by Coding Agents.

Nov 16, 2026 2 min read.

It has been revealed that AWS has released AWS Emulator, a local program that serves an HTTPS endpoint for the public APIs of more than 200 AWS services. AWS Emulator lets developers and coding agents create resources, hit the same errors AWS would return, and iterate without provisioning cloud resources or incurring service charges for the operations it emulates.

Industry observers note that teams point the AWS CLI or an AWS SDK at it with environment variables such as AWS_ENDPOINT_URL, leaving application code unchanged. On Linux it installs as an RPM or Debian package for x86_64 or aarch64; on macOS and Windows, AWS documents a short Dockerfile and does not publish a prebuilt image. Rust tests can use an embedded mode that runs the emulator inside the test process and wires its HTTP client into the AWS SDK for Rust. An aws-emulator skill can start the emulator for coding agents and check a project against published fidelity tests. Written in Rust, it is generated from more than 400 Smithy API models AWS publishes for the SDKs, according to Swaminathan Sivasubramanian.

AWS indicates agents wrote and tested the code. Matthew Goldberg, a senior principal engineer at AWS, describes three teams: one writes fidelity tests from the public API models and verifies them against real AWS, one replays those tests and files challenges, and one implements each fix. Every change must pass a merge gate that checks compilation, coding standards, security, and fidelity regressions. The work runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Instances, AWS CodePipeline, and AWS CodeCommit.

In a recent development, how closely the emulator matches AWS varies by service. AWS publishes versioned fidelity tests and per-service scores with each release; a test passes only when every call matches AWS, including status codes, side effects, and exact errors. Unimplemented operations return HTTP 501 with the error code NotImplemented. AWS notes fidelity is closest on control-plane APIs, while data-plane behavior and support for CloudFormation, Terraform, and the AWS CDK vary by service. Documented limits include no evaluation of IAM or resource-based policies, so it must not be used to test security; a single shared account and Region per process; in-memory state that disappears when the process stops; and no testing for long-running use or load. The evaluation suite includes tests the emulator does not yet pass.

Developers already have several local AWS stand-ins, including LocalStack, Floci, and moto. AWS Emulator is generated from AWS's own API models, ships official fidelity scores, and is dedicated to the public domain, but it is not a drop-in replacement for every workflow those tools cover, especially permission testing and infrastructure-as-code pipelines.

According to recent reports, AWS just released a free local emulator of its APIs, made for coding agents and written entirely by agents. I counted its published fidelity tests: S3, DynamoDB and SQS pass about 2 in 3. CloudFormation passes under 1 in 5.

Yurii Serhiichuk compared it with existing emulators and published a container image and GitHub Action to cover a packaging gap:.

AWS shipped AWS Emulator today - think LocalStack/Floci but native. Rust, built by agents (so hopefully it gets updated pretty fast). No public docker image though, and no GitHub action. So I filled that part.

Sources indicate that AWS Emulator is generally available at no additional service fee. Source is on GitHub under the CC0 1.0 Universal public domain dedication, except third-party code in the vendor/ directory, which is under the Apache License 2.0. Setup details are in the user guide, and fidelity scores ship with each release.

Developer creates a 100% valid ZIP file that doubles as a BIOS-bootable operating system

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that hacking stories these days mostly involve someone using an army of AI agents to find vulnerabilities in networks and software that were carefully hidden in plain sight.
  • You can unpack the ZIP file just like any other, boot it using Linux's GRUB, QEMU, or any other Multiboot-compatible loader (even if imaged to different media), or alternatively, perform the finest party trick: image-write it to a floppy and boot from it directly from BIOS on any compatible PC, without modification.
  • Much like me, that sequence of words may be triggering a head-tilt reminiscent of a confused puppy, so we'll explain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that hacking stories these days mostly involve someone using an army of AI agents to find vulnerabilities in networks and software that were carefully hidden in plain sight. Today, for a change, we have a story about hacking in its original meaning — twisting computing artifacts into purposes not in their design spec. David Oberhollenzer, aka Goliath, a greybeard in spirit if not in shade, crafted a 100% valid ZIP file that's simultaneously an archive, BIOS-bootable, and a Multiboot-compatible OS image.

You can unpack the ZIP file just like any other, boot it using Linux's GRUB, QEMU, or any other Multiboot-compatible loader (even if imaged to different media), or alternatively, perform the finest party trick: image-write it to a floppy and boot from it directly from BIOS on any compatible PC, without modification.

Much like me, that sequence of words may be triggering a head-tilt reminiscent of a confused puppy, so we'll explain. The first thing you need to know is that unlike most file types, the metadata (in this case, file directory) of a ZIP is actually at the end of the archive. Up to that point, the data is comprised of every compressed file in sequence.

According to recent reports, the file packs all have a predictable structure: "PK" followed by bytes 03 04, metadata (including name), some extra/comment fields, and then the file's contents. Notably, any file can be stored uncompressed, and Goliath made use of that for the very first file, called ZIPHEAD.COM — remember, this is the start of the ZIP archive.

According to recent reports, goliath noted that it was "easy" to make the ZIP file a valid Multiboot system image. A valid image only needs to contain bytes 0x1BADB002 in the first 8 KiB, followed by some flags and a checksum. It was trivial to place that datum in ZIPHEAD's data, along with the location of where the bootloader lies.

Sources indicate that grub or QEMU don't care about anything else in the image, as once they have the initialization information, from that point it's the bootloader's problem. The actual bootloader, predictably, is in ZIPHEAD's uncompressed data, and the image will happily boot directly, or, say, from a floppy.

Making the same exact archive bootable via a standard PC BIOS took a little more work and some clever shenanigans. Making a disk bootable is simple enough: the BIOS reads the first exact 512 bytes of the disk's contents, and if they end with bytes 0x55AA, then it's bootable, and the BIOS starts executing whatever code is the first byte.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Placing 0x55AA precisely at position 510 of the ZIP, already in ZIPHEAD's contents, is once again simple, and won't corrupt the Multiboot image, as if you'll recall, the Multiboot spec is flexible with data locations. But you may wonder: once the BIOS runs code in sequence starting from the ZIP's first byte, then ZIPHEAD's header ("PK" + 0x0304, plus all metadata) surely is garbage for practical purposes, and not proper code? Well, yes, but actually no.

Sources indicate that the first four bytes represent CPU instructions that don't write anything to memory, so they're harmless, other than a push-to-stack. The next few belong to ZIPHEAD's metadata, and Goliath massaged those values to represent instructions that would either be innocuous or perform operations he could use, namely using the modification time bytes as instructions to jump further down the data.

Sounds simple, but the actual process of choosing bytes that represent (1) non-crashy CPU instructions, (2) useful code for setting up the boot process, and (3) still represent a valid file header in a ZIP archive is far trickier than the above. The update changes the starting point for a query: instead of relying on details typed into a blank AI prompt, the tool begins with information from the patient’s chart and produces responses containing both chart data and citations.

Industry observers note that elsevier’s patient-context documentation describes five connected steps: start with the patient, bring together relevant record context, connect that context with clinical evidence, deliver cited insights in supported EHR workflows, and support the clinician’s decision. In supported implementations, usable context can include notes, imaging, procedures, laboratory results, medications, orders, allergies, vital signs, and inpatient and outpatient records.

The system is designed to operate across EHR environments rather than being tied to a single provider. The patient-context capability is presently available only in the United States.

In a recent development, traceability runs in both directions. Each patient-context statement can be traced to relevant chart data, while the clinical response links to its supporting source. Clinicians can therefore inspect which record details informed an answer and review the evidence behind it, while the final assessment and plan remain with the clinician.

The announcement follows Elsevier’s acquisition of Wellsheet in June 2026. Wellsheet specializes in aggregating and synthesizing EHR data to surface relevant clinical intelligence at the point of care.

In a recent development, san Juan Regional Medical Center in New Mexico is using the new patient-context functionality. Elsevier describes it as a rural center serving communities with limited access to healthcare, with smaller clinical and quality teams than large academic systems, in a state where nearly 40% of residents rely on Medicaid.

Elsevier indicates user data is encrypted in transit and at rest, support access is limited to authorized personnel under pseudonymization, cloud providers and third-party AI partners receive no access for training purposes, and the product is built to be HIPAA-compliant where country regulators recognize such compliance.

It has been revealed that the revision makes two kinds of verification part of the same clinical interaction: checking the patient facts used by the system and checking the publications behind its response. For resource-constrained providers such as San Juan Regional, the practical question is whether that connected, cited workflow can make a broad evidence base easier to use within existing staffing and EHR constraints.

#532. Microsoft 365 outage led to chlorine gas poisoning of 15 people in Germany

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (800 w)

Microsoft 365 outage led to chlorine gas poisoning of 15 people in Germany

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (800 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Techradar

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you were affected by last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage, chances are you had trouble accessing your email.
  • In a recent development, according to a news report from German outlet WDR (via Notebookcheck), 15 guests at a hotel for the Phantasialand theme park were injured when the park’s swimming pool received excessive levels of chlorine.
  • According to a Facebook post made by the fire department that responded to the incident, 40 first responders were dispatched and 15 guests were triaged after the chlorine gas leak.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you were affected by last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage, chances are you had trouble accessing your email. You probably didn’t expect to be poisoned as a result, yet that’s exactly what happened to over a dozen unfortunate hotel guests in Germany — but Microsoft has reported that the blackout wasn’t caused by a cyberattack.

In a recent development, according to a news report from German outlet WDR (via Notebookcheck), 15 guests at a hotel for the Phantasialand theme park were injured when the park’s swimming pool received excessive levels of chlorine. This was caused by a malfunction in the chlorine monitoring system, but because alerts are sent to park staff over email — and because those email systems were down due to the Microsoft 365 outage — no one knew about the problem until guests started getting sick.

According to a Facebook post made by the fire department that responded to the incident, 40 first responders were dispatched and 15 guests were triaged after the chlorine gas leak. WDR reported that the affected people suffered from respiratory irritation, with four needing to be taken to hospital.

The episode illustrates the serious — and often unexpected — consequences that can arise when something as central to a business’s operations as an email system goes down. When it’s responsible for vital safety procedures, the results can be potentially life-threatening.

Since the outage, Microsoft has mentioned that full service has been resumed. It has since published a post-incident report, which is available in the Microsoft 365 Admin Center portal. The full write up has also been relayed on Reddit.

In the report, Microsoft revealed that the outage was caused by three principal factors: a “latent defect” from July that overwhelmed Windows servers; a Microsoft Teams failure that increased the load on a system shared with Microsoft Exchange; and the fact that 14% of server capacity for the networking system was out of service at the time.

According to recent reports, taken individually, these factors were not enough to cause the global failure. But when the increased load and the lower server capacity combined, they triggered the latent defect. Server requests then piled up until the servers stopped responding — which happened to occur during the peak traffic window for the United States.

It has been revealed that as a mitigation effort, traffic was automatically redirected towards healthy endpoints. However, this process made those endpoints more likely to themselves encounter the latent defect. “This caused a cascading failure from server to server as the same amount of load was spread across fewer servers,” Microsoft wrote. At its worst point, the outage had caused 80% of available servers to become unresponsive.

Due to a separate glitch, Microsoft’s bulwarks against such a cascading failure did not function properly. Recovery took longer than expected because restored servers were immediately overwhelmed by pent up traffic, making them fail once again. And because the latent defect dated back to July, simply rolling back to a recent version was not enough.

To fix the outage once and for all, Microsoft had to return its code path to that of a previously good state, then take servers offline in batches, roll out the patch across its infrastructure, then restart its systems. Eventually, service was restored.

The post-incident report is a sobering reminder of what can happen when several seemingly independent concerns can converge all at once, and of the consequences that are possible when that happens on such a large scale. And as the chlorine incident in Germany demonstrates, these failures often go beyond mere technical disruption and touch on people’s health and wellbeing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, doom now runs on a USB flash drive’s built-in LCD and is played by copying files to and from it, as hardware hacker Aaron Christophel demonstrated in a teardown video. The marking on the drive’s display chip had been removed, but an open debug port let him extract its firmware, which enabled identification. He was then able to use AI to reverse-engineer the hardware and get the game running on the drive’s screen.

The off-the-shelf drive, the MOVESPEED MSSU10, has USB-A on one end and USB-C on the other, and the 128GB model, the smallest capacity in the range, cost him about 50 euros. Its screen normally indicates status data such as transfer speed, how full the drive is, and its temperature.

Sources indicate that the main flash controller is the Silicon Motion SM2320G, one we have reviewed in portable SSDs like the Kingston XS2000 and Lexar SL660 Blaze, with a separate C*Core CCM4101 microcontroller — which has 2MB of flash and a small amount of RAM to itself — for the 428 x 142 color LCD. The NAND carries SanDisk markings. All of this is fairly standard portable SSD hardware, aside from the display.

In a recent development, the drive’s metal body uses heavily glued plastic end pieces but, past that, the display lifts off first and unplugs. The board slides out after the USB-C end cap is removed, in this case with minor cosmetic damage inflicted. The display chip’s marking is scrubbed, most likely with a laser, by the hacker’s reckoning, which can hinder identification and tinkering. Luckily, a probe on the debug pads, ground, and a 3.3V pin connected on the first try, and memory was immediately readable.

The bootloader returned a version string dated 2023, followed by the full firmware, which helped greatly with identification. He claims the chip is marketed as one for security — for fingerprint readers and access control, for example — but no related features were found to be enabled for this drive. He also discovered that, although the data sheet and stock firmware declare a 200 MHz operating clock frequency, it measured 40.2 MHz. This is unexplained.

According to recent reports, one critical concern is immediately apparent: how do you play on a drive with no buttons? The display chip has no USB connection of its own and, from the connected PC or host, it only sees the storage controller’s activity, which it uses to gauge transfer speed. The primary storage controller has read and write counters, and the chip pulls these every 50 ms over I2C. Christophel indicates this is far easier than relying on a single physical button, as he did on a previous power bank mod.

Sources indicate that the solution, then, is a PC script, doomctl.py, which turns key presses into small, timed transfers in each direction. The commands are simply encoded as transfer rates, at five levels per direction, and each read/write pair can map to a certain button combination. Arrow keys are for movement and turning, Space or Ctrl for firing and opening doors, and M for the menu, keeping it simple. Ordinary copying, without the script, can still steer, but the control scheme is much nicer.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Performance is…well, not really playable at about 13 frames per second, although the game logic runs at Doom’s normal 35 ticks per second. This is why he names the chip’s clock as the biggest potential performance gain. The game itself is built on DMC100-DOOM, Artur Bieniek’s port for very small microcontrollers. Only the first map, E1M1, fits in the chip’s flash, and no sound is produced as the drive lacks a buzzer. Christophel did play the level end to end, noting the low resolution.

AI did the heavy lifting: the reverse engineering as well as the port, and Christophel noted, “I would not be able to do such a thing in a few hours.”.

According to recent reports, the open-source project, with its code and prebuilt firmware published, is likely to draw attention and may spawn similar hacks. The tools required are relatively minimal, mainly a debug probe, and he does suggest backing up the stock firmware before trying. For his own unit, he put it back together to use as a normal drive, but one that can still play Doom, if so desired.

Security researchers at Zimperium have discovered that ArcticRAT, an Android remote access trojan, now uses AI-powered analysis of stolen SMS messages and app data to identify victims’ financial status, detect banking activity, and find one-time passcodes. The malware can take near-total control of infected phones, including accessing banking apps, monitoring screens, recording keystrokes, activating microphones, stealing lock-screen credentials, and abusing Android Debug Bridge to lock owners out, making it a particularly dangerous tool for financial theft.

In a recent development, zimperium’s zLabs team has published upcoming research on ArcticRAT. For those of you who are not familiar, ArcticRAT is an Android remote access trojan that has evolved into an AI-powered, full device-takeover tool.

In a recent development, the malware is now capable of sending stolen SMS messages and app data to a commercial large language model (LLM) to determine target victims’ financial standing. Needless to say, this makes it a lot more dangerous.

Recent findings suggest that AI has essentially been added to the attack chain, unfortunately. Prompts that are sent to an LLM API actually filter stolen SMS messages for one-time passcodes, balance changes, and transfer notices.

Industry observers note that on top of that, they estimate each victim’s financial standing. Based on that, targets are being identified. Zimperium notes that this was first seen in samples from mid-July this year.

According to recent reports, arcticRAT can take full control of your phone. The device can look switched off to its owner, but the attacker is essentially using it. The attacker can move through the victim’s banking apps, watch the screen, listen in through the microphone, and log every keystroke.

There’s also the fake lock screen that steals PINs, patterns, and passwords, plus Wireless Debugging (ADB) abuse that can strip the lock screen or lock the owner out of the phone.

Needless to say, Zimperium went into a lot more technical details in the full report, but this is the gist of it. ArcticRAT is now far more capable than it was before, and thanks to the AI element, it’s also a lot more dangerous at the same time.

Its main goal is monetary gain, as is the case for the vast majority of trojans on the market. Some of them are becoming very sophisticated, as more and more AI is being pumped into them.

However, even Nvidia's former chief executive Jensen Huang had apparently begun to question the sustainability of this strategy before his departure, based on reports from The Wall Street Journal and SemiAnalysis.

Recent findings suggest that over the past several years, Nvidia has not only captured the vast majority of the AI accelerator market, but has also secured a substantial proportion of the world's production capacity for advanced logic, high-bandwidth memory (HBM), and various other components required to build AI accelerators and systems, which has limited the ability of its competitors to ramp up shipments of their processors. To support the deals, Jensen Huang personally negotiated agreements with major suppliers in Taiwan and South Korea.

It has been revealed that the massive scale of Nvidia's procurement commitments also enabled the organization to secure more favorable quotes than its rivals. SemiAnalysis estimates that SK hynix could charge Nvidia between $3.00 and $3.30 per gigabit of HBM4 memory in 2027, whereas other first-tier customers, such as AMD, Amazon, Broadcom, and Google, would pay between $3.70 and $4.10 per gigabit. The analysts believe that as part of an informal arrangement between the two companies, Nvidia gives SK Group preferential access to its AI GPUs.

While Nvidia's ability to secure vast production capacities has been instrumental in its success, such commitments also carry considerable risks. At a meeting with senior executives in August, Huang reportedly expressed concerns about the massive volumes of wafers and memory that Nvidia had committed to purchase as major cloud service providers sought to reduce their reliance on the company's hardware in favor of alternative AI accelerator platforms, according to The Wall Street Journal.

In a recent development, in a bid to diversify its customer base and create additional demand for its products, Nvidia offered financial guarantees to emerging cloud service providers and data center developers that otherwise could not afford to procure its hardware at scale. As of the end of its fiscal second quarter, Nvidia had $530 billion in gross off-balance-sheet guarantees, up from $184 billion a quarter earlier, as well as $99 billion worth of equity investments, according to SemiAnalysis. As half a trillion dollars seems gargantuan, here is a breakdown based on a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission:.

Sources indicate that the scale of such commitments raised concerns even within Nvidia. Then-CFO Colette Kress questioned the criteria used to select recipients of financial support and the potential returns on such arrangements. She also reportedly reduced Nvidia's initial financial commitment to OpenAI's massive data center project in Ohio by half before the two companies signed an agreement on August 17. The facility is expected to house some $300 billion worth of Nvidia processors.

According to recent reports, at some point, Huang himself began to question the merits of Nvidia's aggressive financing strategy in the event of his departure, essentially calling the current interim CEO, Colette Kress, a mere 'reporting CFO' rather than an executive capable of making strategic decisions. He also expressed concerns about massive wafer and memory procurement commitments as major cloud service providers sought to reduce their reliance on Nvidia’s GPUs.

It has been revealed that despite questionable commitments, without Huang and his personal relationships with executives at major semiconductor companies, Nvidia may find it harder to secure preferential treatment from its suppliers. SemiAnalysis believes that customers other than Nvidia could account for over 70% of TSMC production capacity in 2028. While this could enable Nvidia’s competitors to significantly increase shipments of their AI processors, it could also affect the willingness of Taiwanese and South Korean suppliers to invest aggressively in additional production capacity without the kind of assurances that Huang used to provide.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New research has warned companies looking to replace human workers with AI could face major reputational consequences later on down the line if their AI strategies fall apart.

Companies that are forced to re-hire human workers after laying them off could ultimately find themselves having to pay higher salaries, offer better contractual terms and include stronger employment protections, the report from JobAssist warns.

But even after offering workers better terms overall, they could have already made reputational and loyalty damages – nearly one-third (29%) of workers say they'd return to their old job, but would immediately start looking for another.

While a relatively low but not insignificant number of workers would likely continue to look for other opportunities, the number of workers looking for a higher salary (71%) is much higher. Nearly two in three (64%) also stated they'd negotiate more aggressively in general when returning to an old job.

It has been revealed that however, workers are still very clearly worried about AI's impacts on their roles, because half (54%) would now prioritize job security over titles and perks, implying they're concerned about experiencing yet another redundancy. Nearly half (44%) also said they'd trust their employer less after AI replaced human workers.

All in all, the study is proof that employer reputation could suffer beyond the original workforce reduction, with laid off workers and re-hires less likely to trust the tech giant.

And even after all the costs associated with laying off workers in the first place, and investing so heavily in artificial intelligence, JobAssist warns that workers could end up demanding more money, benefits and security than they had done before.

"For businesses evaluating the financial benefits of replacing employees with AI, the survey highlights a risk that could emerge if an automation decision has to be reversed," the report summarized.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An early build of Samsung’s Expert RAW app for One UI 9.5 indicates a cleaner layout, custom shortcut buttons by the shutter, and RAW burst shooting. The virtual aperture now goes from f/1.4 to f/22, and hidden settings hint that video recording could come too. It should arrive with the Galaxy S27 early next year.

Samsung’s Expert RAW app is getting its biggest redesign yet, and it looks built around the Galaxy S27. SamMobile got its hands on an early build of the app for One UI 9.5, and it adds a cleaner layout, burst shooting, a wider virtual aperture range, and possibly video. That’s good news if you shoot on Samsung’s Android phones and want more control than the stock camera app gives you.

The leak comes from SamMobile, and Android Police broke down the details. Since it’s an early build, some of this could change before launch.

Industry observers note that the fresh design uses translucent panels and gives the manual controls clearer labels and bigger adjustment panels. The Quick Control menu now opens into a grid with options like the timer, aspect ratio, and resolution. Advanced tools like the virtual aperture, virtual reflector, ND filter, and astrophotography mode move into a new Expert button in the top left.

It has been revealed that the histogram gets more useful, too. Tap the small one to open a larger panel with separate white, red, green, and blue plots.

Two fresh buttons next to the shutter can each be set to one of nine options, including exposure lock, focus peaking, metering, and the timer. If you always reach for the same two settings, that should save a few taps.

Industry observers note that the virtual aperture now runs from f/1.4 to f/22. On the Galaxy S26 Ultra today, it tops out at f/16. Burst shooting is also coming, with up to 30 shots per burst saved as DNG files. The app warns that bursts will eat up storage, which makes sense, since RAW files are much bigger than regular photos.

The most interesting find is video. The leaked build has a Videos section in its settings with a stabilization toggle, and Ocean Mode offers resolution and frame rate options. Video recording doesn’t actually work in this build, though, so it’s not clear what Samsung aims to support.

Expert RAW has always been aimed at people who want to edit their photos later, and RAW video would push it even further in that direction. It’s also a feature Apple already offers with ProRes on the iPhone Pro models.

Sources indicate that the redesign is expected to arrive with One UI 9.5 and the Galaxy S27 series early next year. Samsung is redesigning a lot of its apps for One UI 9.5, including Samsung Notes, so Expert RAW getting a refresh fits the pattern. It’s not clear yet which older Galaxy phones will get the new version.
