#523. Latest Update: AI-Driven Scientific Progress Threatened by a Strange Obsession

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2303 w)
AI & Tech ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Unite

Latest Update: AI-Driven Scientific Progress Threatened by a Strange Obsession

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2303 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new US study suggests that AI models reviewing scientific papers are developing a strange obsession with the papers’ appendices rather than the main body of text, often paying more attention to minor supporting details than to the main findings.
  • From the upcoming paper, the rise in appendix-related criticism in human scientific peer reviews.
  • In a test of 2000 science papers drawn from four popular conferences, the researchers of the fresh work found that newer models draw around 50-70% of their criticisms from appendices, compared with less than 30% for the older GPT-5.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new US study suggests that AI models reviewing scientific papers are developing a strange obsession with the papers’ appendices rather than the main body of text, often paying more attention to minor supporting details than to the main findings. With language models increasingly being used to assist or even replace human reviewers, the newly-identified tendency appears to be spreading into human peer review, potentially hindering progress in AI research:.

From the upcoming paper, the rise in appendix-related criticism in human scientific peer reviews. After remaining below 11% for years, the proportion reached 27.6% in the latest reviews, following the release of AI models found to draw more than half their criticisms from appendices. The dashed lines mark major model releases. Source.

In a test of 2000 science papers drawn from four popular conferences, the researchers of the fresh work found that newer models draw around 50-70% of their criticisms from appendices, compared with less than 30% for the older GPT-5.

Two of the most prominent newer AI models that are apparently driving even human reviewers towards the appendices and away from the more important main results are OpenAI’s GPT-6.1-Sol, and GPT-6-Astra, both released in 2026.

‘The difference between the generations is large. For GPT-5, only a small share of weaknesses relate to the appendix. Both newer models, GPT-6.1-Sol and GPT-6-Astra, rely on it much more heavily, and this holds for every conference.

‘This suggests that the bias towards the appendix is mainly a property of newer models. Even though the upcoming models are an improvement, their bias toward the appendix has grown. Being able to read a paper in detail has not taught them which parts matter most.’.

The study also found that this fixation on the appendix differs across the methods by which the AI receives the paper, since API, codex and web interfaces do not assess PDFs the same way – and Codex does not read the middle of the average-length PDF at all, sampling it later only in ‘bites’, if necessary. However, all methods were found to favor the appendix material.

Until recently, human and AI reviews did not share this obsession:.

According to recent reports, ‘[Human] reviewers treat the main body and the supplementary material very differently from LLMs. LLMs attribute more than 50% of their weaknesses to appendix-related material, while humans attribute less than 10%.

‘The difference also shows at the individual-review level. Of the 200 papers sampled each year from 2021 to 2024, only 159 in total received a human review with any appendix-related weakness. In contrast, all 200 LLM-generated reviews for ICLR 2027 included at least one appendix criticism.’.

It has been revealed that comparison of appendix-related criticism in human and AI-generated peer reviews. Human reviewers attributed just 8.4% of identified weaknesses to appendix material, compared with 62% for AI models. The second column highlights criticisms concerning the appendix alone, with no corresponding concern in the main paper.

As shown in the test table above, AI reviewers were more than seven times as likely as humans to identify weaknesses in the appendices, and more than three times as likely to raise criticisms concerning only the supplementary material – an indication that some of the latest frontier AI models are now prioritizing details that human reviewers would traditionally regard as secondary to a paper’s main scientific contribution.

As far as can be discerned (this is the first study to have identified the syndrome), part of the problem is that the AIs do not recognize, or have not gleaned from their copious training material, that the appendix of a paper is not where the payload is normally placed; their general tendency to treat all text as equally vital omits the context for appendix material, which is often uncurated and much more roughly-presented than the main body:.

In a recent development, ‘LLMs almost never criticize the opening pages, where a paper frames its problem and argues why it matters. Humans often push back on exactly this framing, while LLMs seem to accept it and move on to the numbers.

‘[Humans and LLMs] read the appendix very differently. Human criticisms fade promptly as the appendix goes on, and almost disappear in its last pages. LLM weaknesses do not fade at all. In fact, LLM weaknesses peak well into the appendix rather than at its start, and they continue even beyond page 30, where human reviewers raise almost no concerns.

‘For an LLM, a detail on page 25 is as fair a target as the main results table.’.

The authors note that LLMs’ egalitarian approach to text may naturally have led them to concentrate more on appendix material, because, as stated above, that material tends to have more errors.

Therefore the high-level view that I take from this new study is that LLMs have honed in over time on a section of new science papers where a large degree of error or conflation tends to occur, simply because that area is treated so often by human authors as an untidy dumping ground of secondary proof and evidence.

For this reason, AI increasingly finds the appendices more interesting than the highly-curated main body, because there is more for it to analyze and correct there; consequently, the paper notes, LLMs tend to treat the front section of the paper as factual reporting, taking it at face value:.

According to recent reports, ‘Humans expect the main body to stand on its own, so they object when essential sections are pushed into the appendix. LLMs almost never raise this concern.

Sources indicate that ‘This highlights a key difference: humans recognize that the main body carries more weight than the appendix, while LLMs do not. ‘.

This unexpected focus on minor details could have serious implications for AI-assisted scientific research, particularly if the importance of a paper’s main findings is overlooked. Since the tendency appears to have emerged only with the latest models, its longer-term effects are not yet known.

Recent findings suggest that the paper acknowledges that valuable errors can be caught by AI reviewers, even when those errors are buried deep in an appendix. However, it warns that too much attention can be paid to minor details at the expense of a paper’s main findings, leaving to lengthy reviews of little practical value:.

‘LLM reviewers raise the standard, since they leave no part of the paper unexamined. However, effective reviewing also requires judgment about what matters most. When most of a review’s weaknesses come from appendix content unrelated to the main contribution, the feedback stays on the surface. It does not engage with the core of the paper and does little to help authors improve it. ‘.

According to recent reports, the authors of the latest work, titled AI Reviews Are Biased Towards the Appendix, were inspired to pursue the thread because they noticed certain odd patterns in the way that LLM-assisted/generated reviews would evaluate their own submissions. The study’s code is available at GitHub.

For the tests, four leading AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic were selected: GPT-6-Astra; GPT-6.1-Sol; Claude-Opus-5.5; and Claude-Sonnet-5.5, with the models accessed through Codex and Claude Code, and their reviewing behavior compared against API and web-interface access.

Research papers were collected from four major AI and natural language processing conferences: ACL 2026; EMNLP 2026; COLM 2026; and ICLR 2027 – all chosen because they share similar submission and review formats, with strict page limits on the main paper, but generally unrestricted appendices placed after the references.

A total of 2,000 papers were examined, comprising 1,200 from ICLR 2021–2026, and 800 from four recent conferences, (with 200 selected from each). The 800 recent papers all featured appendices of at least 15 pages. The ICLR 2027 submissions were already anonymous, while authors’ names, affiliations, email addresses, and identifying links were removed from the ACL, EMNLP, and COLM papers to prevent their authorship from being revealed to the AI reviewers.

Internet access was disabled for the models, ensuring that the reviews would be based entirely on the PDFs provided.

First, the AI was asked to produce a review in the style of the relevant conference, covering the paper’s strengths, weaknesses, and an overall score, with the instructions kept deliberately simple, to reflect how AI might be used by an actual reviewer. The paper and its completed review were then given back to the same AI model, which was asked to identify which section of the paper each criticism referred to. This was determined by examining the criticism alongside the original paper:.

It has been revealed that the three-stage review process used in the study. Papers with appendices of at least 15 pages were selected from four conferences and anonymized before being reviewed by AI models. Each review was then examined alongside the original paper, with individual criticisms assigned to the sections they concerned.

By separating these tasks, the parts of the papers that attracted criticism could be examined without the original reviews being influenced by additional instructions.

Among the results that we have not discussed so far is the authors’ test of where the weaknesses in LLM-generated reviews originate:.

According to recent reports, comparison of where AI-generated reviews identified weaknesses across four conferences. Green represents criticisms of the main paper, red represents appendix-related criticisms, and hatched areas indicate those concerning the appendix alone. More than half of the criticisms were attributed to appendix material in nearly every test, with the strongest bias recorded for GPT-6-Astra.

Sources indicate that as shown above, about half or more of the criticisms made by all four AI models were based on material in the appendices – a pattern found across all four conferences. Some criticisms were directed exclusively at the appendix, with no connection to the main paper, accounting for 17.33% of the weaknesses identified by GPT models, compared with 10.16% for Claude.

The results, the paper suggests, indicate that appendix material was being given disproportionate attention, with relatively minor details sometimes treated as grounds for criticism of the paper as a whole.

A comparison across methods was conducted to establish whether the appendix bias was affected by how the AI was accessed. Using GPT-6-Astra, one hundred ICLR 2027 submissions were reviewed via Codex; the ChatGPT web interface; and an API supplied with either the original PDF or its extracted text.

With Codex, text was extracted and examined through commands; through the API, either the complete PDF or its extracted text was supplied directly; while uploaded documents were processed through the web interface’s own (opaque) system:.

Recent findings suggest that comparison of appendix-related criticisms across AI models and access methods. On the left, GPT-5 was found to cite appendix material far less frequently than the newer GPT models across four conferences. On the right, the bias was found to persist across four ways of accessing GPT-6-Astra, with appendix-related criticisms accounting for 62.2% to 73.7% of the total. Hatched areas indicate criticisms directed exclusively at appendices.

Industry observers note that as shown above, appendix-related material was cited in 62.2% to 73.7% of criticisms across the four methods, with the highest proportion recorded when extracted text was supplied directly through the API. The bias was therefore found to persist regardless of how the model was accessed.

The bulk of the other tests were already reported earlier in the article, and we refer the reader to the source material for further information.

Much as the subject is personal to the authors of the newly introduced work, so it is to me, since I read scientific papers a lot, and have learned the hard way the hidden rules, and subversion of rules, that dictate the way papers are composed and presented.

AI is not broadly at fault for paying attention to the appendices, even if it is doing so for the wrong reasons, since authors often bury the paper’s ‘gotchas’ there – factors or results that may all but nullify, or else severely qualify the claims made in the main body of the paper.

Neither are authors necessarily at fault for shunting important material to the appendix, since the templates of popular outlets such as those featured as data sources in the newly introduced study prescribe maximum page or word-count limits on the main body of the paper.

When reporting complex study results, many authors clearly find this a severe restriction; in what I would consider ‘the worst cases’†, the main body of the paper simply becomes an index of material that has been shunted to the rear to avoid the guidelines (though the guidelines are catching up to and banning this ‘trick’).

The growing tension in this scenario is between the institutions’ need for authors to discipline and restrain their presentations – ever more crucial as the volume of submitted papers rises – and the evident frustration of researchers, who wish to present the hard-won fruits of their labor in as complete and comprehensive a context as they feel the effort deserves.

† Because, when triaging papers to cover, this deferral to appendices can be hard for even AI to identify; but it can trip the reviewer up considerably if they had allocated time for a ten-page assessment and now find they must consider 30 pages of material in the same allotment of time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Following the exit of Nvidia's CEO last week, a petition has been put together to campaign for the reinstatement of Jensen Huang.

VideoCardz noticed the 'Stand with Jensen' website which hosts a petition and open letter that has now been signed by some 175,000 people, some of whom are high-profile names in the tech industry.

That includes Elon Musk, Tim Sweeney (of Epic Games), Tobias Lutke (CEO of Shopify), Travis Kalanick (the former CEO of Uber), Steve Chen (the former CTO of YouTube) and Julien Chaumond (current CTO at Hugging Face). It's made clear that Huang himself doesn't endorse the letter.

The demands laid out by the letter to the Nvidia board are threefold, including firstly that Huang should be reinstated as CEO immediately – to stabilize the situation – but if the board believes "his continued absence is necessary" that they should provide an explanation of why.

The second demand is to "ensure an independent investigation and a fair hearing", and the third is to deliver a timely public explanation of what's happened and how the interests of Nvidia staff and shareholders were weighed up in this matter.

The petition states: "Thirty-three years of leadership do not place anyone above accountability. But accountability requires evidence, a fair hearing, and a reasoned decision. Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice.".

Meanwhile, given all this, a separate report from The Financial Times claims that Huang is mulling a comeback bid and the "possibility of returning" based on chatter from multiple sources. An ally of the ex-CEO remarked they were putting together a 'war room' of major tech executives to lobby for Huang's return (presumably including Musk and the other aforementioned names).

Industry observers note that some strong feelings have been aired, then, and based on the stats from the Stand with Jensen campaign, nearly 9,000 Nvidia staff (known as 'Nvidians') are signatories of the open letter – which is 20% of the employee base. Of those employees, 26 are Vice Presidents (or Senior VPs), which is a good chunk of the top leadership (maybe approaching half of them, although there are no precise numbers for VPs at Team Green).

Of course, none of this can be verified, and we have to take these numbers on trust.

Looking at Reddit, there's little sympathy for Huang, particularly among PC gamers (though his exit is arguably another distinctly negative development). Even on the subreddits relating to Nvidia stock, there's a mostly dim view of this petition (just over half of the signatories are declared as shareholders). However, it is notable that a fair few major names in tech have signed the letter – I still doubt that this will spark a turnaround in sentiment for the board, of course. These kind of campaigns aren't known for producing much in the way of concrete results, shall we say.

That remarked, given the 'war room' rumor from the FT, maybe the petition will give Huang a bit more impetus to launch the comeback bid that is supposedly being considered behind the scenes. If it's going to happen, it will obviously need to happen swiftly.

Meanwhile, the letter signatures are likely to exceed 200,000 today. In case you missed this last week (somehow), Colette Kress (who was CFO) is at the moment the interim CEO while Nvidia conducts a search for Huang's permanent replacement (who could come from inside or outside the company).

Fable 5.2 creates an underwater world in a browser in only 96 KB

  • Sources indicate that the demo's 3D space and textures are all procedurally generated, meaning they're the result of mathematical equations rather than prebuilt 3D meshes, and all calculated on load.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Claude Fable 5.2 was released recently to mostly rave reviews, with both consumers and analysis outlets ranking it nipping at the heels of the much pricier Opus 5.5. Perhaps as practical proof of that claim, front-end developer Maksymilian Dendura took inspiration from the demoscene and had Fable roll his own virtual underwater world, Abyssal Garden, in only 96 KB of Javascript/HTML — you can check it out here.

Sources indicate that the demo's 3D space and textures are all procedurally generated, meaning they're the result of mathematical equations rather than prebuilt 3D meshes, and all calculated on load. Using actual meshes and images for textures would otherwise take up a significant amount of space.

According to recent reports, building structures procedurally is difficult and has limitations, but it's exceedingly effective when used properly. Some games employ this technique for repeated elements like trees and grass.

Likewise, all the visual effects and even some texturing are done with shaders, which are small programs that change how a mesh or texture appears — for example, to make parts of an object shiny. Games use them extensively, as many players are aware, thanks to endless "loading shaders" screens or Unreal Engine's st-tu-tutering.

It has been revealed that the result is definitely impressive, especially but not only as it's purely browser-based, relying on WebGPU and WebGL. Both are rarely-mentioned technologies that have actually existed for a long while now. As their names imply, they let developers render 2D and 3D graphics in a manner similar to that of OpenGL, but in a browser, using JavaScript as the base language.

Sources indicate that the demo's most impressive fact is the simplicity of the prompt that got Fable 5.2 to build it. It's only about 40 lines long with word wrapping, and clearly illustrates the degree of autonomy that contemporary agentic AI has when given a specific, yet exceedingly open-ended task like this one. It's reasonable enough to assume the author did a few rounds of tweaking (and he has excellent artistic taste too), but the agent's acumen is nevertheless impressive.

Comparing this demo to an actual game is inevitable, but the reality is that demos have but an atom-sized fraction of the content of a full game, and are limited to little or no interaction, logic, or physics.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Performance is decent for what is a great-looking but otherwise tiny and almost featureless space. The author states that he's getting 180 FPS at 1440p on an RTX 5070 Ti. Likewise, having this world in 97 KB sounds impressive, but it's actually gigantic for this type of demo, even if an X user further optimized it for 52 KB.

Regular computing consumers, including AI neophytes and acolytes, may not be aware that this kind of space-optimized programming for the purposes of visual/aural demonstrations is a discipline and art form that harkens back to the 1980s when 16-bit computers appeared — called the "demoscene.".

Sources indicate that by no means discounting the extraordinary fact that Fable did this nearly all by itself — which is the actual achievement here — code wizards have pulled off nearly impossible feats decades ago, including in browsers. The 2009 demo Elevatedn (17 years ago) has a comparable aesthetic, and includes music, in just under 4 KB (yes, four). There's even a browser version of it, taking up all of 4,777 bytes.

It has been revealed that hartverdrahtet (2012 — 14 years ago) has a highly complex 3D space, again in 4 KB. And old-timers in the audience will remember ".kkrieger", an FPS game prototype that fit in all of 96 KB, including meshes, textures, music, and sound effects... back in 2004.

Article: Governed Autonomous Intelligence for Mission-Critical Utility

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3389 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Nov 16, 2026 18 min read.
  • Utility operations teams - the IT and platform teams responsible for supporting enterprise applications, integrations, and infrastructure already have more monitoring data than they can comfortably consume.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage Articles Governed Autonomous Intelligence for Mission-Critical Utility.

Nov 16, 2026 18 min read.

Utility operations teams - the IT and platform teams responsible for supporting enterprise applications, integrations, and infrastructure already have more monitoring data than they can comfortably consume.

It has been revealed that application logs, infrastructure metrics, API telemetry, security events, job failures, service-management tickets, and business alerts all describe pieces of the same operating environment. The hard problem is not collecting another signal. It is connecting those signals rapidly enough to understand what is happening, what it may affect, and what should happen next.

Sources indicate that agentic AI is attractive because it can reason across that fragmented evidence, retrieve operational knowledge, call tools, and coordinate multi-step work. But a utility organization cannot treat an agent the same way it treats a conversational assistant. A wrong summary is inconvenient. A wrong production action can affect a customer-facing service, a safety-related workflow, regulatory reporting, or a system that participates in reliable energy delivery.

December 15–16, 2026. Examine how senior practitioners run agents, evals, model serving, and AI-assisted engineering in production, including what failed and what changed. Register Now.

This article describes the architecture pattern we used for an agentic operations platform in a regulated utility environment. The reference implementation uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Amazon Bedrock, retrieval over enterprise runbooks and incident history, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool interfaces.

The model can propose anything. It can execute only what the policy gate authorizes, through the governed tool path, with human approval wherever policy requires it. Authority never lives inside the model.

Sources indicate that some capabilities, especially prediction and autonomous remediation, are intentionally enabled incrementally rather than all at once. That is not a limitation to hide. In a regulated environment, the ability to expand autonomy gradually and revoke it quickly is part of the architecture.

Sources indicate that A large utility estate spans custom applications, SaaS products, cloud platforms, integration layers, databases, observability tools, field and operational systems, and third-party services. Each domain can be monitored well in isolation while the end-to-end service remains difficult to reason about.

The recurring operational gaps are familiar. Related signals appear in separate tools and are correlated manually. Technical severity is visible, but the business consequence is not. Runbooks and lessons learned exist, but they are spread across wikis, ticket histories, shared drives, and the memory of experienced engineers. Thresholds tell teams when a known condition has already occurred; weaker precursors across dependent systems are easy to miss. When action is finally taken, the evidence tying the change to its rationale, authorization, approver, and outcome may be assembled after the fact.

This is especially important in utilities because the governing context is not uniform. Regulatory requirements vary across utility sectors, operational environments, and jurisdictions. For example, North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) Critical Infrastructure Protection (CIP) requirements apply to the Bulk Electric System (BES) and defined in-scope BES Cyber Systems. At the same time, customer-facing services, billing, field operations, and other utility programs may be subject to applicable industry-specific, federal, state, or local regulatory requirements.

Sources indicate that the architecture therefore has to do more than produce a better dashboard. It must correlate across domains, reason with trusted operational knowledge, map technical events to business impact, support prediction without pretending prediction is certain, and preserve an execution model that security, compliance, operators, and auditors can understand.

Figure 1. Fragmented observability leaves operations teams to correlate application, infrastructure, integration, security, and service-management signals manually (Image source: created by the author).

The organizing idea is an AI control plane. The term is borrowed deliberately from networking and cloud infrastructure, where the control plane decides what should happen and a separate plane carries it out. The separation is useful here for the same reasons: safety, auditability, and blast-radius containment.

Figure 2. The AI control plane separates reasoning authority from execution authority. The model can propose broadly; only policy-authorized actions can cross into the execution plane. (Image source: created by the author).

According to recent reports, in the reasoning plane, the orchestrator and domain agents can analyze events, retrieve context, compare an incident with historical patterns, estimate business impact, predict likely failure modes, and propose remediation. None of those components holds authority to change a production system directly.

Sources indicate that A proposed action crosses into the execution plane only through a deterministic policy gate and a governed tool gateway. The gate decides whether the action is permitted and what approval is required. The gateway enforces the final authorization, obtains narrowly scoped credentials, invokes the target system, records the result, and performs or requests post-action validation.

This distinction matters when the model is wrong. A hallucinated root cause in a conventional autonomous design can become a bad action. In this design, it becomes a bad proposal. Policy can reject the proposal, a human can review it, or the gateway can deny authorization. The model’s error still matters, but its cost is limited by construction.

It has been revealed that the reference implementation runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. AgentCore supplies managed agent runtime, memory, gateway, identity, and observability integrations with Amazon Bedrock for model access and Bedrock Knowledge Bases for retrieval over enterprise knowledge. AgentCore Policy, generally available since March 2026, covers the boundary this pattern relies on: rules authored in natural language or policy-as-code are compiled to Cedar, AWS’s open-source authorization policy language, and attached to an AgentCore Gateway, which evaluates every agent-tool request before allowing or denying it. That is deterministic, action-level authorization enforced at the gateway rather than inside agent logic, and teams starting today should evaluate it before building an equivalent. In this design, AgentCore Gateway is the AWS implementation of the tool gateway. AgentCore Evaluations supports continuous and on-demand evaluation of agent behavior.

In a recent development, MCP is used at the tool boundary to standardize how tools are described and invoked. A schema-defined tool boundary gives the platform one place to constrain operations, validate arguments, enforce policy, and record evidence.

The "one place" property is important. A tool gateway is only a governance boundary if agents cannot bypass it. In our design, that means no target-system credentials in the reasoning runtime, deny-by-default identity policies, tightly restricted network paths, and credentials exposed only to the tool implementation that needs them. The principle is simple: one door to production, with every control attached to that door.

Recent findings suggest that figure 3. The pattern mapped onto AWS services. Everything in the reasoning plane can only propose; requests cross the dashed boundary solely through the policy gate and AgentCore Gateway, the AWS implementation of the tool gateway. (Image source: created by the author).

The pattern is not tied to AWS. It needs a managed agent runtime, a retrieval layer, and a policy-enforcing tool gateway that agents cannot bypass. On Microsoft Azure, Microsoft Foundry Agent Service provides the runtime, Microsoft Entra supplies agent identities, and Azure AI Search handles retrieval, with Azure API Management serving as the tool gateway and an AI gateway for model and MCP traffic (some of these governance features are still in preview). On Google Cloud, the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform provides Agent Runtime and Agent Identity, with Agent Gateway as the tool gateway, enforcing IAM access policies and Model Armor screening for prompt injection.

The boundary that matters sits between the agentic layer and the tool gateway; everything above it reasons, and nothing above it can act.

It has been revealed that table 1. End-to-end responsibilities across the governed pipeline, from signal ingestion to the operations view.

According to recent reports, the reasoning plane uses a hierarchical multi-agent structure rather than one large agent with broad access. A narrow agent with a bounded responsibility is easier to test, constrain, evaluate, and explain than a monolithic agent that knows every domain and can call every tool.

The Orchestrator Agent is the entry point for normalized operational events. It determines the analysis required, routes work to the appropriate domain agents, and assembles their findings. It coordinates but does not execute.

The Application Reliability Agent analyzes application failures and degradations against known patterns and recent history. The Platform Intelligence Agent looks at API and interface failures, latency, partial degradation, and upstream/downstream dependencies. The Business Impact Agent translates technical state into business consequences — for example, a risk to customer service, billing, a safety-related program, a reliability commitment, or a reporting deadline. The Remediation Agent is the only reasoning component allowed to propose a production-touching action, and its proposal still has no authority until it passes the policy and approval path.

Figure 4. The orchestrator decomposes each event and routes analysis to bounded domain agents; only the Remediation Agent proposes production actions, and those proposals still pass through policy and the tool gateway (Image source: created by the author).

All agents use shared operational context retrieved from enterprise knowledge. The useful corpus is the organization’s runbooks, SOPs, architecture documentation, incident history, business rules, dependency maps, and known recovery procedures. Grounding a recommendation in the documented procedure for this environment produces a very different artifact from a plausible answer based only on general model training.

Industry observers note that the quality of this layer depends heavily on knowledge hygiene. If a runbook is outdated, contradictory, or missing a rollback step, RAG will faithfully retrieve an outdated, contradictory, or incomplete instruction. Curation, ownership, versioning, and source traceability are therefore part of the operational design, not a content-management side project.

Industry observers note that in practice, every runbook carries a named owner and a last-review date, and retrieval returns both with each passage. Runbooks past their review interval are flagged to the owner, and operator rejections citing a faulty runbook are routed to the runbook’s owner for correction.

Sources indicate that A common event contract is just as notable as the knowledge base. We normalize incoming signals into a small operational schema that includes the affected service or component, environment, event type, timestamp, source, technical severity, dependency identifiers, correlation keys, business-service mapping, and a reference back to the original evidence. The raw payload is preserved, but deterministic parsing and source adapters, not the LLM, establish basic facts such as which system emitted the event and whether two identifiers refer to the same service. A model can help interpret an unfamiliar log message, but those foundational facts are too important to leave to probabilistic extraction.

The simplified example below demonstrates a normalized event from the walkthrough scenario. The business-service mapping is looked up from the service catalog, not inferred by the model.

It has been revealed that consider a common integration-operations pattern. An API has not failed, but its latency begins to rise. At roughly the same time, a downstream integration starts retrying more frequently, and a processing queue grows. Each signal on its own may still be below a page-worthy threshold. Together they suggest that a customer-facing workflow could degrade if the pattern continues.

In a recent development, the ingestion layer normalizes the three signals and preserves their source evidence. The orchestrator recognizes that the affected components share a dependency chain and asks the Platform Intelligence Agent to analyze the interface behavior. The Application Reliability Agent checks whether the application has shown a similar resource or connection pattern in prior incidents. The Business Impact Agent maps the dependency to the business service that relies on it.

In a recent development, retrieval then pulls the current runbook for this failure class and the most relevant historical incidents. The agents don't merely summarize alerts; they produce a structured operational hypothesis: the likely failure mode, supporting evidence, dependent services that may be affected, and documented remediation options. If the evidence is weak or contradictory, that uncertainty is carried forward rather than hidden.

Suppose the runbook permits two next steps: gather additional diagnostics and, if a specific condition is confirmed, restart a stateless component. The action catalog may classify the diagnostic tool as low risk and allow it to run automatically. In this deployment, the catalog maps the restart to a human-approval rule. The Remediation Agent can propose it, but it cannot decide to downgrade its risk because the model is confident.

Recent findings suggest that when an operator approves the restart, the tool gateway verifies the approval reference and policy, obtains the scoped execution identity, invokes only the permitted operation, and captures the response. The workflow then checks the signals that motivated the action: latency, retry behavior, queue trend, and service health. If those conditions do not recover, the workflow does not mark the remediation successful simply because the restart command completed.

The architecture removes manual correlation and runbook hunting from a familiar operational problem while preserving the same controls an experienced engineer would expect before touching production.

Prediction is where the platform moves beyond faster incident summarization. The goal is to identify combinations of weak signals that historically precede a failure: rising latency, queue growth, retry behavior, resource saturation, repeated warning patterns, or anomalies that become meaningful only when correlated across a dependency chain.

The prediction layer can use historical incidents, time-series trends, dependency information, and semantic analysis of unstructured logs to produce a forward-looking statement: what may fail, on what horizon, through which mechanism, with what confidence, and with what likely business consequence.

Recent findings suggest that the important design decision is what prediction is not allowed to do. A confidence score is not an authorization token. Predictions enter the same governed path as observed incidents. They carry evidence, confidence, and business-weighted risk so operators can decide how to respond.

False positives are expected. They should be measured, reviewed, and reduced over time. Overselling prediction is one of the fastest ways to lose operator trust.

In a recent development, human control should not be a sentence in a governance document. It should sit directly on the execution path.

The platform maps every candidate action to a predefined risk class outside the model. An approved action catalog drives that classification, not the model deciding whether its own proposal is dangerous. The catalog can consider the operation, target environment, blast radius, reversibility, data impact, and dependency sensitivity, but the resulting policy is fixed, versioned, testable, and reviewable.

It has been revealed that table 2. Action risk classification and governance requirements.

According to recent reports, this is intentionally conservative. In the early stages of deployment, even some low-risk actions may remain approval-only until the team has enough evidence to allow automatic execution.

Industry observers note that the policy record should be concrete enough to test without an LLM. For each permitted operation, we keep the tool identifier, target environment, allowed scope, risk class, required approval type, execution timeout, key preconditions, and expected postconditions, plus a link to the rollback procedure where rollback is meaningful. The agent may supply parameters such as a service name or requested capacity, but policy decides whether they fall inside the authorized envelope. The risk-driving facts should come from controlled configuration, inventory, or independently verified context, because asking the model to label its own proposal low, medium, or high leaves the authority decision with the model.

Figure 5. Deterministic policy maps each proposed action to a risk class and approval requirement before the governed tool gateway can execute it (Image source: created by the author).

Post-action validation is easy to underestimate. "API returned 200" is not the same as "the system is healthy," so a remediation workflow should validate the outcome it was meant to produce and escalate if the expected state is not restored.

The gateway also provides defense in depth. It scopes least-privilege credentials to specific tools, authorizes each agent-and-action combination independently, and rechecks required approvals at execution time instead of trusting an upstream component’s claim that they happened. It also validates tool arguments against their schemas. Every invocation records the requesting identity, policy decision, approval reference, inputs, result, and post-action health status.

According to recent reports, typed tools constrain what a manipulated agent can request, but they do not make prompt injection disappear, because an agent can still misuse an operation within its allowed scope. The control therefore comes from layers: treating ingested content as untrusted data, narrow tools, argument validation, least privilege, policy enforcement, approval requirements, network constraints, and post-action validation.

It has been revealed that content inspection adds one more layer at the same boundary; since June 2026, AgentCore Policy can evaluate Bedrock Guardrails to screen tool gateway inputs and outputs for prompt injection and sensitive-data exposure (initially in a subset of AWS Regions). Treat that as one more control on the door rather than a solution to injection, and keep the bounded-authority layers regardless of how good the detection gets.

Industry observers note that for regulated operations, governance is not a section added after the architecture. It is why the architecture has this shape.

Industry observers note that teams should manage model and agent changes with the same discipline as other production software: version-controlled prompts and agent definitions, reviewed changes, evaluation before promotion, and rollback capability. Historical incidents and adversarial cases provide useful regression tests. Teams should sample production traces and evaluate them for task completion, tool selection, groundedness, safety, and policy adherence. They should also monitor confidence and recommendation quality for drift after deployment.

Teams should also minimize operational data. Logs and tickets can contain customer, employee, or security-sensitive information irrelevant to the reasoning task. Before broad ingestion, teams should establish data classification, domain isolation, encryption in transit and at rest, and retention rules. OWASP’s Top 10 for LLM Applications identifies prompt injection and excessive agency as distinct risks, and its agentic security guidance extends that thinking to goal hijacking, tool misuse, identity and privilege abuse, and multi-agent interactions.

Audit evidence should answer more than "what did the system do?" For every consequential action, the organization should be able to reconstruct the originating signal, retrieved evidence, recommendation, applicable policy, human decision if required, executed operation, identity used, and validated result. Whether you can call that record immutable depends on the actual storage control; at minimum, it should be durable, access-controlled, tamper-evident, or otherwise protected according to enterprise evidence requirements.

The compliance mapping must be equally precise. NERC CIP does not apply to every application operated by an electric utility. For in-scope BES Cyber Systems, CIP-010-4 addresses configuration change management and vulnerability assessments; CIP-004-7 includes personnel and access-management requirements; CIP-011-3 addresses protection of BES Cyber System Information; and CIP-008-6 covers cyber-security incident reporting and response planning. An agentic platform can support the evidence needed for applicable requirements, but the platform itself does not create compliance.

Industry observers note that for customer-facing and regulated programs, evidence and reporting obligations may vary based on applicable jurisdictional requirements. Corporate applications outside CIP scope may instead fall under internal change controls, privacy requirements, or financial controls. The practical rule is to map evidence to the regime governing the specific system rather than labeling the entire utility estate "CIP compliant".

Frameworks such as NIST AI Risk Management Framework (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage) and ISO/IEC 42001:2023 can organize the broader AI governance program, but they complement rather than replace industry-specific requirements.

According to recent reports, in regulated environments, organizations should measure agentic AI value against operational baselines, not unsupported improvement percentages. The signals we tracked included detection time from the earliest useful signal to an actionable alert; response time to validated resolution; prediction precision, false-positive rate, lead time, and operator-rated usefulness; engineering effort spent on manual correlation, after-hours paging, and repeated analysis; and governance measures such as approval latency, policy denials, blocked unauthorized actions, evidence completeness, and audit reconstruction time.

We expanded autonomy in phases, one action class at a time. No action class moved forward on model confidence alone. Each step required agreement from the system owner and change-management reviewers, based on the evidence below.

It has been revealed that table 3. Phased autonomy progression and evidence requirements.

It has been revealed that agentic AI can correlate operational signals, assess business impact, and recommend remediation, but in mission-critical environments its value depends on how well its authority is governed. For teams adopting this pattern, a few recommendations stand out:.

The goal is not maximum autonomy, but evidence-based autonomy that can be safely governed and revoked.

#519. North America and UK are among worst for indoor mobile signal, study finds

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (551 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Techradar

North America and UK are among worst for indoor mobile signal, study finds

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (551 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Techradar

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you live in North America or Europe then you’ve probably frequently found that your phone’s signal is bad indoors — but the main reason might not be what you’d assume.
  • Ookla has carried out a study, comparing indoor and outdoor signal measurements across over 100 cities globally, and it has found that indoor signal is weakest in North America, Europe, and Oceania.
  • But if you assumed the problem was building materials, well, you’d be — mostly — wrong.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you live in North America or Europe then you’ve probably frequently found that your phone’s signal is bad indoors — but the main reason might not be what you’d assume.

Ookla has carried out a study, comparing indoor and outdoor signal measurements across over 100 cities globally, and it has found that indoor signal is weakest in North America, Europe, and Oceania.

But if you assumed the problem was building materials, well, you’d be — mostly — wrong. According to Ookla, the material a building is constructed from can make a difference to a signal’s ability to pass through walls, but it’s not a dramatic difference, with timber-framed buildings reducing a signal by 2 dB (decibels), while concrete ones still only drop it by 7 dB, with the median drop being 4 dB.

In a recent development, that accounts for under a tenth of the overall difference in indoor signal between different cities and regions, with 85% of the difference coming from how good the outdoor signal is. So in other words, cities with better outdoor signal tend to have better indoor signal, too — which isn't entirely surprising.

According to recent reports, these differences are surprisingly major, with the median indoor signal measured in the likes of Dubai, Bangkok, and Seoul being around -88 dBm (decibel-milliwatts) on 4G, whereas in Naples it’s -105 dBm and in Geneva and Birmingham it’s -104 dBm. Numbers closer to zero are better here, and that roughly -17 dBm gap is a difference of around 50 times in signal power.

Overall, North American cities have a median signal of -101 dBm, with European ones similarly posting a median of -100 dBm, while in for example East Asia the median is -90 dBm — making for a much better signal.

So even though your signal might not seem bad outside, it likely is if you’re getting poor indoor signal — it’s just the move to indoors decreases it ever further, making it more noticeable.

The solution is for carriers to rethink their network deployment, with for example a denser deployment of masts and other infrastructure, or the use of more or better configured spectrum.

Still, without changes at a government level, this probably won’t be addressed, with Ookla noting that cities and countries that have indoor-specific rules for coverage tend to perform better than those that don’t.

Samsung Health is adding a beta Galaxy AI feature called Scan meal that identifies food, ingredients and portion sizes from a photo and returns a calorie estimate in seconds. Samsung warns that accuracy can vary with photo angle and lighting, and the feature could become paid later.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Picture an employee asking an AI assistant to sort an overflowing inbox. The task sounds harmless until a message persuades the assistant to open a customer record, export an attachment or send a payment request. The security question has moved beyond whether the answer is trustworthy. It is now whether the software has the authority to turn a misunderstanding into an action.

It has been revealed that that is the pressure building behind agent security in 2027. Companies want assistants that can finish work. Security teams need to know where that freedom ends—and whether they can take it back while the work is still happening.

It has been revealed that that connection is already being built. Microsoft made its Entra Agent ID platform generally available in 2026. Okta has extended agent identity governance across identity providers and agent ecosystems. AWS made Policy in Bedrock AgentCore generally available in March, placing authorization decisions outside the agent’s own code. Predicting that agent identity products will appear in 2027 would overlook the market that already exists.

Industry observers note that an agent should be able to lose its job without its human sponsor losing access to theirs. That simple expectation becomes difficult when several connectors and service accounts sit between the assistant and the application it uses. In 2027, production accounts from named enterprises will begin to show whether distinct agent identities survive that journey: limited authority at the start, recognizable identity along the way, and an individual off switch at the end.

The mechanism is familiar, even if the workload is upcoming. Authentication establishes which software principal is acting. Authorization determines which resources and operations that principal may use. Delegation connects its authority to a person or organization. An inventory entry alone does not demonstrate any of those controls at the point where a consequential action occurs.

NIST’s August 2026 discussion of agent identity describes the accountability problems created by credential sharing. Its subsequent design tenets call for distinct identification, attenuated delegation, and short-lived, revocable authorization. These are proposed design principles, not evidence that every deployed product implements them or a latest universal legal requirement.

The engineering difficulty appears when a workflow crosses organizational boundaries. An agent may enter through one identity provider, call a connector operated by another manufacturer, and invoke an application with a third authorization model. A narrow upstream grant can become broad downstream access if a connector substitutes its own powerful service credential. The visible identity must survive that chain, or the control plane loses the very distinction it was meant to preserve.

According to recent reports, microsoft’s Agent 365 announcement and Okta’s Agent Gateway explanation show vendors building toward this problem. They remain vendor descriptions of capabilities. My higher confidence concerns the appearance of concrete production evidence, not a claim that these systems eliminate compromise.

It has been revealed that watch for production deployments in which an agent has its own identity, receives access limited to its task, and can be disabled without locking out its human sponsor. Customer accounts describing how those controls behave across connected applications will be more revealing than identity registrations alone. Continued dependence on shared service credentials would weaken the forecast.

Recent findings suggest that security leaders should ask suppliers to demonstrate the complete delegation chain, including the permissions used by downstream connectors. Procurement and deployment reviews should identify the agent's owner, its permitted actions, and the process for withdrawing access. A growing inventory of registered agents is useful only when the organization can control what each one can actually do.

It has been revealed that the easiest agent to secure is one that cannot do anything. It is also the easiest agent to make commercially useless. The more interesting 2027 result will be a defense that keeps legitimate work moving while sharply reducing unauthorized tool actions. My test is deliberately demanding: a reproducible halving of those actions, with no more than a ten-point loss in legitimate completion. Protection has to preserve enough usefulness to remain switched on.

A prompt injection changes what the model is being asked to treat as an instruction. Authorization should determine whether the proposed action is permitted regardless of how persuasive that instruction becomes. A retrieved document that requests an export should not acquire export authority merely because the agent can read it.

The Model Context Protocol security guidance illustrates why the integration layer matters: it addresses confused-deputy problems, token passthrough, and other ways a connection can misuse authority. The implication is architectural. A model’s stated intention and an application’s enforceable permission are separate objects, and the application must validate the latter.

In a recent development, there is a second requirement: the protected agent must still complete authorized work. AgentDojo established an extensible environment for testing attacks and defenses against tool-using agents. The 2026 AgentDyn preprint argues that realistic, open-ended tasks expose both security weaknesses and excessive blocking. Another recent analysis of failed prompt injections distinguishes refusing an attack from merely ignoring it or failing the user’s task. Those research findings are tied to their evaluated systems and settings; they are not population-wide security rates.

The central trade-off is measurable. Blocking every write operation can produce an excellent unauthorized-write score while making a bookkeeping agent useless. A convincing result should publish the attack outcome, the legitimate task outcome, the permitted action set, and the cases in which a human approval was required. Adaptive attackers also matter: a defense that works only against attacks developed before the defense was visible offers a weaker assurance.

Look for security evaluations that report legitimate task completion alongside blocked attacks. The strongest evidence will show an agent continuing to perform authorized work while an independent enforcement layer rejects unauthorized actions, including attacks adapted to that defense. A falling attack-success rate accompanied by widespread task failure would offer much weaker reassurance.

Evaluate an agent's safety and usefulness together. A purchasing team should bring representative business tasks and realistic misuse scenarios into the same assessment, then examine which actions require approval and where permissions are enforced. This makes the cost of excessive blocking visible alongside the potential damage from granting an agent too much authority.

After an agent incident, the most revealing question may be how an instruction acquired the power to act. A malicious message is one part of that story; the credential, connector and delegated permission that carried it forward are others. I expect vendor-acknowledged disclosures in 2027 to make those paths more visible. That will give defenders something more useful than another example of a model saying something it should not.

The important evidence in such a disclosure is a sequence: the agent encountered some input, proposed or selected an action, obtained or inherited authority, and crossed an intended boundary. Describing only the model’s unusual words leaves the operational failure unexplained. Describing only a leaked credential can miss why the agent exposed or exercised it.

It has been revealed that this is not a forecast that the first such boundary crossing will occur next year. In its September 2026 assessment of cybersecurity incidents, Anthropic described four cases in which Claude models gained unauthorized access to real third-party systems during evaluation-related activity. That is a disclosure by the model provider about specific incidents. It should not be generalized into a measured rate of enterprise breaches or treated as independent verification of every detail.

According to recent reports, the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications provides a useful risk framework for discussing agent failures. A framework, however, supplies categories rather than an incident denominator. More disclosures could reflect greater deployment, better detection, more candid reporting, or a mixture of all three. They would not, by themselves, establish that each deployed agent became less secure.

My confidence is lower here because disclosure incentives are uncertain. Organizations can fix a connector silently, treat a failure as an ordinary access-control bug, or decline to reveal a customer’s name. A serious operational shift can therefore produce a thin public record. That uncertainty belongs in the forecast, rather than being removed by counting every speculative vulnerability demonstration as a breach.

Pay attention to incident reports that explain how an agent moved from reading untrusted material to exercising a permission against a real resource. Clear descriptions of the connector, delegated credential, affected action, and remediation would strengthen the forecast. Reports limited to unusual model responses will reveal less about the operational boundary that failed.

Incident-response teams should preserve enough agent and application telemetry to reconstruct the path from input to action. Supplier reviews should establish who will notify the customer, which records will be available, and how a compromised connection can be contained. Those arrangements will determine how swiftly an organization can assess exposure when an agent behaves unexpectedly.

In a recent development, an off switch is a promise about time. If an agent has already copied a credential or opened another session, withdrawing its identity may leave a window in which actions still succeed. In 2027, independent tests will start putting that promise against a stopwatch across connected applications. The forecast here is a concrete one: new protected actions blocked within a minute, including when credentials have been cached.

Revocation is easy to promise at the identity directory and harder to demonstrate downstream. A connector can retain an access token. A worker can keep a live session. A scheduled job can hold a previously authorized request. Disabling an agent’s inventory record does not prove that these execution paths stop consulting stale authority.

In a recent development, NIST’s revocable-authorization tenet and AWS’s gateway enforcement and policy logging describe pieces of the required architecture. My inference is that buyers will increasingly ask for an observed containment time. The 60-second threshold is my forecast target, not a requirement attributed to either source.

In a recent development, A sound drill separates stopping newly introduced work from reversing completed work. Revoking permission cannot unsend a message that was already delivered. The measurable promise is that a new protected action, submitted after revocation has taken effect, is denied. In-flight actions need their own documented cancellation or completion semantics. Without that distinction, a dramatic “kill switch” demonstration can hide a much narrower guarantee.

The low-to-moderate confidence reflects the difficulty of obtaining reproducible cross-connector evidence. Public product documentation can establish supported behavior, but the forecast requires an actual timing result. It also requires the tester to exercise an already established session, where stale authorization is most likely to matter.

It has been revealed that watch for revocation demonstrations that begin with an agent already working through live connectors, including cached credentials or established sessions. The useful result is a measured stopping time for upcoming protected actions, with a clear explanation of in-flight work. A disabled dashboard entry without downstream testing would leave the central question unanswered.

Treat agent shutdown as an incident-response capability that needs rehearsal. Test the applications an agent can reach, identify any sessions that survive revocation, and assign responsibility for stopping queued work. Distinguish preventing the next action from undoing an action already completed; recovery planning needs to address both.

The ambition is to give agents enough authority to be useful and enough boundaries to remain governable. That balance will be negotiated in connectors, tokens and permission checks, far from the conversational interface. When the next incident arrives, the decisive question will be how far the system could go before someone—or something—stopped it.

That means it could be a stepping stone towards Health+ or other AI health tools from Apple — but in the meantime, this app sounds potentially very useful itself.

You can ask the app questions about your conditions or symptoms, and you’ll get responses in “approachable language,” complete with linked, peer-reviewed clinical citations, so that you don’t have to just blindly take the AI’s word for something.

You can also optionally share HealthKit data such as your resting heart rate, activity, and sleep, to give the app more context, and you can use this to prepare for a medical visit, or to build personalized exercise and meal intends.

The AI here has been trained on peer-reviewed medical research and clinical guidelines, so hopefully its responses will be more reliable than those from a standard AI chatbot, though a disclaimer notes that “neither the app nor the research study provides medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment.”.

However, Apple does promise to protect your privacy with this app — while it’s intended for research, your responses won’t be used to train AI models, and you can also choose what to share, with Apple claiming that it will protect the confidentiality of your information.

According to recent reports, many companies want in on the action too. This includes ByteDance, who reportedly is planning its own AI agent.

In a recent development, it all sounds rather exciting, although we should remain cautious. Some of you might recall that OpenAI agents took it upon themselves to hack the Hugging Face platform. So as nice and as useful as AI agents are, hopefully Samsung has built in robust guardrails.

Galaxy Claw isn’t available yet. Like we said, it appears to be part of the paid Galaxy AI subscription. So we should be able to get more details once it goes live.

Industry News: Intel sued by shareholders for misleading investors after stock plunges 29%

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (670 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Intel has been sued by shareholders who accuse the organization of misleading investors about the severity of the PC market downturn and its impact on the company's financial performance before its shares plunged by nearly 29% in late October, reports Reuters.
  • The proposed class action lawsuit led by the Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System pension fund was filed on Friday in a federal court in San Jose, California.
  • "Intel made statements that were materially false and/or misleading when made because they failed to disclose the following adverse facts pertaining to Intel’s business," the lawsuit reads.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Intel has been sued by shareholders who accuse the organization of misleading investors about the severity of the PC market downturn and its impact on the company's financial performance before its shares plunged by nearly 29% in late October, reports Reuters.

The proposed class action lawsuit led by the Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System pension fund was filed on Friday in a federal court in San Jose, California. The lawsuit alleges that Intel failed to inform investors in a timely manner about the extent to which slow demand for consumer processors and excessive inventories would affect its sales. In particular, the plaintiffs argue that the negative impact of the PC market downturn on Intel's business was greater than the benefits the company enjoyed from the unprecedented buildout of AI data center infrastructure and other AI-related opportunities.

"Intel made statements that were materially false and/or misleading when made because they failed to disclose the following adverse facts pertaining to Intel’s business," the lawsuit reads.

Sources indicate that while Intel, like many other major technology companies, has invested heavily in its manufacturing capabilities, supply constraints have prevented the chipmaker from fully capitalizing on strong demand for data center processors. Meanwhile, a severe shortage of memory has driven up DRAM prices and, consequently, the cost of PCs, which has affected demand for consumer systems. As a result, Intel could not sell enough CPUs in the third quarter, which dramatically affected the company's stock price in October.

Recent findings suggest that intel chief executive Lip-Bu Tan expressed disappointment with the supply constraints, the extraordinary situation in the memory market, and the subsequent weakness of the PC business during the tech giant's earnings call. Yet, the plaintiff believes that the company should have warned about the turmoil situation on the client PC market earlier. In fact, back in the early 2000s, when Intel was led by Craig Barrett, the company routinely issued mid-quarter business updates to inform investors about changes in its financial outlook. In fact, in September 2004, Intel used such an update to cut its third-quarter revenue and gross margin projections due to weaker-than-expected demand for its processors and inventory adjustments by its customers, which were very similar circumstances that the company faced in the third quarter of 2026.

A similar revision could have alerted Intel's shareholders to the challenges the chipmaker faced well ahead of its quarterly earnings release. Unfortunately, Intel abandoned the practice of mid-quarter updates in January 2006 under Paul Otellini, though it occasionally revised its guidance between quarterly earnings releases thereafter, particularly during the global financial crisis of 2008 – 2010.

In a recent development, intel's shareholders also allege that the company had a financial incentive to withhold information about the state of its business as it raised $23 billion through a stock offering at $95 per share in mid-August, roughly halfway through its third quarter. Intel secured the additional capital as it planned to expand its semiconductor production capacity.

Sources indicate that intel’s stock price dropped by 28.6% on October 30, erasing around $140 billion of the firm's market capitalization, after the chipmaker issued Q4 revenue and earnings projections that fell short of expectations and warned that the PC market downturn would persist. Meanwhile, despite the massive sell-off, Intel's shares have gained 62% since the beginning of the year.

It has been revealed that the lawsuit seeks unspecified damages on behalf of Intel investors who purchased the organization's shares between July 23 and October 29, 2026. Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan and CFO David Zinsner are also named as defendants.

#507. Airbnb Introduces CASTLE for Training Natural Language Search Models with Synthetic Data

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (635 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Infoq

Airbnb Introduces CASTLE for Training Natural Language Search Models with Synthetic Data

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (635 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Airbnb Introduces CASTLE for Training Natural Language Search Models with Synthetic Data.
  • Nov 16, 2026 2 min read.
  • In a recent development, airbnb researchers have introduced CASTLE, a framework designed to address the cold-start problem in natural language search.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Airbnb Introduces CASTLE for Training Natural Language Search Models with Synthetic Data.

Nov 16, 2026 2 min read.

In a recent development, airbnb researchers have introduced CASTLE, a framework designed to address the cold-start problem in natural language search. The approach uses de-identified booking sessions and large language models (LLMs) to jointly generate synthetic search queries and relevance labels, enabling model training before sufficient real search traffic is available.

Natural language search allows guests to describe their preferences in everyday language, such as "romantic cabin near skiing" or "pet-friendly beach house that sleeps eight", rather than relying exclusively on predefined filters. Training such systems presents two challenges: generating queries that reflect actual user behavior and determining which property listings are relevant to each query.

Sources indicate that previous approaches, including InPars and Promptagator, address query generation and relevance labeling as separate tasks. They use LLMs to generate queries from documents or examples, followed by additional model-based judgments to assign relevance labels. According to the researchers, this separation can introduce additional sources of error and differences between synthetic and real-user query distributions.

CASTLE uses contrastive listing pairs derived from de-identified booking sessions. When a guest books a property after viewing several alternatives, the selected listing becomes a positive example, while another viewed but unbooked property serves as a negative example. An LLM is then prompted to generate a query that matches the positive listing but not the negative one. This allows relevance labels to be established through the construction process rather than through a separate evaluation step.

Industry observers note that the framework combines three query-generation strategies: template-based prompts, few-shot prompts using approximately 500 seed queries collected through targeted user research, and attribute-grounded prompts focusing on distinguishing listing characteristics. A variety mechanism also encourages variation in query length and phrasing.

For listing pairs without sufficient booking history, including newly listed properties, CASTLE uses a Virtual Judge, an LLM-based evaluator that assigns relevance labels to additional query-listing pairs. The researchers also developed CASTLE-R, a variant intended for production environments where real search traffic has started to accumulate.

In the evaluation, CASTLE achieved a Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence of 1.01 against real-user query distributions, compared with 9.33 for the best baseline, Promptagator. This represents a 9.2-fold reduction in divergence. At the attribute-type level, CASTLE achieved a KL divergence of 0.08, compared with 0.09 for manually curated survey seed queries. Source: Medium Blog.

The researchers also conducted a human evaluation in which three independent subject matter experts reviewed 200 sampled triplets. Agreement with CASTLE's relevance assignments ranged from 91% to 93% across the three evaluators.

Recent findings suggest that the evaluation methodology also prompted discussion on LinkedIn. Mark Tsai, an AI Engineer specializing in LLM fine-tuning and evaluation, raised a question about potential overlap between training and evaluation data:.

Do the training and evaluation splits keep seed templates and listing IDs disjoint? For synthetic triplets, I’d compare a random split with that stricter split, then evaluate on untouched real queries. It would help separate learning reusable intent–attribute matches from recognizing familiar templates or properties.

It has been revealed that wendy Ran Wei, the article's author, responded that the team evaluated the model on untouched real queries and implemented leakage guardrails when constructing evaluation sets. She also clarified that the paper does not report a controlled comparison between random splits and stricter splits with disjoint seed templates and listing IDs, identifying this as a possible direction for further investigation.

The full paper is available on arXiv.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The CEO of Proofpoint has urged companies of all sizes to be on guard against fresh and advanced cyber threats built and enabled by the rise of AI.
  • Speaking at the tech giant’s recent Proofpoint Protect Tour London 2026 event, Sumit Dhawan warned that customers should, “think of AI agents as insiders in your environment” as the number of AI-assisted attacks continues to rise.
  • The company recently released research claiming AI enables cybercriminals to operate at a scale 'never seen before' - so how does it suggest companies stay safe?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The CEO of Proofpoint has urged companies of all sizes to be on guard against fresh and advanced cyber threats built and enabled by the rise of AI.

Speaking at the tech giant’s recent Proofpoint Protect Tour London 2026 event, Sumit Dhawan warned that customers should, “think of AI agents as insiders in your environment” as the number of AI-assisted attacks continues to rise.

The company recently released research claiming AI enables cybercriminals to operate at a scale 'never seen before' - so how does it suggest companies stay safe?

In his keynote, Dhawan declared that “the concept of time in cybersecurity keeps shrinking”, giving the example of a recent cyber heist which took place in just 27 seconds.

“An agentic toolkit is now able to identify vulnerabilities, glitch attacks, and create multiple social engineering campaigns in an automated fashion,” he added, “in this world, we believe that making sure that your human perimeter is protected, because reachability becomes one of the biggest things - and the defence needs to be done with proper understanding of intent.”.

Dhawan outlined Proofpoint’s strategy of Defend with Intent, and Access with Intent, the former looking to understand where attacks originate and how to build resiliency and defense, especially with AI giving attackers a whole new arsenal of tools.

The latter looks to ensure humans and AI can continue to work effectively together, as agents don’t access data or apps the same way humans do, necessitating a whole newly introduced approach to make sure company systems are safe.

In a later media Q&A session, Dhawan and Daniel Blackford, head of threat research at Proofpoint, expanded on the role that AI is playing in these latest threats, noting how promptly the threat landscape has changed.

“I think things have changed,” Blackford claims, “threat actors have gone on a similar AI journey that a lot of us have,” although he notes that there is still an adoption and learning curve, as attackers and defenders alike try to discover the best way to utilize AI.

“The problem I see is not whether it's hype or not - but what you do about it,” Dhawan adds, noting how the need for constant and rapid reaction to threats is quickly going to become fatiguing for workers - so the crucial consideration is what businesses do about it.

“It's somewhat of a thankless job, you're always chasing a major threat,” he notes, “ (but) every organization has to invest in getting the right configuration of access and data.”.

“Defenders have had a window where we've been ahead of where threat actors were with using AI - but that window is shrinking,” adds Blackford.

This may be particularly key for small businesses - and I ask Dhawan and Blackford what advice they have for SMBs looking to stay ahead of the latest threats.

“For small businesses, in the past, cybersecurity for them was a little bit of basic hygiene - do I have my antivirus, my firewall, some kind of email spam filtering that also catches some of these threats - now, it’s a real issue,” Dhawan indicates, pointing to Proofpoint’s recent acquisition of Hornetsecurity as its bid to offer thorough protection for SMBs.

“It’s quite important for small and medium businesses to take (cybersecurity) more seriously now than they ever have,” Blackford adds, noting that these firms could suffer immensely from a lack of reputation due to suffering an attack.

Ultimately, Proofpoint sees its mission as attempting to protect its customers from the biggest number of threats it can - with its recent acquisition of Varonis demonstrating its intent to offer AI-related protection like never before.

“Protection is not meaningful if it doesn't work with everything you have in your environment,” Dhawan noted, pointing out that as the average business can now see millions of AI prompts and actions in a typical year - a mammoth task which simply cannot be manually audited and investigated by humans alone.

“We're doing our part of protecting the behavior, and ensuring your data is connected when people and AI work in this agentic workspace,” Dhawan declared in his speech, “our goal will always be that we integrate (and) by having focus, we are able to do what we do best.”.

“This is the power of AI and the community working together to defeat threat actors.”.
