Recent findings suggest that knit is targeting the mechanisms that connect patients with existing care: referrals depend heavily on professional relationships, scheduling on rigid rules and appointment availability, and clinical pathways on simplified categories and scores. The company argues that these mechanisms can leave patients waiting for suitable care while clinicians spend time on work others could do more effectively. Its example is a surgeon whose clinic is filled with patients who do not need surgery while patients who could benefit from an operation wait weeks or months.

In a recent development, knit intends to provide a shared clinical-intelligence foundation rather than own every application or workflow. Health systems, technology companies and developers could build on that foundation instead of independently developing the underlying intelligence, giving Knit a platform role beyond its initial navigation and operations products.

Industry observers note that separate benchmark documentation published November 16, 2026 tested Med-BEAM against Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Sonnet 5 and Claude Haiku 4.5. The task used records for 200 patients admitted to the hospital from the emergency department, none of which had been used to train Med-BEAM.

Given each patient’s history through admission and a full list of possible actions, the models predicted what would happen over the next 24 hours across medications, procedures, laboratory orders, imaging, nursing actions and referrals. No particular outcome was selected in advance.

According to recent reports, knit reported an average precision of 0.565 for Med-BEAM, using a 0-to-1 measure of how well each model ranked the care that actually occurred. Opus 4.8 scored 0.228, Sonnet 5 scored 0.222 and Haiku 4.5 scored 0.124, giving Med-BEAM an advantage of 2.48 to 4.56 times on this task.

Sources indicate that the speed and cost comparisons used different methods. Measured language-model response times ranged from 216 seconds for Haiku 4.5 to 408 seconds for Opus 4.8, with 307 seconds for Sonnet 5; Med-BEAM’s roughly two-second figure was an estimated processing time. Knit estimated per-patient costs at 37 to 257 times lower than the language models, using actual Anthropic benchmark usage at published rates for those models and, for Med-BEAM, inference time and hourly compute cost multiplied by three to match the provider margin.

In a recent development, knit characterized the evaluation as an initial result on one defined prediction task and prepares broader benchmarks across additional tasks, models and clinical settings. The distinction is significant: predicting subsequent clinical actions is an early test of the model, while the tech giant’s causal-AI objective concerns how alternative decisions would change patient outcomes.

In a recent development, the Series A follows an $11.6 million seed round co-led by Uncork Capital and Frist Cressey Ventures, according to a firm-hosted account dated May 12, 2026. Moxxie Ventures led the pre-seed round with participation from Coalition Operators. Knit is a UC Berkeley spin-out, and its earlier model used Truveta data covering more than 130 million patients to learn real clinical-practice patterns.

Broader evaluation is therefore central to the financing’s purpose: Knit’s clinical deployments and shared developer foundation depend on translating an early predictive advantage into routing and operational tools that work across institutions with different clinicians, resources and practice patterns.

#504. Industry News: Jailbroken PS4 runs 9-billion-parameter AI model at up to 43 tokens per second

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (862 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware

Industry News: Jailbroken PS4 runs 9-billion-parameter AI model at up to 43 tokens per second

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (862 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, developer Leonardo Alegría’s open-source project Garlic LLM lets a jailbroken PS4 run the 9-billion-parameter Qwen3.5-9B AI model offline on the console’s 2013-era GPU.
  • Recent findings suggest that the project, named after the memory the GPU reads directly — its sibling memory type is “Onion” — relies on a PS4 running GoldHEN, which is a homebrew enabler for exploited consoles.
  • It’s capable of voice conversation, with spoken replies in seven languages through the Chatterbox speech model and the chat model running at about 22 tokens per second.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, developer Leonardo Alegría’s open-source project Garlic LLM lets a jailbroken PS4 run the 9-billion-parameter Qwen3.5-9B AI model offline on the console’s 2013-era GPU. The app talks to the GPU directly, and the model is shrunk to about 4.5GiB to fit in the console’s memory, running at 31 to 39 tokens per second.

Recent findings suggest that the project, named after the memory the GPU reads directly — its sibling memory type is “Onion” — relies on a PS4 running GoldHEN, which is a homebrew enabler for exploited consoles. Garlic LLM is a free, single 5.66GB download, available on Hugging Face and installable through the PS4’s Package Installer, with about 6GB free needed, or 12GB if the package is first copied to the console’s internal disk. The developer tested it on a base/Slim PS4 on firmware 11.52.

It’s capable of voice conversation, with spoken replies in seven languages through the Chatterbox speech model and the chat model running at about 22 tokens per second. A held controller button also lets it take dictation with Nvidia’s Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 speech-to-text model, which supports 25 European languages. Parakeet models also power local transcription and dictation apps such as Meetily and Hex. The main model is Alibaba’s small open-weight Qwen3.5-9B, which, at the claimed 31 to 39 tokens per second in text chat — the prompt and test method are not given — is usable on the console.

In a recent development, the closest comparison is the PS5LM fork, which runs llama.cpp as a native app on the PS5 and reaches the console’s AMD GPU through PS5_Vulkan, a port of the RADV driver. The open-source llama.cpp is a widely used program for running language models locally, and RADV is the open-source driver that lets AMD GPUs run Vulkan, the graphics and compute API. On the PS4 there is no such driver layer for homebrew; Garlic LLM uses neither llama.cpp nor a Vulkan port, or so it would appear.

According to recent reports, the model’s operations, such as matrix multiplies over 4-bit weights, are compute kernels written in OpenCL C and compiled with LLVM for AMD’s Graphics Core Next (GCN) architecture. The weights are kept in that “Garlic” memory, while the CPU side, in plain C, handles the tokenizer, the interface, text rendering, and audio. The pipeline runs from the prompt to the CPU tokenizer, then, for each token, a PM4 command buffer — the low-level commands a graphics driver would normally generate, which, in this case, the app builds itself — and the GCN kernels, before the token is displayed or spoken. The whole thing is built with the open-source OpenOrbis PS4 toolchain.

One immediate question is how you fit a 9-billion-parameter model in the console’s 8GB of memory, which the CPU and GPU share. At 8 bits per weight, you have one byte per parameter, meaning you’d need at least 9GB, with typically more than that required overall. Part of the answer is 4-bit (“Q4”) weights, which take half as much, although 3-bit (“Q3”) weights, at about 3.5 bits with scales, are used for the two largest matrices in each layer.

Using the combination gets you to about 4.5GiB, versus about 4.9GiB if it were all 4-bit. The attention, or KV, cache is also 4-bit, which lets a 16K-token context fit, in comparison to the model’s native 256K. The Parakeet dictation model adds 0.33GiB and the Chatterbox voice models 0.29GiB and 0.09GiB, for a grand total of 5.23GiB, or 5.62GB, which closely matches the 5.66GB package size.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The next question is performance. Qwen3.5 comes with a multi-token prediction (MTP) head, and Garlic LLM uses it to draft up to two tokens ahead, with the full model verifying. This matches what the model was trained for, and the vLLM instructions on Alibaba’s model card use two speculative tokens. The project credits this for its chat speed on 2013 hardware.

Code also comes out faster with this setup, at up to 43 tokens per second. Also detailed is the default temperature, or model variability, which is 0.7 — Alibaba recommends 0.7 for general tasks with thinking off and 1.0 with it on — although the demo video uses 0, so it is predictable. At 35 tokens per second, the middle of the reported performance range, a 300-token answer takes under nine seconds. As a comparison, the PS5 ran the three-times-larger Qwen3.8-27B at about 20 tokens per second and the smaller Gemma 4 E4B and Llama 3.2 3B at 61 and 124, respectively, which is potentially quicker.

The PS4 Pro is “not tested yet,” but the developer is asking customers for reports on GitHub. The PS5 is not supported as the app is written specifically for the PS4’s GPU and system software. The app itself contains no exploit, but GoldHEN is installed at the user’s own risk.

OpenAI confirmed healthcare computer-use agents on November 16, 2026, making them available through ChatGPT for Healthcare, ChatGPT for Clinicians and the OpenAI API, and reported that 99% of 325 reviewed GPT-6 Astra tasks in electronic health record inboxes were rated clinically safe.

Sources indicate that the agents operate existing software interfaces to complete multistep work, including authorization requests, referrals and discharge planning. In a synthetic-patient demonstration, a message about lower back pain prompts a review of visit notes, physical-therapy records and prior imaging. The agent drafts an MRI order, encounter note and patient reply for clinician review, then prepares an insurer-portal authorization request for an authorization specialist to review.

Recent findings suggest that the safety assessment examined whether inaccuracies, omissions or actions in the model’s work could plausibly lead to patient harm. Reviewers assessed Astra’s interface actions alongside the notes, orders and patient messages it produced. OpenAI also reports that physicians selected the two highest helpfulness categories, very helpful or extremely helpful, in 93% of 646 assessments on a five-point scale.

On HealthAdminBench, an independent benchmark from Stanford researchers, OpenAI reports that GPT-6 Astra earned 94.3% of available rubric points and GPT-6 Luna earned 91.8%. Luna’s cost of 8.5 cents per task was 98% lower than Astra’s, and both models ran at maximum reasoning effort.

The benchmark contains 135 tasks and 1,698 subtasks spanning prior authorization, durable medical equipment orders and appeals. Agents observe live web portals through screenshots, accessibility trees or both, then navigate forms, review clinical documentation, check coverage criteria and submit decisions through standard browser interactions.

OpenAI reports that a CVS Health production agent cleared a months-long document-sending backlog over a weekend, while another handles system steps for tens of thousands of specialist consults each day. The agents navigate existing applications to complete steps that application programming interfaces do not fully support. CVS Health uses validation checks, human oversight, screenshots and action records to verify actions and application state. Data remains within its enterprise-controlled infrastructure, and production data is not used to train foundation models.

CVS Health has also published its CUA Agent Kit under an Apache-2.0 license. The kit uses an OpenAI computer-use agent to discover browser or Windows workflows, then turns successful runs into inspectable Playwright or pywinauto code that runs without model calls. This removes repeated model reasoning from stable workflows, while Codex-assisted diagnosis and updates remain subject to engineer review, testing and verification.

Sources indicate that cigna Healthcare reports that its case managers previously navigated more than 10 separate clinical and administrative systems to gather benefits and coverage, provider, appointment and prior-interaction context. Its deployment assembles that information for member outreach and moved from concept to deployment in under eight weeks. The work is part of The Cigna Group’s broader collaboration with OpenAI and is intended to give case managers more time to support members around care looks established by treating providers.

Abridge is developing a cross-system assistant that can coordinate discharge work across medication access and home health, with concurrent agents and escalation for clinical judgment. Its own announcement claims the experience is live in early environments with a few select partners, and that oversight must show what information was used, whether each step completed, when the assistant escalated and whether a payer received a submission.

In a recent development, ambience’s demonstration applies similar oversight to prior authorization. The agent prepares a request from chart evidence, stops to ask a clinician when the record is ambiguous and waits for approval before submitting. Health systems can restrict permitted actions, pause the agent and inspect a step-by-step audit log.

ChatGPT for Healthcare provides role-based access controls and audit logs, and organizations can add approval steps and limit agents to the applications, records and actions needed for each task. To support HIPAA-compliant workflows involving protected health information, organizations must use eligible services covered by an OpenAI Business Associate Agreement and the required security and retention settings. OpenAI states that organization data is not used to train its foundation models.

In a recent development, the contrast between CVS Health’s production administrative agents and Abridge’s early care-coordination environments defines the rollout’s central tension. Computer use is already handling high-volume interface work, while broader clinical coordination makes audit trails, access limits and escalation points essential to safe deployment.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • And LIFTOFF of the first Vulcan Amazon Leo mission, carrying 40 broadband satellites to low Earth orbit!
  • Shortly after the triumphant takeoff clip was shared by the ULA, above, the space tech firm updated its X feed with a confirmation that its mission on behalf of Amazon failed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon has suffered a major setback in its aims to offer a viable Starlink rival, after 40 satellites destined for low Earth orbit (LEO) were destroyed. Just ten minutes after the Vulcan vehicle debuted from Space Launch Complex 41 in Cape Canaveral, Florida, on Sunday, there was an “anomaly,” meaning that the rocket “failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit.” The language seems quite vague, but the United Launch Alliance (ULA) claims that data needs to be analyzed “to understand what occurred today.”.

And LIFTOFF of the first Vulcan Amazon Leo mission, carrying 40 broadband satellites to low Earth orbit! https://t.co/dv1MSjJUMFNovember 15, 2026.

Shortly after the triumphant takeoff clip was shared by the ULA, above, the space tech firm updated its X feed with a confirmation that its mission on behalf of Amazon failed.

Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle debuted from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit. Every flight generates data, and every flight teaches us something. Since the anomaly just occurred, we don’t have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today. ULA exists to provide assured access to space for our nation and for the customers who depend on us. That purpose is why we take on some of the hardest missions in spaceflight, and why we hold ourselves to the standard of mission success. Today, we did not meet that standard. We will work closely with our customer and other appropriate organizations to find the cause, determine the appropriate corrective action, and return to flight as swiftly as possible. ULA is committed to full transparency with our customers, and they will have visibility into the investigation process, which utilizes rigorous methodology and corrective action. We will provide further updates when fresh information becomes available.November 15, 2026.

In a recent development, sadly for Amazon, the ULA, and folks who want a viable substitute for Starlink in the satellite internet business, this failure will surely delay the full commercialization of this service. ISPReview notes that Amazon has successfully launched 392 Kuiper communications satellites, but needs at least 500 for basic global coverage. Moreover, Amazon Leo service’s transition from the current commercial beta phase to launching properly at the end of 2026 now looks uncertain.

Sources indicate that reports indicate Amazon has already manufactured 1,000 satellites, but ULA, which is a joint venture of Boeing and Lockheed Martin, will need to analyze and assure customers that Sunday’s failure won’t be repeated. ULA's Vulcan vehicle had already been out of action for nine months after technical investigations into issues with its solid rocket side boosters and core BE-4 engines (made by Amazon Blue Origin).

It has been revealed that for some context, the ULA has (or had) a great track record. Sunday's incident was its first total mission failure in its 20-year history. Early telemetry from the organization is already pointing towards some suspected causes of the destruction of the 40 satellites. Likely fault candidates include the first-stage BE-4 engines burning longer than planned, and there may have been some altitude problems near staging.

The headline failure and essential careful analysis of the anomaly won’t hold up Amazon’s other launch partners, though. A week from today, the Amazon Leo constellation is set to grow by 36 more satellites. They will be sent into orbit aboard a European Ariane 64 Block 2 (LE-04) rocket.

Amazon has approval for an initial constellation of 3,236 LEO broadband satellites, with 392 now in orbit, plus 5,105 for 5G service. Satellite tracking sites suggest Starlink already has 11,200+ satellites in orbit.

Recent findings suggest that “Delivering the infrastructure that will power the next era of superintelligence requires us to optimize compute platforms and models together,” Su said. The approach is intended to make World Labs’ model research an input to AMD’s future hardware, software and systems, connecting infrastructure planning more directly to emerging AI workloads.

Industry observers note that world Labs’ work spans interactive 3D environments and robotics. Its AI models generate and simulate those environments, while other technology supports robotic learning and simulation. Under AMD’s integration proposal, the researchers will keep pursuing foundational models. Their work with AMD engineers is meant to turn lessons about emerging model capabilities into future infrastructure for customers and developers in the open AI ecosystem.

Founded in 2024, World Labs had an established technical relationship with AMD before the transaction. The lab said the companies’ technical partnership began in 2025, initially focusing on model training and inference optimization on AMD GPUs. Its leadership strategy called for Li, Justin Johnson and Ben Mildenhall to continue leading the team as it joined AMD.

Industry observers note that world Labs describes Atlas, released on November 12, 2026, as its next-generation world model: it creates and reconstructs 3D environments, while accompanying tools and APIs let developers use the results in their own workflows. The release provides a current example of the research and product workflows AMD has acquired.

According to recent reports, world Labs says Viewfinder starts with a user’s photos or generated images, reconstructs the scene and supports upcoming viewpoints and rendered camera paths. Chisel provides a way to lay out and adjust a scene, with each camera view responding when objects move. Other tools turn scene representations into meshes with real geometry for games and interactive environments, while Relight changes how those scenes are lit. A developer API and integrations, including Blender, extend Atlas into outside applications and existing 3D tools.

World Labs claims film and visual-effects owners can build a set, direct a camera through it and render shots. Architecture and design users can shape spaces from photos or rough scene layouts, explore them from any viewpoint and take a mesh into their existing tools. Robotics users can create spatial environments from real or generated scenes for research and simulation workflows.

AMD has added a team working on generated environments, editable 3D scenes and simulation, and connected that work to its own engineers. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Uber’s Legal AI Agent Cuts Contract Review Time by 20% with Rules and RAG.
  • Nov 16, 2026 2 min read.
  • Uber’s Legal Redlining Agent has reduced average contract review time by more than 20%, with 91% accuracy in AI-generated decisions, according to the company.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Uber’s Legal AI Agent Cuts Contract Review Time by 20% with Rules and RAG.

Nov 16, 2026 2 min read.

Uber’s Legal Redlining Agent has reduced average contract review time by more than 20%, with 91% accuracy in AI-generated decisions, according to the company. Integrated into Microsoft Word, the agent analyzes proposed contract changes, assesses legal risks, and recommends policy-aligned responses using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), historical lawyer feedback, and deterministic rules. Lawyers retain responsibility for reviewing and approving its recommendations.

The agent identifies edits proposed by external parties, interprets their intent, compares changes with legal policies, and suggests whether to accept, reject, or modify clauses. It also generates comments explaining recommendations and flags changes requiring closer scrutiny. Uber began developing the first generation in early 2024 and piloted it with its Legal team in 2025.

High-level workflow of the Legal Redlining Add-in / Agent (Source: Uber Blog Post).

According to recent reports, an initial RAG implementation retrieved relevant sections from legal playbooks to guide language model responses. However, the system struggled with semantic retrieval accuracy, negotiation tone, and scenarios not covered by existing examples. Uber subsequently added a feedback loop that captures lawyers’ decisions, reasoning, and final edited text.

In a recent development, this change allowed the agent to retrieve examples of how similar clauses had been handled rather than relying only on whether a previous recommendation was accepted or rejected. At runtime, similarity search and metadata filtering narrow thousands of historical interactions to approximately 20 candidates. A second language model-based filtering stage evaluates their relevance. Exponential decay weighting, with a configurable half-life right now set to 365 days, prioritizes recent decisions while retaining older examples. The implementation also gives domain experts control over language and negotiation style.

Uber Engineering framed the challenge in its LinkedIn post:.

How can AI help streamline repetitive contract review while keeping lawyers in control?

It has been revealed that the legal team defines the desired tone and style, while engineers maintain the prompt structure and application workflow. The architecture combines a React and TypeScript Word add-in with a Python backend orchestrated through LangGraph. Parallel workflow nodes handle intent detection, risk assessment, and policy lookup. OpenSearch stores vectorized legal rules and historical feedback, while Redis maintains session state for follow-up questions.

Legal Redlining Agent system architecture (Source: Uber Blog Post).

A deterministic rules engine enforces non-negotiable legal requirements and overrides model recommendations when a matching rule applies. Language models handle tasks requiring contextual interpretation, including clause recommendations and negotiation tone. A final verification step checks generated responses against retrieved rules.

In a recent development, uber is also exploring agentic harnesses, including Claude Code and OpenCode, alongside skills to structure and automate workflows across its agentic AI efforts. The team plans to investigate legal ontologies and knowledge graphs to represent legal concepts and relationships, providing a semantic foundation for more consistent interpretation and reasoning.

Microsoft is hiking cloud prices in India — but dropping costs in China and other markets

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft has confirmed the details of its latest currency adjustments in a bid to keep local pricing more closely aligned with its global pricing levels and to account for exchange rate fluctuations, and it's bad news for India which is set to see cloud pricing increases of 15.7%.
  • Newly introduced Zealand will also see a 10% rise, while the two nations will also see rises of up to 20% and 10% across on-prem pricing.
  • But not all countries are seeing price hikes – China (-8.5%), Norway (-5.9%) and Australia (-4%) will each see a decrease in cloud pricing in line with currency exchange rates.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft has confirmed the details of its latest currency adjustments in a bid to keep local pricing more closely aligned with its global pricing levels and to account for exchange rate fluctuations, and it's bad news for India which is set to see cloud pricing increases of 15.7%.

Newly introduced Zealand will also see a 10% rise, while the two nations will also see rises of up to 20% and 10% across on-prem pricing.

But not all countries are seeing price hikes – China (-8.5%), Norway (-5.9%) and Australia (-4%) will each see a decrease in cloud pricing in line with currency exchange rates. These three countries see no change to on-prem pricing.

It's worth noting that individual products may see slightly different adjustments based on rounding rules and also how the prices are calculated, but the above percentages offer a preview into the sort of changes customers in these five nations can expect to see in the latest year.

The organization confirmed in a blog post that the changes will come into effect from January 1, 2027, as part of a new scheme it introduced in July 2026 whereby the hyperscaler would adjust prices each January for greater predictability, rather than at random points throughout the year.

Microsoft is also looking to adjust its Brazil pricing following the implementation of the nation's tax reform, while Japan will remain on its previous annual April cadence (with an announcement on track for February 2027).

It's argues that the revisions will help maintain competitive and regionally consistent prices for its cloud services, but some customers worry that currency fluctuations can make identical services more expensive or cheaper depending on where customers are billed.

Crucially though, these adjustments are purely a response to global currency fluctuations, and it's not a sign that Microsoft is raising its prices across the board.

AI Is Entering Latin American Classrooms: Are We Prepared?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1220 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI is making its entrance into Latin American classrooms, offering teachers new ways of organizing their classes, personalizing learning methods, and supporting their students.
  • However, while educational institutions begin to incorporate these technologies, a fundamental question arises: are the educational systems prepared to face the challenges that come along with them?
  • In a recent development, in a great number of Latin American countries, educational institutions, along with specialists, are exploring the opportunities and risks of incorporating artificial intelligence into teaching and learning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI is making its entrance into Latin American classrooms, offering teachers new ways of organizing their classes, personalizing learning methods, and supporting their students.

However, while educational institutions begin to incorporate these technologies, a fundamental question arises: are the educational systems prepared to face the challenges that come along with them?

In a recent development, in a great number of Latin American countries, educational institutions, along with specialists, are exploring the opportunities and risks of incorporating artificial intelligence into teaching and learning. While these tools promise to transform education, they also raise questions regarding teacher preparation, students’ privacy, educational inequalities, and the development of critical thinking.

According to Tamara Diaz, Director General of Education at the Organization of Ibero- American States (OEI), educational systems are still trying to understand how to incorporate these technologies.

¨We are experiencing a time of great bewilderment; not only in Latin America, but in the whole world, ¨ Diaz told Unite AI.

Diaz explains that even though artificial intelligence is already being used to prepare classes, create educational material and support students with learning difficulties, its implementation is still limited.

To take absolute advantage of its potential, she considers it necessary to implement clear public policies, evaluate the results of these tools and offer teachers training and support.

In Chile, artificial intelligence is already part of many teachers’ professional work. According to the TALIS 2024 results cited by Fundación Santillana, 55% of Chilean lower secondary education teachers surveyed in the study remarked they had used artificial intelligence in their work. Among their uses are lesson planning and the creation of feedback texts for students.

In an interview with Unite AI, Fundación Santillana de Chile shared the case of Deina Sepúlveda, an English teacher at Liceo Agrícola El Carmen de San Fernando, a technical high school in the country.

Industry observers note that sepúlveda used artificial intelligence to develop a web page that lets her students practice pronunciation in English, listen to words and texts, and adjust the playback speed of the audio files. Her experience was also published by the Chilean educational portal Educarchile.

In Brazil, the incorporation of artificial intelligence is also sparking debates about its possibilities and challenges. Ricardo F. Alvares, CEO of IA Instituto, shared his perspective on the role that these technologies can play in learning, especially in areas like the personalization of teaching, educational inclusion, and teacher preparation.

Industry observers note that one of the examples that Alvares shared is that of the Escola Estadual Santo Afonso, in Belo Horizonte, Brazil. As Alvares told Unite.AI, during 2026 the school participated in a pilot project called Jemas ( Jornadas Educativas en el Mundo del Alumno), which combined teachers’ knowledge with artificial intelligence tools to prepare classes that are adapted to the students’ interests, experiences and contexts.

It has been revealed that another example mentioned by Alvares is from the EMEF do CEU Pêra Marmelo, a public school in São Paulo, where eighth-grade students participated in math activities supported by artificial intelligence. This initiative involved the participation of the Institute of Mathematics and Statistics at the University of São Paulo and focused on topics such as algebra and problem-solving. In addition to strengthening mathematical learning, the activities sought to foster a critical attitude towards the use of these technologies.

Even though some Latin American schools are already using artificial intelligence in their educational activities, its incorporation is still facing notable challenges.

Recent findings suggest that teacher training, the protection of student data, and the risk of becoming overly dependent on these tools are among the primary concerns. However, one of the greatest challenges is not merely introducing technology into schools, but ensuring that teachers have the necessary preparation and support to use it responsibly.

In Colombia, the Institute for Educational Research and Pedagogical Development (IDEP) has been providing AI- related teacher training since 2023.

Recent findings suggest that A spokesperson for IDEP told Unite AI that teachers have shown interest in learning practical uses of these tools, but have also expressed concerns about their ethical implementation. However, IDEP points out that it still doesn´t have enough systematic evidence to determine how teachers are subsequently applying this knowledge in the classroom.

In Costa Rica, the Omar Dengo Foundation has also pointed out that the inclusion of artificial intelligence into education requires careful attention in the way in which students learn and develop their own abilities. In a written statement provided to Unite.AI, the foundation warned about the risks of exclusively depending on these tools, and highlighted the importance of strengthening critical thinking. From this perspective, the challenge not only consists in teaching students how to use artificial intelligence, but in helping them evaluate their answers and understand its limitations.

These concerns are not limited to specific countries. Across Latin America, the incorporation of AI in education has raised questions about the preparation of teachers, inequalities in access to technology, and the role of schools in the development of students´ critical thinking. Even though these tools offer opportunities to personalize the learning process and support teachers, their implementation also requires clear guidelines and educational strategies that take into account the different realities faced by all schools in the region.

It has been revealed that the OEI has also addressed the challenges represented by the incorporation of artificial intelligence in the educational systems of the region. Díaz pointed out that one of the main obstacles is ensuring that the integration of these tools serves clear pedagogical objectives and is not limited solely to the use of upcoming technologies. In that sense, teacher training and the development of critical thinking in students are fundamental to taking advantage of the opportunities that AI has to offer.

Recent findings suggest that in her responses, Díaz also identified two risks related to students´ learning: The convenience trap, which involves turning to artificial intelligence for immediate answers without putting in the intellectual effort required for learning, and the illusion of competence, which occurs when students believe they have acquired knowledge simply because a tool has provided them with an explanation. Both, according to Díaz, are risks that can lead to confusing access to information with actual learning.

Experiences in Latin American schools show that artificial intelligence is now finding its place inside the classrooms, even though its use remains uneven.

While some institutions experiment with tools that allow new ways of learning, others still face difficulties related to access to technology and the preparation of their teachers.

The future of artificial intelligence in education in the region will depend not only on the availability of these tools, but also on how educational systems manage to integrate them without sidelining critical thinking, student autonomy, and the fundamental role of teachers.

Ana Hoy is a contributor to Espacio Media Incubator and Latin America Reports based in Bogotá, Colombia. A graduate of Washington State University, Ana has also reported for Colombia One, BLENDtw, and others.

The second enhancement is ‘Ask Maps in directions’. As you’re about to head out, you can ask Google Maps to pull up your itinerary. There, you’ll see real-time details like live traffic conditions, whether a place is open, and even what the vibe is at your next stop.

The third option that Google mentioned is ‘Know before you go’. You can pull up your directions to see helpful ‘Know Before You Go’ tips about your route. That includes where to park or charge your car, and real-time conditions such as weather, potential delays, and tolls.

‘Find Appointments’ is the fourth feature that Google noted. The company says that Ask Maps’ upcoming agentic capabilities can find appointments online and call local businesses for you, thus saving you time.

The last Ask Maps feature that the manufacturer mentioned is ‘Search saved lists’. You can now ask Maps to find saved places on your lists in seconds. All you need to ask is: “Which spots saved in my lists have availability for 5 in the next 30 minutes?” Gemini will look across your lists and check live availability so you can easily pick a place.

According to recent reports, google did say that it will also publish some traffic trends about the best times to drive home for Thanksgiving, least busy times for holiday errands, and popular holiday activities. All of those will be based on Google Maps insights.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in an attempt to resurrect ASRock's discontinued SkyOC overclocking feature, an enthusiast has vibe-coded a motherboard BIOS using AI, potentially bringing non-K CPU overclocking to modern Intel CPUs.
  • Recent findings suggest that for context, Intel offers multiplier-based overclocking only on its unlocked K-series processors like the Core i9-14900K and the newer Core Ultra 270K Plus.
  • In a recent development, ASRock's SkyOC technology, which was introduced for Intel's Skylake processors in 2016, allowed customers to overclock locked non-K CPUs through BCLK adjustments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in an attempt to resurrect ASRock's discontinued SkyOC overclocking feature, an enthusiast has vibe-coded a motherboard BIOS using AI, potentially bringing non-K CPU overclocking to modern Intel CPUs. According to a post on X, Hardware 360º used Chat-GPT Astra to decompile and compare two versions of an ASRock BIOS, one released with SkyOC and another with the feature disabled. The AI reportedly identified the code responsible for enabling the overclocking workaround and modified it to create a BIOS ready for implementation on a compatible motherboard. Unfortunately, it remains to be seen whether the modified firmware can restore SkyOC on modern Intel platforms, as the workaround is yet to be fully tested.

Recent findings suggest that for context, Intel offers multiplier-based overclocking only on its unlocked K-series processors like the Core i9-14900K and the newer Core Ultra 270K Plus. Non-K models have locked multipliers, which restrict people from pushing CPU frequencies. However, there’s another way to raise the speed of a processor by pushing the base clock itself. The base clock, or BCLK, typically runs at 100 MHz and works alongside the CPU multiplier to determine its operating frequency. For example, raising the base clock speed of a CPU to 105 MHz increases the clock speed by 5%. The only downside is that BCLK adjustments can also affect the entire motherboard, including memory and PCIe-based components, thereby potentially causing system instability.

In a recent development, ASRock's SkyOC technology, which was introduced for Intel's Skylake processors in 2016, allowed customers to overclock locked non-K CPUs through BCLK adjustments. Certain motherboards also featured independent clock generators, allowing CPU clock adjustments without affecting the rest of the system. Intel was not particularly pleased with the workaround, and ASRock eventually had to remove SkyOC from its motherboards via BIOS updates. Additionally, Intel introduced microcode changes to prevent non-K overclocking.

The current experiment revisits that workaround by identifying the original BIOS code and adapting it for modern motherboards. Hardware 360º claims Intel's restrictions include a mechanism that triggers a shutdown when BCLK exceeds 103 MHz, and that SkyOC originally worked around this by tricking the processor with a false report of the actual BCLK value.

In a recent development, finding the original code for SkyOC does not necessarily mean it can be successfully ported to a modern motherboard BIOS. Newer Intel processors use different firmware, microcode, and clock-management mechanisms, which would make adapting the workaround considerably more complicated. Flashing modified motherboard firmware also comes with its own set of risks, including the possibility of rendering the board completely unusable. Nevertheless, it is interesting to see how AI-assisted reverse engineering can help gain access to BIOS modifications that would otherwise require a considerable amount of effort.

An inpatient nurse admitting a patient who uses an insulin pump can combine Aiva’s hospital-policy information, including required nursing checks and documentation, with Amion’s on-call directory to find and contact the covering endocrinologist.

A care-navigation example extends the same approach to cost and access. IMO Health identifies the procedure code for a knee MRI without contrast, Stedi checks insurance eligibility and benefits, and Turquoise Health supplies the blueprint’s negotiated rate for that code at two hospitals. The workflow also identifies additional information needed to estimate what the patient would owe. Other examples use Luma Health and TriZetto to build a pre-visit confirmation list, or Assort Health and Ferry Health to combine referral trends with outstanding scheduling work.

Industry observers note that the plugin expansion accompanied OpenAI’s separate computer-use announcement for healthcare teams. OpenAI described work with Abridge, Ambience, Cigna Healthcare and CVS Health. Organizations can configure application access and approvals and record audit logs.

The clinical-search changes affect how ChatGPT finds, evaluates and cites medical evidence in both healthcare products. The answers are designed to connect relevant evidence to clinical questions and practical next steps, with citations clinicians can inspect. In a blind evaluation, physicians reviewed responses to real-world questions across multiple specialties, including multi-turn conversations, comparing the previous and updated ChatGPT for Clinicians experiences.

OpenAI reports that across more than 1,300 reviews, physicians rated the updated experience more highly on all eight measured dimensions: factual correctness, safety, actionability, calibration, source authoritativeness, locality alignment, temporal alignment and goal satisfaction. Organizations must use eligible services covered by that agreement, apply required security and retention settings, and extend protections to connected systems. OpenAI states that content shared with ChatGPT for Healthcare is not used to train models. Claude impressed me with its responses and powerful productivity features, but in many areas, I preferred Gemini.

Claude is an excellent chatbot, but Gemini feels like a complete Android assistant.

#484. Breaking: WhatCable is saving me from slow and incompatible USB-C cables

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Androidpolice

Breaking: WhatCable is saving me from slow and incompatible USB-C cables

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1231 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Androidpolice

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that irene Okpanachi is a Features writer covering Android devices, laptops, portable projectors, VR headsets, software, and AI recorders for Android Police and Talk Android.
  • Charging on Android isn't complicated.
  • In a recent development, I've learned that an expensive charger is no better than a budget one if it doesn't support your phone's fast-charging protocol.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that irene Okpanachi is a Features writer covering Android devices, laptops, portable projectors, VR headsets, software, and AI recorders for Android Police and Talk Android. She has five years' experience across the Tech, E-commerce, and Food niches, with over 1,000 posts published. The Tech space is where she geeks out most, particularly Android. Irene holds certifications in Graphic Design (HerTechTrail), Writing in Plain Language (LinkedIn), and English for IT (Cisco Networking Academy). Beyond writing, Irene is a gamer, singer/songwriter, food lover, and a Jack of all trades.

Charging on Android isn't complicated. Yet, it's more than simply plugging your charger into your phone.

In a recent development, I've learned that an expensive charger is no better than a budget one if it doesn't support your phone's fast-charging protocol. Surely, there are nuances, like heat and battery protection.

But you can rule out most slowdowns when you know your cable's power rating.

Sources indicate that A MacBook app has been my saving grace in sorting out the USB-C cables I charge my Android phones with. Here's how I tested them.

Recent findings suggest that there's much to praise in a USB-C-centric PC like Apple's product. The brand was among the first to go all-in on the port, with the 12-inch MacBook's single USB-C port in 2015. Now, most laptops on the market use it.

The design made my recent cable test easier to run, because I could plug both ends of each cable into my computer's two USB-C ports and read it without any extra hardware.

Sources indicate that under the USB-C standard, a cable needs an electronic marker (e-marker) to carry more than 60W or to support USB 3 data. Cables without one, like most USB 2.0 charging cables, are capped at 60W.

I charge my Google Pixel 8 with a 65W Yesido charger and a 240W cable, though the phone draws at most 27W. I believed both were original, but I still wanted proof that the cable lived up to its 240W label.

So I tested it alongside two other cables with WhatCable. The PC software is available for free on its official website and GitHub page, but not on the Mac App Store.

Sources indicate that the download is a 21.5MB zip file that expands to 82.2MB after you unzip it. Because it comes from outside the App Store, your Mac may refuse to open it the first time and warn you that it's from an unidentified developer.

Go to System Settings > Privacy & Security, scroll down to the Security section, and click Open Anyway next to the WhatCable message. Then enter your password to confirm.

According to recent reports, the app then opens as a small cable icon in the menu bar in the upper-right corner of the screen. I clicked it, and a panel listed each USB-C port on my Mac as Port-USB-C@1 and Port-USB-C@2.

In a recent development, you'll see a summary of any connection and a cable's e-marker data on WhatCable. A Show technical details toggle in the lower-left corner adds connection data and raw system properties.

A settings menu covers launch at login, empty-port visibility, font size, the menu bar icon, and charging watts in the menu bar.

Much of the app is inaccessible unless you pay for the Pro license, which offers live power graphs, negotiation diagnostics, display diagnostics, cable pin maps, and MagSafe pin diagrams.

According to recent reports, the Pro license costs $13 as a one-time purchase for two Macs, which seems fair, although I'm hesitant to throw money at most offers. With the app's basic version, you're good to go.

Of the cables I tested, two are originals: the 1-meter USB-C cable that came with my Meta Quest 3S headset and the 2-in-1 USB-C cable that came with my Maono PD200W mic.

The third is a 240W USB-C cable I share with my phones and PC. For my first test, I plugged both ends of each cable into my PC.

That way, one port supplies power and the other receives it, so the computer can read the cable's e-marker without another device attached.

macOS asked me to allow the accessory to connect, and I clicked Allow. The 240W cable's e-marker reported a rating of 50V at 5A, or 240W, which matches its label.

It's a passive cable, and its data speed is USB 2.0, or 480Mbps. The software noted that the e-marker doesn't report a vendor ID, which is common even on authentic cables.

Many cable makers skip the paid registration with the USB Implementers Forum and leave the field blank, even when the cable performs as rated.

It has been revealed that so, a blank vendor ID claims more about the maker cutting registration costs than about the cable's quality. That aside, WhatCable couldn't read an e-marker for my USB 2.0 Quest 3S and Maono cables, which was expected.

Recent findings suggest that they don't meet either condition that requires one under the USB-C standard. Also, they were undocumented because Meta and Maono didn't publish ratings for them.

According to recent reports, for my second test, I connected my Pixel 8 to the MacBook with the 240W cable. WhatCable identified the phone and showed a USB Power Delivery (PD) 3.0 connection, which is a protocol that covers charging only.

However, data moves at the speed of the slowest part of the chain, and the 240W cable can only carry USB 2.0 data. So my data connection ran at USB 2.0 speed, even though both devices could go faster.

These results are largely consistent with a previous test I ran, which confirmed that my Pixel 8 charges at its full 27W on this cable, picking 9V at 3A from my Yesido charger.

Sources indicate that what I didn't know until now was that it was the wrong cable for moving files to my computer. USB 2.0 maxes out at 480Mbps, which is about 30 to 40MB per second.

A batch of 100 photos should take under 20 seconds, but backing up my 12GB photo folder will take several minutes.

According to recent reports, for my third test, I charged my MacBook with the Yesido charger and the 240W cable. WhatCable listed the charger's power options, from 5V at 3A (15W) up to 20V at 3.25A (65W).

The MacBook took the top option, 20V at 3.25A, for the full 65W. For my fourth test, I swapped in my Maono cable. The charger's top option dropped to 20V at 3A, and the MacBook charged at 60W, costing my MacBook 5W.

However, WhatCable still labeled the connection "Charging well." I only spotted the drop by comparing the two results.

In a recent development, the Maono cable works with my MacBook, but it isn't fully compatible with my charger's top power option. It's a clear case of a cable limiting the charge, and it gives a strong reason to use the software to catch mismatches.

Sources indicate that all my cables look similar in a drawer. But apps like WhatCable offer deeper visibility into my charging system beyond battery capacity and wattage.

Sources indicate that they help me rule out the weak links before I trust them with my devices. Incompatible cables aren't necessarily dangerous. Slower charging produces less heat, which is gentler on batteries.

But you'll face bottlenecks if fast charging and transfer are the priority.

Anthropic told IPO investors that its Claude Mythos Preview model did the software work required to get its AI running on AMD’s GPUs in about three days, with “basically no human intervention,” a job it indicates used to take six to 12 months. The three days cover prompt processing for one Anthropic model on AMD MI355X GPUs “at a useful level of performance,” with Mythos porting or writing “almost 100% of the kernels.” That kind of low-level code, which ties an AI model to one tech giant’s chips, has long been part of Nvidia’s CUDA moat, and an AI that can write it in days would suggest that moat is eroding.

Tom Brown, Anthropic’s co-founder and chief compute officer, made the time comparison, noting to investors that the original meant using a team of “dozens of engineers.” The firm already runs its models on multiple kinds of chips — on GPUs from Nvidia and AMD, Google’s TPUs, and AWS Trainium — and its fleet is managed as “one fungible pool of compute.” Brown called the early multi-chip decision “an unconventional bet.” It may have been a wise one, given that Google’s TPUs can now natively run AI models built in PyTorch, and Meta uses them in production.

Anthropic's claim that the job used to take six to 12 months comes from past work, from its “historical experience bringing up fresh accelerators using traditional engineering approaches,” where tailoring the code to each hardware platform was a challenge. Removing that onboarding barrier could reduce things to a purchase decision, and Anthropic started working with AMD GPUs for the first time this year, with an agreement for up to 2 gigawatts now in place.

According to recent reports, CUDA, Nvidia’s programming platform, is very mature at nearly two decades old. AMD has an equivalent, ROCm, with HIP as its programming layer. Code written for CUDA has to be transformed to work there, and AMD even built a tool called HIPify for the process. There is still a conversion cost to switching, and AMD’s vice president of AI software, Anush Elangovan, told EE Times in April that “Claude is better than HIPify because it has web search built in.”.

It has been revealed that AMD has been making the argument that AI can write this type of code since August of last year, presenting a research agent that fell short of human experts at the time. In September of that year, AMD CEO Lisa Su said on the Possible podcast that much of AI software is written in CUDA, which needs to be “translated to AMD,” and “a ton of that can now be done in software.”.

Moving forward to July earlier this year, AMD’s senior vice president of AI, Vamsi Boppana, said its engineers were using AI models to generate GPU kernels, and Su said that when she asked whether her team was helping the Anthropic engineer working on the MI355X, she was told they didn’t need any help. Boppana said that in some cases, the resulting kernels were even “better than the most manually tuned versions.” Under its July agreement with Anthropic, AMD is also using Claude to optimize workloads for its Instinct GPUs and to speed up ROCm development.

At AMD’s Advancing AI event in July, OpenAI’s Philippe Tillet stated that once OpenAI got its Helios racks, a single engineer confirmed everything worked within a few days, and that “agents are taking over our jobs, in a sense, as kernel engineers.” Before the event, AMD’s Andrew Dieckman, corporate vice president and general manager of the company’s data center GPU business, told reporters that he has had practically zero conversations with AMD’s customers about CUDA.

Published GEAK, an AI agent that writes GPU kernels; against 30 expert-written kernels it got 19 right, at 0.92 times the experts’ speed on average.

Tom Brown, Anthropic co-founder and chief compute officer.

Mythos “got Claude running on AMD in just three days with basically no human intervention”; the slide footnote limits the three days to prompt processing for one model.

Sources indicate that until this week, though, all of this came from AMD or its stage, not from Anthropic to its own investors. Anthropic buys the chips rather than selling them, and it’s heading into its IPO next week, so its multi-chip approach — now with at least some numbers to back it up — carries more weight than a chipmaker’s claims. Its prospectus indicates it in writing, too, though without a number: “We can onboard newly introduced chip platforms in a fraction of the time it once took.”.

AMD’s Advancing AI keynote, July 23.

Not stated; left running “over the weekend”.

Its “leading model” on an MI355X rack, with performance climbing.

Sources indicate that IPO roadshow video, narration, Nov. 10.

Mythos, with “basically no human intervention”.

Three days (“in just three days”).

Getting “Claude running on AMD”; Claude “ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels”.

Work that “took dozens of engineers months”.

Sources indicate that IPO roadshow video, slide footnote, Nov. 10.

About three days (“~3 day timeline”).

Bringing up “prompt processing for one Anthropic model on AMD MI355X GPUs at a useful level of performance”.

Six to 12 months (“~6-12-month estimate”), from “historical experience bringing up fresh accelerators”.

Prospectus (S-1/A No. 2), Nov. 10.

Its engineering teams, “leveraging Claude”.

Bringing “upcoming chip platforms into production”; no chip named.

What it calls “intense engineering effort over many months”.

The prompt processing (prefill) part of the workload is the step where a model reads and processes what it’s been given before it starts replying, and Anthropic hasn’t remarked whether the replying step (decode) was included as well. Anthropic’s chart, with its axis labeled “Time to onboard new silicon,” highlights both lines reaching the same “~100%” mark without saying 100% of what. The company also hasn’t said how fast the model ran on AMD’s GPUs versus Nvidia’s, and that’s the comparison we want to see to show whether AMD’s chips, running AI-written code, can match Nvidia silicon.

It has been revealed that on the other hand, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in an April interview with Dwarkesh Patel that Nvidia already uses AI on its own kernels and knows its chips best — “nobody knows our architecture better than we do” — and can get the most out of them. Asked why labs like Anthropic use other accelerators, he called Anthropic “a unique instance, not a trend.” Nvidia and AMD, among seven companies, are buying $26.0 billion of Anthropic’s stock at the IPO price, so Nvidia is investing in the very organization Huang called the exception.

In late July, SemiAnalysis published an article, “Can AMD break the CUDA Moat?,” which essentially mentioned that software creation is not the same moat it was even a year ago. That said, the catch for AMD is that with agentic coding, “each agent requires GPUs to test their code against,” which means that the AI writing the code still needs the hardware. It has found a constant lack of GPUs inside AMD for this type of development, which has held AMD back and may be a fresh bottleneck.

In a recent development, that leaves CUDA’s moat somewhere in between. Getting a model running on a latest chip, once the expensive part, appears to be getting cheaper, and better AI may wear down Nvidia’s claim that it knows its hardware best. As for Anthropic’s fungible pool, the chips in it aren’t fully interchangeable — Google’s TPUs are increasingly specialized, for example — and getting the most out of any of them still takes the hardware to test on. The moat is narrowing, but is not gone.

Anthropic’s first AMD MI450 chips, in Helios racks, are expected in the first half of 2027. That’s a newly introduced generation and an opportunity to see if the three-day bring-up can be repeated. Anthropic’s IPO comes sooner, after which it will report as a public company.

Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.

Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) has identified threat actors using large language model frameworks to fully automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation without human involvement for the first time, according to a quarterly AI Threat Tracker produced with Mandiant and published November 16, 2026.

Sources indicate that one detailed example was an exposed staging server hosting a multi-agent vulnerability research and weaponization framework that GTIG dubbed exploit_agent. The framework integrated multiple frontier and local LLMs. It was configured to continuously compare code before and after patch announcements for popular web application software, analyze the differences for potential vulnerabilities, draft exploits, and execute those exploits automatically.

According to recent reports, the server also contained data exfiltrated from targeted victims, alongside scripts for internal reconnaissance, brute-forcing, installing webshells, and removing webshells left by other attackers. Victim telemetry suggested the operator was particularly interested in French websites associated with the media and entertainment industries and the education sector. Russian-language configuration comments referred to LLM API keys for autonomous exploitation.

GTIG stated attackers may find patched n-day vulnerabilities, meaning flaws with fixes already released, more efficient targets than zero-days because the available research material is finite. Agents can compare source code versions, including pre-release or preview channels, and examine release notes, security research, and proof-of-concept code related to a specific flaw. Research into previously unknown zero-day flaws requires a broader search.

Sources indicate that automating differential patch examination and proof-of-concept weaponization can reduce the interval between patch disclosure and weaponized exploitation. The lower barrier to entry has a second effect: GTIG stated LLMs have helped produce exploits described as working when they do not, creating additional verification work for defenders who must distinguish functional attack code from broken claims.

Industry observers note that the exploit_agent finding is part of a broader shift from manual prompting to multi-agent intrusion tooling. GTIG and Mandiant observed multiple threat actors abusing open-source agentic penetration-testing frameworks, including ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI, to automate discrete phases and operational tasks during live intrusions. Shared capabilities include discovering and exploiting low-complexity vulnerabilities, generating single-use payloads on demand, and adjusting tactics based on real-time execution feedback.

GTIG independently observed CAIRN and PentAGI deployed in the wild, alongside experimentation with CyberStrikeAI and HexStrike AI. CAIRN coordinates specialized agents through an Observe, Orient, Decide, Act loop and a shared blackboard. GTIG observed it in intrusion activity against targets including the US aerospace sector. Between late August and early October 2026, a threat actor used a customized PentAGI-based orchestration platform for systematic reconnaissance and vulnerability scanning against a wide range of organizations in Asia.

These frameworks can compress attack timelines to machine speed, but GTIG assesses that they at the moment trade stealth for velocity. Unrestricted autonomous execution generates forensic traffic, uses recognizable identifiers, and leaves distinctive code-level traces. Those artifacts can aid detection and mitigation, although the tools remain capable of achieving their operational objectives.

Sources indicate that the report also documents a market for compromised cloud and AI resources. Throughout 2026, Mandiant responded to several LLMJacking incidents in which financially motivated actors used compromised cloud environments to consume victims’ compute or LLM resource quotas. Some single-day fraudulent charges exceeded $100,000, and the most severe cumulative abuse reached $1 million before remediation, Mandiant reported.

GTIG is also tracking LLM Mixers, illicit storefronts that sell unauthorized access to LLM services and supporting proxy infrastructure. They route buyer traffic through pools of stolen credentials and compute instances and can spread query volume across multiple victim environments to reduce detection. GTIG observed advertised prices ranging from $0.10 to $25 per million tokens on Russian- and Chinese-language underground marketplaces, with pricing dependent on the service, model, and credentials offered.

In a recent development, the findings point to a near-term defensive problem of speed and scale. Public patches can supply the comparison material for automated exploit development, while stolen credentials and proxy services can supply access to AI capacity. Those same automated operations leave forensic traces and contribute unreliable exploit code, giving defenders detection opportunities even as they face shorter exploitation windows and more material to verify.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that this type of buoy will have an equal number of blue and yellow stripes.
  • The IALA uses buoys with yellow and blue vertical stripes to mark the locations of upcoming wrecks and hazards.

In a recent development, understanding the meanings of various types of buoys is essential for any boater. For example, a boater familiar with the buoyage system will know that a buoy with black and white stripes is warning them of a hazard or obstruction between the buoy and the shore. Thus, they'll know to avoid this area accordingly. Similarly, you might spot a buoy with blue and yellow vertical stripes out on the water. Per the buoyage system established by the International Organization for Marine Aids to Navigation, once called the International Association of Lighthouse Authorities (IALA), this type of buoy indicates the location of an emergency wreck.

It has been revealed that this type of buoy will have an equal number of blue and yellow stripes. The minimum number of total stripes is four, and the maximum is eight. Its shape is either a pillar or spar. In addition, it will typically include a vertical or perpendicular yellow cross as the top mark. The buoy may also feature an alternating blue and yellow light. Like a solid yellow buoy, it can help boaters avoid danger by alerting them to the presence and general location of a hazard.

The IALA uses buoys with yellow and blue vertical stripes to mark the locations of upcoming wrecks and hazards. Such buoys serve as temporary warnings. They may remain in place until the hazard has been dealt with properly. What this consists of may vary depending on the nature of the hazard. Sometimes, this involves removing the hazard. There are also instances when it's impossible to remove a hazard, and instead, addressing it consists of promulgating information about it.

It has been revealed that in general, it's always critical to pay attention to buoys and to make any necessary adjustments based on the information they're communicating. For instance, an orange buoy could indicate a speed limit or other such regulation that might apply in a given area. You may need to slow down or make other such changes to comply with said regulation. By familiarizing yourself with the meanings of various buoys and by acknowledging them properly when you encounter them, you'll boost your odds of staying safe while boating.

5 V8 Engine Cars Most Likely To Last 250,000 Miles

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A car with a well-built V8 engine can last a long time.
  • Sources indicate that we'll focus on those that offer a V8 engine either in the current or previous model years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, V8 engines have earned a reputation for offering impressive power and performance. That's why they have been the go-to for full-size trucks, SUVs, and luxury sedans, despite many modern cars shifting toward small turbocharged engines and hybrid powertrains. Like other engines, V8s have their fair share of problems, which might turn away some potential owners from getting a car with a V8. However, generalization isn't the best in this case because not every V8 engine is created equal.

A car with a well-built V8 engine can last a long time. In fact, some V8-powered vehicles are capable of covering 250,000 miles or even more, provided you take good care of the car by adhering to the recommended maintenance schedules. If you're shopping for a V8-powered vehicle and want the most reliable models with longevity, iSeeCars has done an extensive analysis of data from over 395 million cars to identify models that have a higher chance of hitting that milestone.

Sources indicate that we'll focus on those that offer a V8 engine either in the current or previous model years. We've selected the top five models, starting with those with the highest chance of reaching 250,000 miles and going down to the lowest.

In a recent development, the first model powered by a V8 engine that can hit 250,000 miles is the Toyota Sequoia. According to iSeeCars' data, the Toyota Sequoia has a 42.3% chance of reaching the quarter-million-mile milestone. In fact, the Sequoia had the highest overall chance of reaching the milestone, beating other car models with much smaller engines. Per the data, the Sequoia is nearly eight times more likely to reach 250,000 miles than the average car.

According to recent reports, so if you need a V8-powered car to keep for the long term, you should definitely have the Sequoia on your wishlist. The Sequoia is a full-size SUV featuring three rows of seats. Although the 2026 model year of the Sequoia uses a smaller 3.4-liter V6 with twin turbos, earlier generations actually had V8s under the hood. For instance, in the second generation of the Sequoia, Toyota offered both a 5.7-liter and 4.6-liter V8, although it later dropped the latter, leaving the former as the sole option.

In a recent development, to get a V8-powered Sequoia, you'll have to look for a used model from 2022 and earlier, since the third-generation models starting in 2023 don't have it. You can begin your search by going through our list of the most reliable Toyota Sequoia model years for help in selecting the right V8-powered model. A used 2022 Toyota Sequoia starts at around $37,100 according to Kelley Blue Book (KBB) Fair Purchase Price data.

The second V8-powered model with a higher chance of hitting that milestone is the Lexus LS. According to the list, the Lexus LS has a 38.8% chance of lasting 250,000 miles, just a few points less than the Sequoia. According to iSeeCars data, the Lexus LS is more than seven times more likely to hit that milestone than the average car.

This isn't a surprise, as Lexus is known to be one of the most reliable car brands. Unfortunately, the Lexus LS doesn't offer a V8 engine in the current 2026 model year. However, if you're willing to look in the used market, you can find older Lexus LS models powered by a V8. For example, the 2017 Lexus LS sedan came with a 4.6-liter V8 engine making either 386 hp in rear-wheel-drive configuration or 360 hp in all-wheel-drive variants.

Actually, the 2017 Lexus LS was the last model with a V8 — Lexus dropped the V8 engine from the LS nameplate starting with the 2018 model year. The 2026 model uses a smaller V6 mated to a 10-speed automatic transmission. If you'd like to get the last V8-powered model, KBB data show you can expect to spend about $25,000 to $26,000 depending on the trim.

The 4Runner is yet another V8-powered model from Toyota on iSeeCars' list of long-lasting vehicles, which includes 27 different cars. The 4Runner clinched the third position on the list. Data from iSeeCars indicates that the 4Runner has a 33.1% chance of hitting the milestone, which is pretty solid as well, just like the other two models we've discussed.

Sources indicate that the 2026 Toyota 4Runner comes in 12 trims, none of which offer a V8 engine. Only the fourth-generation 4Runner had a V8 under the hood, so if you need one, you'd have to shop for used models between 2003 and 2009. Alongside a standard 4.0-liter V6 making 245 hp and 283 pound-feet of torque, the 2003 4Runner also offered a 4.7-liter V8 producing 235 ponies and 320 pound-feet of torque. Yes, the optional V8 made less horsepower than the smaller V6, but it offered more torque.

For the 2005 model year, Toyota stepped up the V8 engine's output to 270 hp in the 4Runner. According to KBB, a used 2009 4Runner, the last model year with a V8, starts at around $11,600. The V8 engine was an optional upgrade, so you'll have to ensure the model that you get did receive the eight-cylinder treatment before you purchase.

Japanese automaker Toyota has earned a reputation for building reliable cars, and as expected, most of its models can actually serve you for a long time. Like the Sequoia, the Tundra is another solid choice in the company's lineup for people who'd like a car that has been proven to last. Based on iSeeCars' data, the Tundra has a 28.2% chance of making it to 250,000 miles. While its chances are considerably lower than the previously mentioned models, the Tundra was actually ranked fifth overall and finished higher than other reliable Toyota models like the hybrid Camry.

According to recent reports, although the Tundra doesn't offer a V8 in the current model year, it used to in previous generations. That means the used market is, unfortunately, your only option if you must drive a V8-powered Tundra. However, the good news is that Toyota only dropped the V8 from its full-size pickup truck starting with the 2022 model year, so you don't have to go far back to get a model with such an engine.

Sources indicate that alongside the 2022 redesign, the manufacturer replaced the 381 hp 5.7-liter V8 with a 3.4-liter V6. The 2021 model used a 5.7-liter V8 with a six-speed automatic, standard rear-wheel drive, and optional four-wheel drive. According to KBB data, the Tundra right now starts at around $29,200 in the used market and debuted at a starting MSRP of $33,675.

It has been revealed that the GX is yet another V8 model from Toyota's luxury brand Lexus that is more likely to last 250,000 miles. Data from iSeeCars indicates this SUV has a 23.3% chance of hitting the quarter-million-mile mark. The GX ranks seventh in longevity across all the car models that the team at iSeeCars analyzed. Per the data, that makes the Lexus GX more than four times as likely to achieve this feat compared to the average car.

Lexus introduced the GX in 2003, just as the SUV body style started to attract a lot of attention in the luxury car market. ​​The first model, the GX 470, launched with a 4.7-liter V8 engine, and a V8 remained the go-to for most of the car's years. That was until the 2024 model year, when the company axed the V8 for a 3.4-liter twin-turbo V6. So if you'd like a V8-powered Lexus GX, consider models that were released in 2023 and earlier.

According to recent reports, the 2023 Lexus GX offered a 4.6-liter V8 producing 301 hp, sending power to all four wheels via a six-speed automatic transmission. At launch, the 2023 Lexus GX started at an MSRP of $59,950; however, data from KBB shows you can find one used starting at around $52,400.

It has been revealed that to build this list of V8-powered vehicles that are most likely to hit the quarter-million-mile mark, we relied on data from iSeeCars. The site analyzed data from millions of vehicles from different manufacturers and compiled a list of 27 models with a higher probability of hitting that milestone. We relied on the list for our selection, but only picked models that offered V8 engines at some point in the past.

The five models we've discussed are the ones that had the highest chances of hitting the milestone. None of them offer V8 engines in the current generation. So, to make it easier for you, we've gone the extra mile to highlight which model years to go for if you need a V8 engine.
