#475. POCO F9 Ultra Review: Last Year’s Chip, This Year’s Endurance

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2805 w)
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Androidheadlines

POCO F9 Ultra Review: Last Year’s Chip, This Year’s Endurance

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2805 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Androidheadlines

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The POCO F9 Ultra is the most powerful smartphone the company has to offer.
  • I’ve had the pleasure of using this phone for well over a week now, and I’ve had a nice time with it.
  • A big, bright, great-sounding flagship alternative that cuts very few corners.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The POCO F9 Ultra is the most powerful smartphone the company has to offer. As many of you know, POCO is owned by Xiaomi, so you can expect HyperOS on this device. Furthermore, some of you may have instantly noticed some design similarities with the Xiaomi 17T series. This phone basically looks like the Xiaomi 17T with an extended camera bar on the back. That’s not a bad thing, though; we’ll talk about that soon.

I’ve had the pleasure of using this phone for well over a week now, and I’ve had a nice time with it. The POCO F9 Ultra is not perfect, of course, and we’ll talk about why in this review. There is plenty to love here, though, and it’s a nice alternative to some more expensive flagship smartphones out there. In any case, let’s get down to specifics.

A big, bright, great-sounding flagship alternative that cuts very few corners.

POCO supplied us with a review unit of the POCO F9 Ultra, but didn’t have a say in our opinion, nor did they see this review before you. We’ve been using the device for over a week before forming an opinion.

The POCO F9 Ultra is heavier than both Xiaomi 17T series phones, while it’s about the size of the Xiaomi 17T Ultra. As I said in the intro, there are a lot of design similarities here. The only true differentiating factor is the camera bar on the back. The POCO F9 Ultra features a flat display with thin, uniform bezels, and a centered display camera hole up top. Its power/lock and volume rocker buttons are on the right, and those are the only buttons on the phone.

The phone’s corners are rounded, and the device is made out of aluminum, glass, and a glass-fiber-reinforced back. Many people will think it’s glass on the back, though, as you really can’t tell the difference. So that plastic back is not exactly a bad thing, as it can’t shatter like glass can, not to mention that it makes the phone lighter than it would otherwise be. The device is also IP68 certified for water and dust resistance. Its backplate is flat.

Industry observers note that the frame is mostly flat, though it curves towards the sides, which makes the phone quite pleasant to hold. Yes, the device is very slippery, as you’d expect considering the build materials. That’s the case for the vast majority of modern flagships, though. It is what it is. The back camera plateau does protrude a bit, but the phone does not wobble on the table due to the design of that camera bar. You don’t really see the wobbling as a problem until it keeps annoying you day in and day out, so I’m glad this phone doesn’t have that glitch. On that camera bar, in addition to the cameras themselves, you’ll find an LED flash and a Bose-powered speaker and woofer. More on that later.

In a recent development, the weight distribution is good. In all honesty, the only thing that bothered me about the device is the slippery factor, but most of you will probably use a case, so that won’t be a problem. All in all, POCO did a really nice job of adapting the Xiaomi 17T design for this device.

It has been revealed that what’s the situation with accessories? Well, POCO could have done better in that regard, in all honesty. First and foremost, you do not get a charger in the box. There is a Type-A to Type-C cable, but no charging brick. So, you’ll need to get one on the side if you don’t already own it. There is a case included in the box, but… it’s a basic, hardshell plastic case. I much prefer soft-touch silicone cases over this, as it really does feel cheap, it’ll get scratched like crazy, and it’s more slippery than silicone cases. That’s better than nothing, though. Many OEMs don’t include a case at all, so….

The POCO F9 Ultra features a 6.9-inch HyperRGB AMOLED display. That display offers a refresh rate of up to 185Hz, and its brightness goes up to 4,500 nits. The resolution here is 2608 x 1200 pixels, and the Gorilla Glass 7i protects the panel. Dolby Vision is supported, as is HDR10+. The display is flat, and it has very thin bezels around it, as you can see in the provided images. Those bezels are also uniform, thus completing the phone’s premium look.

Sources indicate that the display, by default, is set to the ‘Original color PRO’ scheme. You can change that to ‘Vivid’, or set everything manually. The point is, you have options. The default option is perfect, in my opinion, though, so I didn’t really mess with that. The colors are vivid in that color mode, and everything seems well-balanced. The colors are not too warm or too cool. In the ‘Xiaomi Vision Care’ menu, you can enable reading mode, enable nighttime eye comfort, and more. This display offers quadruple TUV Rheinland eye comfort certifications, including flicker-free DC dimming.

Recent findings suggest that the bottom line is, this display is great. It’s well-balanced right out of the box, but you do have additional options for fine-tuning if you need them. It has great viewing angles, and it can get immensely bright if you need it to. By default, it’s vibrant enough, and the touch response is quite good too. It does have high refresh rate support as well, so scrolling and navigating it is very smooth. All in all, it’s very good.

The POCO F9 Ultra is fueled by the exact same chip as the POCO F8 Ultra, the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5. That’s a 3nm chip from Qualcomm, and the company’s former flagship chip at this point. The model POCO sent us comes with 16GB of RAM and 1TB of internal storage. The company is using LPDDR5X RAM and UFS 4.1 flash storage here, by the way. The storage is not expandable. Other versions are also available; there’s a 12GB RAM model with 256GB of storage, and a 16GB RAM variant with 512GB of storage.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to benchmarks, we were able to test out Geekbench only. The phone still doesn’t allow us to run 3DMark Wildlife Extreme Stress Test or AnTuTu, unfortunately. It seems to be blocking both benchmarks. The phone did reach nice results in Geekbench, though, as you’d expect from that processor. What we’ve also noticed is that the phone does get quite toasty under duress. I’ve specifically run demanding tasks to see how it’ll handle them, and the phone did get very warm during gaming with hotspot included, followed by plenty of camera use.

The good news is that while you’ll feel the heat on your hands, the games were not affected by it at all. Also, you really do have to push the phone to its limit for the heat to be noticeably annoying. I specifically put it in duress, though that’s not my normal use. In my normal use, the phone was perfectly fine in terms of heat; it did not feel that warm to the touch at all. That’s probably what you can expect as well.

It is capable of flying through anything you throw at it. Day-to-day use is incredibly smooth, and it also does a fantastic job when it comes to games, heat aside. The performance itself is great, as long as you don’t mind a bit of heat.

3DMark (Wildlife Extreme Stress Test):.

3DMark (Wildlife Extreme Stress Test) thermals:.

POCO equipped this phone with a truly beefy 8,050mAh battery, so it’s not surprising that the battery life is great here. This is, of course, a silicon-carbon battery, as the phone is not thick at all, nor heavy. You’ll be glad to know that the phone delivers when it comes to battery life. Our battery life benchmarks are visible below, but what most of you are interested in is actual day-to-day use, how did the phone hold up?

It held up great, actually. I was able to cross the 8-hour screen-on time on two occasions, and the phone still had plenty of juice left in the tank. It had over 30% left on those days, and I really didn’t pull back punches. What I did notice, however, is that the battery does drop noticeably faster during more demanding gaming sessions and camera use, especially if you’re shooting 4K content at 60 FPS. That is the case with almost every phone out there, so it’s not surprising.

The point is, even if you’re a demanding user, there’s a good chance this phone will be able to last you a full day without a problem. In fact, for some people, this could easily be a two-day phone, even a three-day phone for people who don’t use their phones much. The battery life is that good.

It has been revealed that the charger is, unfortunately, not included in the retail box. However, we did have a 100W Xiaomi charger at hand, and it was able to fully charge this smartphone in 55 minutes. So, under an hour for an 8,000mAh+ battery, that’s not bad at all. In 30 minutes, you can reach around a 60% charge, by the way. The phone also supports PD3.0, QC3+, and PPS charging, so finding a charger for it should be fairly easy, if you don’t grab the official one. Do note that the phone may not charge at full speed with an unofficial charger.

Recent findings suggest that the POCO F9 Ultra has three cameras on the back, and only the main one is different in comparison to the POCO F8 Ultra. The new model uses a 200-megapixel main camera with a 1/1.56-inch sensor size and an f/1.7 aperture. There is also a 50-megapixel ultrawide camera with an f/2.4 aperture and a 1/2.88-inch sensor size. That camera offers a 102-degree FoV. The third camera is a 50-megapixel periscope telephoto snapper with an f/3.0 aperture and a 1/2.76-inch sensor size. It also offers a 5x optical zoom.

The thing is, despite the fact that the phone is now using a higher-res sensor, it is smaller than the one in the POCO F8 Ultra. I’m talking about the main camera, of course. With that being mentioned, the main camera is good when it comes to daytime photos. The colors are good, images don’t end up oversaturated, and the dynamic range is spot on as well. There’s plenty of detail provided, and the images are sharp, but not too sharp. The images, by default, are getting pixel-binned, and that’s the ideal mode to take pictures in, in my opinion. There is a full 200MP mode, but despite the added detail, your subject will have to be perfectly still, and there’s a good chance you’ll need to do some light editing as well.

According to recent reports, when it comes to low-light, the main camera takes good photos overall. It has good highlight control, and the images overall end up looking good in terms of shadows and the general feel. They don’t end up looking too bright or too dark. There’s enough detail in them, and the colors also look good… well, most of the time. While the camera is rather consistent in low light, I did have several situations where the highlights did get blown out a bit, and the details were not as great as they usually are.

The ultrawide camera does a good job, but the lack of autofocus is an matter. That’s by far the most obvious problem with it. Other than that, it does well in terms of colors and dynamic range. Ultrawide images do look notably softer in low-light, and the representations of shadows is not that great either. The same goes for colors, especially if we’re talking bright neon lights. The periscope telephoto camera is the best performer right after the main camera. It provides plenty of detail, good colors, and good dynamic range. 5x is the sweet spot for it, but even photos at 10x end up looking good most of the time. In low light, there’s plenty of detail, good colors, and good dynamic range. A slightly brighter exposure wouldn’t hurt, though. 10x images do look notably worse in low-light, though.

The POCO F9 Ultra comes with Android 16 out of the box, with HyperOS 3 on top. Do note that POCO promised to start updating the device to Android 17 and HyperOS 4 in mid-November, but that hasn’t happened yet. If you’ve used the POCO F8 series, you’ll be right at home, as this is basically the same software. It’s also worth noting that POCO promised 4 major Android OS updates for the device, along with 6 years’ worth of security patches.

In general, the feel of the software is quite good. It feels very responsive, with great animations. They’re quick and nice-looking in general. The OS is filled with various features, such as the Hyper Island, which is inspired by Apple’s Dynamic Island. It does a good job of providing contextual information and a number of other things, but it is limited, as is on any other Android phone. Third-party app support is not great for it, which is the main problem. First-party apps from Xiaomi will work great with it, though.

According to recent reports, hyperAI is also a part of the package. It can help with your writing, translation, transcription, and more. There are some gestures you can take advantage of as well, such as a swipe down with three fingers to take a screenshot, and many more. All the usual features you’re used to in HyperOS will be here, basically. You can also choose whether you want an app drawer or to have all the installed apps spread across the home screens. There’s some customization on offer here as well, though this is definitely not the most customizable Android skin.

Notifications worked well, and you can actually feel an improvement in the optimization of the software. It simply feels smoother and more polished than it did before. There are still some challenges here and there, though. I would love to see more customization options for HyperOS, and one of the main ones is… third-party launchers. The phone flat-out blocks you from using a third-party launcher if you’re using navigation gestures. Third-party launchers don’t play nice with many Chinese phones, but none other than Xiaomi (including POCO and Redmi) flat-out blocks them if you’re using navigation gestures. It’s about time the company optimizes for third-party launchers.

You do get a number of first-party apps pre-installed here, along with some additional third-party ones. For example, TikTok comes pre-installed, as do WPS Office and Prime Video. Those are just some examples. You can easily remove all of them, though, if you don’t intend on using them, so I don’t really see that as a negative. First-party ones are mostly non-removable, which is to be expected. The situation is better than it was in the past, though. You can remove some of them.

All in all, HyperOS 3 is better now. It was buggier when it first rolled out, but it’s obvious that it has been improved. Even when compared to the Xiaomi 17 series I’ve reviewed. The Xiaomi 17T was already an improvement, but this is even better than it was earlier this year. I’m really wondering about HyperOS 4 at this point. I hope it will keep evolving in the right direction.

The POCO F9 Ultra has stereo speakers. IN fact, it has Bose-tuned speakers. There are two symmetrical stereo speakers included, both 1115D in size. That’s basically the same as last year. POCO refers to these speakers as “master-grade,” and there is a separate subwoofer included. That woofer fires toward the back. Now, this phone may not have the loudest speakers out there, but they’re very good.

Recent findings suggest that don’t get me wrong, they’re plenty loud, but not the loudest around. However, the overall sound quality is excellent. The mids and the highs in particular are very clear, and we enjoyed these speakers very much. I don’t remember the last time I enjoyed speakers on a phone this much, so kudos to POCO.

Should you buy it? Well, if the price tag ended up being lower by around €300, this would be a great value. At €1,099, it’s a harder sell, that’s for sure. Still, it’s more affordable than a number of its competitors, and it’s worth considering, that’s for sure. It offers very good performance, an excellent display, outstanding battery life, very good camera performance, and better sound than you’ll find with its competitors. There’s plenty to like when it comes to the POCO F9 Ultra, as even HyperOS is better than it was.

#474. AI Is Moving Onto Our PCs — But Who Controls What It Can See?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (810 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Unite

AI Is Moving Onto Our PCs — But Who Controls What It Can See?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (810 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI agents are beginning to move beyond chat windows and into the operating systems, applications and files people use every day.
  • Latest Windows PCs and software released in recent months are ushering in a new era of multistep autonomous AI workflows for the ordinary user and into enterprise environments, and the transition is no longer just a technology forecast.
  • NVIDIA’s RTX-powered Windows PCs support locally running AI agents, while Perplexity has expanded its agent capabilities to compatible Windows computers, enabling workflows involving local files and connected applications.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI agents are beginning to move beyond chat windows and into the operating systems, applications and files people use every day.

Latest Windows PCs and software released in recent months are ushering in a new era of multistep autonomous AI workflows for the ordinary user and into enterprise environments, and the transition is no longer just a technology forecast.

NVIDIA’s RTX-powered Windows PCs support locally running AI agents, while Perplexity has expanded its agent capabilities to compatible Windows computers, enabling workflows involving local files and connected applications. Meanwhile, Microsoft is developing safeguards to control how agents access resources and take action.

But greater autonomy brings greater security risks. On October 19, Microsoft’s Executive Vice President of Security, Hayete Gallot, warned that organizations must do more to secure “agentic insiders,” noting that AI agents are frequently overprivileged and can access sensitive data, tools and systems while making decisions in critical processes.

Sources indicate that microsoft’s Windows security strategy is based on containment, limited permissions, limited oversight, and increasing concern that an agent’s error could have repercussions beyond a simple wrong answer. It may reveal sensitive information, alter critical files or cause unwanted activities within business applications.

Using AI agents on a PC can help minimize the amount of sensitive data being transferred to cloud-based services, but local processing is not an all-out security safety net.

Even an on-device model can still have too many files accessed, poor security or unsafe links to other apps.

The problem isn’t always the AI model; it’s often the organizational governance, mentioned Bayron Quintero, CEO and co-founder of iData Global, a organization specializing in AI solutions across the Americas.

According to recent reports, companies can give too much or too little access to data, applications and business processes, he told Unite AI. Agents may be given rights that are not congruent with what they are expected to do.

It has been revealed that “The challenge is ensuring that an agent operates under the principle of least privilege, with access only to the data, systems, and actions required for a particular workflow,” Quintero noted. That means granting access only to the data, systems and actions required for a specific workflow.

He identified clear data ownership, role-based access controls and continuous monitoring of interactions with internal and third-party systems as essential safeguards.

There is no such thing as safe local AI, Quintero emphasized.

Excessive permissions, weak encryption, insufficient monitoring and insecure integrations can make an on-device agent as risky as a cloud-based one – or even riskier.

Security is not just about where a system’s model is running; it’s also about how it’s configured and managed.

The question for the ordinary user is whether an AI agent’s access is appropriate for its task.

An agent should not have to scan an entire drive if it is only asked to summarize one document. An organizing tool for photos should not automatically read financial data or be able to send messages. Permissions must be tight, transparent and revocable.

The agent-account and workspace model in Microsoft is a step towards the separation of an agent’s activity from a person’s session. However, the protections need to be effective beyond the demonstration.

Microsoft’s Windows agent-security guidance calls for user authorization, logs of activity and a mechanism to approach that limits agents to the access they need. Employers and developers need to monitor the agents’ reaction to misguided instructions in documents, websites, or messages.

During an authorized task, agents can come across untrusted content. When an agent sees hostile text as a command, it could be a big security glitch because the information can be easily accessed.

Human approval and least-privilege access must go hand-in-hand with containment for sensitive actions.

The AI PC will not only be evaluated on the amount of work agents can automate, but also on the user’s trustworthiness to share personal and professional data.

While local processing, the agentic AI can enhance speed and minimize certain data exposures, it doesn’t remove the need for permissions and oversight.

The principle should be straightforward: agents should only have access to what is necessary for the job, and owners should be able to comprehend, track and block what an agent does.

Control must not be an afterthought, as computers become more capable of acting for us. It needs to be within the design.

Adlin Pertishya is a technology and business reporter who has worked for Finance Outlook India, Silicon India, StartupBeat and others.

Sources indicate that why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Industry observers note that minisforum’s Intel-based M2 line includes mini PCs with powerful processors such as the Core Ultra X7 Processor 358H (with 16C/16T CPU and B390 graphics), and the Core Ultra 7 356H (16C/16T). But there are more modest systems, too. The M2 Air-304 here is the most affordable option, based around the Intel Core 3 processor 304 with its 5C/5T CPU (1x Cougar Cove P-core and 4x Darkmont LP E-cores) and an iGPU with just a single Xe3 core.

Recent findings suggest that no surprise, the little brother in the pack, both in terms of physical size and computing resources, is the most affordable. It right now starts at $263 for a barebones version. However, our test sample with 16GB DDR5-5600, a 500GB SSD, and Windows 11 Pro is listed at $559 - direct. That’s an introductory price, and Minisforum’s small text threatens that our configuration will bump up to $699 at some point in the future. Such a rise would put this product offering on very shaky ground, and we see B&H Photo has already raised the price at $729.

In a recent development, overall, this Mini PC was pleasant to use, though. It ran quietly and only strained in gaming and productivity benchmarks which put it under loads that casual owners aren’t going to be running on such a machine.

The Mini M2 Air looks stylish enough, and feels solid. Looks can be deceiving, though, and the top shell is a silver colored plastic, not a metallic alloy. Sometimes a metal shell can be used to help conduct away heat, but that seems less important with this actively cooled machine with a 15W processor. We note that there are thermal pads connecting the installed RAM and SSD to the bottom of this mini PC, which is metal.

According to recent reports, A VESA mounting bracket is provided in the box if you prefer to hide the tiny device out of sight. It doesn’t have a remote power switch like the MSI Cubi NUC AI+ 3MG we reviewed earlier in the year, though, so you’ll have to consider reachability. A simple LED-lit power button is on the front of the device, alongside a couple of handy ports (more on the ports later). It also has a reset / clear CMOS hole on the front, and a Kensington lock slot on the rear.

Minisforum’s component choices mean this is a particularly small and light mini PC. The official M2 Mini specs state it is 112 x 112 x 37.15mm, which is roughly 4.4 x 4.4 x 1.5-inches. That’s a volume of 0.47 liters. It weighs in at just 440 grams, which is 0.97 pounds.

The power supply isn’t built-in. There’s a surprisingly bulky 65W power brick in the box, which connects to using a detachable figure-eight cable. However, this mini PC can be powered by USB-C, too, so you could pack a far more compact multipurpose power brick if portability is important.

Intel Core 3 304 (5C/5T) ‘Wildcat Lake,’ up to 4.3 GHz, 15W.

16GB in single SODIMM slot which can fit up to a 64GB DDR5-6400 module.

112 × 112 × 37.15 mm (0.47 L chassis).

Windows 11; barebone model available without OS.

$559.00 limited-time price(16GB RAM, 500GB SSD, Windows 11 Pro).

Recent findings suggest that on the front of the Minisforum Elite Mini M2 Air-304 there are 2x USB-A 3.2 Gen 2 ports and a 3.5mm audio jack. Turn it to the side and you’ll see the microSD card slot. Then, around the back you have access to 1x USB4 (40Gbps, DP Alt Mode, PD), 1x USB-C 10Gbps, 1x USB 2.0, 2x HDMI 2.0, 2x RJ-45 2.5GbE LAN, and a DC-IN barrel jack.

Some might like to have at least one of the Type-C ports on the front, instead of two Type-As. But for its size the Mini M2 Air packs quite a few ports, including the very capable USB4, two HDMI ports, and two Ethernet ports. Realistically, a machine like this won’t be connected to oodles of wired peripherals, but if you found the port count lacking, USB4 allows for a capable and fast dock.

It has been revealed that wireless connectivity seems adequate, with an M.2 2230 card inside providing Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 5.4. I had no problems with either during the test period. The wireless card is socketed. It's located under the SSD, making it easy to repair or upgrade down the line.

Accessing the components inside the Minisforum Mini M2 Air is straightforward, but you need to peel off all the four rubber feet to get to four long fastening screws. When they’re removed, just flip off the metal bottom to access the M.2 slots and SODIMM. Be aware there’s some adhesive force holding this metal plate in place, due to the sticky thermal pads on the RAM and storage.

It has been revealed that there’s just a single M.2 2280 storage slot and one SODIMM slot, both populated. That means, there’s no way to upgrade the RAM than swapping the module you already have in place. Our sample came with a 16GB DDR5-5600 SODIMM, but the system supports up to DDR5-6400. This only non-barebones configuration also came with a 500GB SSD in the M.2 slot.

We have Intel’s latest 18A silicon inside this tiny PC, but not that much of it. Our review unit came with an Intel Core 3 304 "Wildcat Lake" chip that runs up to 4.3 GHz. Previous mini PCs based on Intel 300 series mobile silicon like the previously MSI and the GMKtec Evo-T2 came with a 16C/16T CPU. However, here we have just 5C/5T, and that’s just one performance core supported by four low power efficiency (LPE) cores.

In a recent development, still, single core performance continues to be important for system and app responsiveness. The proof of the pudding is in the testing, though. And while this system felt perfectly usable in Windows 11, internet browsers, and word processing — preparing and writing this review, for example — the benchmarks are somewhat tougher.

As we expected, the single core tests show Wildcat Lake has some bite. It easily beats its AMD-based rivals in the POV Ray single core rendering tests, for example. Moreover, in tests like Cinebench 2024 single core, the Mini M2 Air might trail the pack, but not by very much. It's roughly 107 points is actually within touching distance of the 120 points scored by ‘high performance’ mini PCs like the Beelink SER10 MAX (Gorgon Point) and MSI Cubi NUC AI+ 3MG (Panther Lake).

Multicore tests exposed obvious weaknesses of the 5C/5T CPU configuration with single-channel RAM. All the other mini PCs we’ve tested this year come with 12C/24T (AMD) or 16C/16T (Intel), so the productivity benchmarks we run which can take advantage of multithreading for demanding rendering or encoding tasks make the Minisforum here seem weak. However, it might still be acceptable for transcoding a short video or two, occasionally, as long as you aren’t in a rush. If you are coming from an older, less efficient desktop sporting something like an i7-7700K or i5-10400, this 15W Wildcat Lake chip is an improvement in both single and multicore performance.

During our demanding tests, the Minisforum Elite Mini M2 Air-304 stayed cool and quiet thanks to its 15W processor and capable cooling.

For anything other than the most casual gaming or emulation of older consoles you should look at other devices. We’ve looked at Intel 300 silicon powered devices with iGPUs packing 12 Xe3 cores, and four Xe3 cores, but this just has one, and it is further hampered by sharing the single-channel system RAM.

Prepare to see some low frame rates / scores in our standard tests. I felt that some of these tests probably shouldn’t be run on this mini PC, but did it anyway, for completeness. However, some 3DMark benchmarks simply wouldn’t run, as Intel has pruned the features that work on this iGPU due to limited resources. For example, 3DMark Solar Bay doesn’t run on this system, and neither does Speed Way. Error messages about unsupported hardware pop up when you try these tests.

Steel Nomad ran, though, and the Minisforum and its solo Xe3 core achieved a score of 135. The aforementioned Evo-T2 with Intel Core Ultra X7 358H and (B390) iGPU with 12x Xe3 cores scored 1,624. That’s incredibly close to 12x faster than the Core 3 304’s ‘Intel Graphics.’ A score of 135 means Steel Nomad ran at just a little more than 1 FPS, which actually doesn’t hurt your eyes to watch as much as 10 FPS.

Using the multi-scene benchmarks built into Shadow of the Tomb Raider and Cyberpunk 2077 using our standard settings selections resulted in some unpleasant experiences. Performance of no better than 10 or 12 FPS was observed in these tests. To achieve 25 or even 30 FPS in these titles I found that reducing the game resolution to 720p and low/lowest settings would just about get there.

Industry observers note that so, for some actual fun on the Mini M2 Air I decided to try the latest version of the Sony PSP emulator PPSSPP and play some Wipeout Pure. I managed to run this game on my 1440p monitor with a 6x render resolution, and it achieved a nice steady 60 FPS, delivering an enjoyable futuristic racing experience. It would also therefore likely be good for retro emulation of similar era and older consoles as well as home computers.

Sources indicate that during my day-to-day use, the Minisforum system consumed around 9W when idling on the desktop. When under the heaviest loads I threw at it, the highest system power consumption I saw was around 31W.

I didn't find it surprising that this low-power system ran cool and quiet. System tools revealed that during light activities like browsing the web the CPU temperature remained in the low 30s Celsius. Playing games or benchmarking for length periods, I never saw the reported CPU temperature rise beyond the low 70s Celsius.

In a recent development, minisforum’s tiny mini PC was a quiet operator at idle and under load. My measurements from about half a foot in front of the device show noise levels under 30 dBA at idle, which is very quiet and actually remarked to be beneath the measurement threshold of my meter. Stressing the system with simultaneous CPU and GPU loads I managed to observe just a reading of a little over 37 dBA from the system.

The Mini M2 Air ships with Windows 11 Pro installed in the configuration we received. I found no pre-installed bloatware. The official specs don’t mention compatibility with other OSes like Linux.

Minisforum sells this mini PC with a two-year warranty and a 30-day money-back guarantee.

Recent findings suggest that minisforum sells only two Elite Mini M2 Air-304 configurations in the U.S. There’s a barebones model, or the configuration we tested with pre-installed RAM, SSD, and OS.

At the time of writing our 16GB / 500GB / Windows 11 Pro configuration is listed by the mini PC maker at $559 but the product page says the price is normally $699. The barebone model is currently $263, discounted from $329. We don’t know when the prices might get adjusted. However, we’ve noted U.S. retailers like B&H Photo are now selling the 16GB / 500GB model at $729.

Though the Mini M2 Air’s performance may lack in performance, it also probably the smallest cheapest, and least power-hungry mini PC we’ve tested all year. If these kinds of qualities are important to you, the Minisforum might be appealing.

According to recent reports, it is admirable that this mini PC is so small but leaves RAM and storage upgrades on the table for later. Other positives are the sturdy build, despite the use of plastic for the top shell, and a good port selection considering its size. In addition to being easy to hide due to its small stature, and supplied VESA mount, you probably won’t hear it very much, either.

Of course, the performance is a weakness that can’t be ignored, especially in the context of our ever-growing tested mini PCs chart from 2026. It is great to see this latest-gen processor barebones at just over $260 direct from Minisforum. If you have a spare DDR5 SODIMM and SSD, perhaps from a laptop upgrade or wherever, this might help you get a latest mini PC system up and running cheaply. However, the 16GB RAM and 500GB SSD (and Windows 11 Pro license) currently more than doubles the list price (it adds $296). That’s a bit painful.

Furthermore, if the Minisforum Elite Mini M2 Air ever rises to its apparent MSRP of $699, we’d definitely look elsewhere. Around this price, especially during sale periods, you can shop for mini PCs employing far more powerful previous-gen processors. One good alternative candidate might be the Geekom IT13 Max 2026 we reviewed in August at $799. Price trackers show this Core Ultra 185H machine with 24GB RAM has been available for under $600 with discount / coupon over the last few months. There are also a lot of capable older gen AMD mini PCs to ponder over at attractive prices.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you love spending time out on the open water, you may already captain your own vessel.
  • America is home to about 342 million people, and 85 million of us go boating every year.
  • Founded in 1954 and headquartered in Minnesota, Polaris pioneered the snowmobile.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you love spending time out on the open water, you may already captain your own vessel. Perhaps you're just starting out on your boating journey, nervous about launching your Bayliner for the first time. Or maybe you spend your weekends fishing off a friend's Grady-White. Boating is big business in the U.S. According to the National Marine Manufacturers Association, the industry's annual economic impact is $230 billion, and it supports more than 812,000 jobs.

America is home to about 342 million people, and 85 million of us go boating every year. There are about 16 million recreational boats in use on our waterways, many of those in Florida and on the Great Lakes. In a deviation from what has become the norm, about 95% of the boats sold in the U.S. are actually made here. There are thousands of manufacturers, massive and small, but only three are owned by Polaris.

Founded in 1954 and headquartered in Minnesota, Polaris pioneered the snowmobile. The organization added all-terrain vehicles, or ATVs, in the mid-1980s, and today it also offers on-road adventuring options, a line of commercial products, government and defense vehicles, and pontoon and deck boats. Did you know your favorite winter ride also rules the water?

It has been revealed that bennington makes luxury pontoon boats. These types of boats feature a wide deck built on top of hollow metal tubes that keep the vessel afloat. They offer a roomier design than boats with V-shaped hulls, and they typically feel very stable on the water. They are a great option for fishermen, but they also have plenty of room for your friends and family, from pleasure cruising to tubing and swimming.

Industry observers note that when they go with Bennington, buyers have their choice of length, layout, and premium options. The entry-level Versatile Luxury line includes the S-ONE, with a starting price of $34,326 and lengths from 16 feet to 22 feet. The best-selling brand is known for its high quality, with strong aluminum frames and luxury finishes. Owners also appreciate the smooth, quiet ride.

In a recent development, additional offerings include the Upgraded Luxury line, the Premium Luxury line, the Ultimate Luxury line, and the top-tier Pinnacle of Luxury. Prices in these lines range from about $91,200 to $188,100. Bennington offers a host of warranties, including a limited lifetime structural warranty, a limited lifetime deck warranty, a limited 10-year electronic warranty, and a 10-year bow-to-stern warranty. These warranties are transferable through Bennington dealers, but buyers looking at used models should be aware that the warranty period begins on the original owner's purchase date.

Recent findings suggest that named after the powerful tropical cyclones, Hurricane makes deck boats, which offer plenty of room for both passengers and gear. They have a wide, flared bow and a hull that is made for more seating and deck space than you get with other types of boat designs. The interior can be customized for fishing, lounging, water sports, and more.

Industry observers note that hurricane's lineup includes four models of deck boats and three yacht-certified options. Yacht-certified boats are at least 26 feet long and meet several other criteria, including safety standards and inspections. Hurricane's most affordable deck boat is the FunDeck, which starts at $27,926. It has what the manufacturer calls a "pontoon-inspired layout" and can hold up to 15 people. Buyers can also choose the SunDeck Sport, the SunDeck, or the Center Console model, the most expensive deck boat at $72,848.

According to recent reports, the yacht-certified options include the high-end SunDeck 3200, which costs $388,189 and is Hurricane's most expensive offering at the time of writing. This boat is made for entertaining and has an onboard grill station, a swim platform, a JL Audio sound system, and a power shade to keep boaters cool on hot days. The cabin has a refrigerator, microwave, and a 32-inch TV. If the SunDeck 3200 is a bit out of reach, Hurricane also offers the SunDeck 2690 for $125,384 and the SunDeck 2600 for $124,051. Both are spacious boats with swim platforms and premium options.

Sources indicate that godfrey has 60 years of experience making pontoon boats, and the company is responsible for the world's first aluminum pontoon. The boat manufacturer offers seven different lines of pontoon and tritoon boats made for watersports, entertaining, fishing, and cruising.

Sources indicate that the Mighty G Series is Godfrey's entry-level option and includes the Mighty G Cruise for $23,596 and the Mighty G Fishing for $25,060. Both are 15 feet long and have a capacity of six passengers. They are easy to handle, especially if you're fresh to boating. At the other end of the spectrum is the top-of-the-line XP Series, which Godfrey advertises as providing speed, luxury, and advanced tech. There are two 26-foot models in this line. Each starts at over $250,000 and has a capacity of at least nine.

Recent findings suggest that the luxurious Sanpan Series features tritoon boats, which are pontoons with three tubes instead of two. The Sanpan Lounge has a fiberglass exterior and offers several layouts with comfortable seating for up to 13 people. Features include onboard wireless charging, heated and cooled cupholders, and exterior aft-mounted speakers. Prices start above $150,000. If you're all about speed, the Monaco Series is more affordable and is performance-focused. If you'd rather own a one-of-a-kind Godfrey model, the company has an option to 3D-build and price your dream boat. #469. AI is reshaping the creator economy: trust will decide who wins it

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1088 w)
AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Techradar

AI is reshaping the creator economy: trust will decide who wins it

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1088 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Techradar

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that there’s always been a balancing act between creators and creator platforms over profit, value, and ownership.
  • Recent findings suggest that as creators compete for engagement against low-effort AI “slop,” they must also navigate opaque monetization policies and inconsistent enforcement.
  • At the same time, as more platforms and revenue streams emerge, creators have greater choice about where to build an audience.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that there’s always been a balancing act between creators and creator platforms over profit, value, and ownership. Now, AI tools are upsetting that balance and reshaping commercial dynamics, while raising new concerns about transparency and control.

Recent findings suggest that as creators compete for engagement against low-effort AI “slop,” they must also navigate opaque monetization policies and inconsistent enforcement. These pressures are rapidly increasing the friction between creators and the platforms they rely on.

At the same time, as more platforms and revenue streams emerge, creators have greater choice about where to build an audience.

As the terms creators operate under keep changing, creators are pushing for more control. They want their voices to be heard, their work protected, and the value they generate recognized.

For platforms, this raises the stakes for attracting and retaining top creators. Trust is becoming a competitive differentiator, and the platforms that recognize this are protecting their creators and paying them reliably in the age of AI.

Today, high-volume, low-effort AI-generated content has become an inescapable part of the online experience. But for creators, lax moderation of that content can directly impact earnings by creating an uneven playing field and increasing competition for engagement and views.

Not only must creators compete with AI-generated content, but concerns are also mounting that their work is being used to train the models producing it, without their consent or compensation. Trust is eroding as a result, and inaction risks alienating the very people whose work underpins the success of digital platforms.

These challenges are becoming increasingly evident. Recently, a US court approved a $1.5 billion settlement relating to Anthropic’s use of pirated books to train its AI models. While the case represents a clarification for rights holders, smaller creators and artists often lack the resources required to pursue litigation in the first place.

Industry observers note that concerns have also been raised about YouTube reportedly using AI to alter creators’ videos without their consent. Even where there is no evidence of financial loss, the incident highlights a potential broader imbalance in the relationship if platforms can make unilateral changes to creators’ work without meaningful consultation.

Industry observers note that creators rely on platforms to distribute, monetize, and govern their work fairly. But platforms need creators too. Their business models depend on compelling content that attracts and retains audiences. It’s a mutual dependency that makes listening to and responding to creators’ concerns a strategic imperative.

Questions about trust extend beyond how content is used to how creators earn a living. In just a few decades, the creator economy has evolved from a relatively informal ecosystem into a multibillion-dollar global industry. The decisions made by the platforms shaping this industry now directly affect how millions of creators build their careers and earn income.

Even before AI, changes to recommendation algorithms, monetization models, and advertising guidelines meant creators had to become accustomed to their earnings changing overnight. These realities have encouraged them to move away from relying on individual platforms for predictable income and monetizing their content and brands across multiple platforms and revenue streams instead.

Whether they earn through commission-based selling on ecommerce platforms, livestreaming, brand sponsorships, or content views, creators’ incomes are becoming increasingly fragmented. While this diversification reduces their dependence on any single platform, it also creates greater complexity for the businesses responsible for managing and paying them.

According to recent reports, across the industry, poor payout experiences are already damaging creator relationships. Tipalti’s recent global payments research revealed that 26% of businesses lost contributors because of payment-related concerns in the past 12 months, with creators accounting for 36% of those losses. Payment friction can directly affect a platform’s ability to retain the people generating its content.

Failing to address these pain points creates a commercial risk, particularly when creators have more options than ever to build and monetize their audiences. If a platform is frustrating to work with or fails to provide reliable payouts and transparent breakdowns of earnings, creators can move to a competitor that offers a better customer experience.

To keep creators engaged and earn their trust, platforms must address two priorities: protecting creators' work and paying them reliably and transparently.

Industry observers note that first, creators need confidence that their interests are protected and that they remain in control of their work. Platforms must acknowledge the problems posed by AI, introduce safeguards for creators’ content, and ensure that any resulting benefits are shared fairly.

Sources indicate that second, platforms must offer a transparent and reliable payout experience. At the end of each payment cycle, creators should receive a clear breakdown of how their payout was calculated, including the factors responsible for any monthly variations. They should feel confident that the economic value they create is recognized and that they will be paid accurately and on time.

In a recent development, both priorities carry more weight as creator economies grow worldwide, presenting latest opportunities for global partnerships. New markets often bring inconsistent standards for content protection and payments, and incompatible financial infrastructure can bottleneck growth.

To compete for creators in these regions, platforms need protections that hold up regardless of where a creator is based, and payout infrastructure capable of supporting an expanding range of currencies, payment methods, and regional requirements.

AI is changing what creators make, how platforms distribute it, and how value gets created. But the fundamental relationship hasn’t changed: creators need platforms to reach audiences, and platforms need creators to keep those audiences coming back.

Industry observers note that as that relationship becomes more complex, trust will matter more, not less. Creators need to know their work is protected, their earnings are transparent, and they’ll be paid accurately and on time, no matter where they are. These aren't minor priorities. They show whether a platform actually values its creators, or just profits from them.

It has been revealed that in the age of AI, trust won’t just shape the creator economy. It will shape who succeeds in it.

#467. Industry News: Can You Use Mulching Blades With Side Discharge And Bag Lawn Mowers?

Industry News: Can You Use Mulching Blades With Side Discharge And Bag Lawn Mowers?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (751 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashgear

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that though it is a pretty simple task, lawn mowing does have some degree of nuance to it.
  • Mulching blades are just good enough for both of these mower types, though not perfect.
  • Evidently, between the two, using mulching blades with a side-discharge mower is the way to go over pairing such a blade with a bag.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that though it is a pretty simple task, lawn mowing does have some degree of nuance to it. One element to consider is the type of mower blade to attach to your mower deck, with mulching blades being one of the many options. The design of a mulching blade sets it apart from a regular one, as it's meant to chop grass into finer clippings than most standard blade types. This reduces unsightly clumping throughout your lawn. This design makes them a great fit for most lawn mower types, whether you have a side-discharge model or one with a bagger attachment.

Mulching blades are just good enough for both of these mower types, though not perfect. In the case of a side-discharge model, these blades are fine to have around. In creating smaller clippings, these blades can send their finer, soil-enhancing debris out the side of the mower, reducing the amount stuck to the mower deck at the end of the job. As for bagging mowers, they don't really benefit from mulching blades. The design of the mulching blade isn't meant for sending grass clippings backward and into the bag itself, so you're not going to pick up as many clippings as you would hope. At that point, neither the bag nor the mulching blade is living up to its fullest potential, so why even bother pairing them?

Evidently, between the two, using mulching blades with a side-discharge mower is the way to go over pairing such a blade with a bag. Beyond the latter scenario, in other instances, a mulching blade can be more of a hindrance than a help.

In some scenarios, mulching blades are far from ideal. For example, if you mow infrequently and your lawn tends to grow tall and thick, a mulching blade isn't the best option. It will struggle to effectively mulch up this extra grass, resulting in clumping and piling that it's supposed to prevent. Similarly, mulching blades aren't great on wet or even damp grass. Grass that's supposed to be discharged is likely to stick to the blade and deck, meaning even with the right lawn mower-cleaning tools, you still face more extensive cleanup. Worse yet, on the job, your blade may struggle to move due to debris accumulation under the deck.

Even though they will largely work fine on a side-discharge mower, if you want optimal performance with such a model or a bagger, you'll want to grab a different yet similar blade over mulchers. A high-lift blade is specifically designed to pull grass clippings up and out of the mower deck, sending them into a bag or out of a designated discharge port. They're also better at handling taller, thicker lawns than their mulching counterparts. The only major downside here is that your grass clippings will be larger and potentially more noticeable, but if you're more concerned with dischargeability, bagging, and plowing through a thick or damp yard effectively, then it's the blade for you.

Bearing in mind which mower types and lawn conditions aren't ideal for a mulching blade, this begs the question: which mowers are? As it turns out, there's a specific mower variety to make the most of this type of blade.

Industry observers note that if you plan to try a mulching blade, you'll want the right mower for the job. As the name implies, a mower created with mulching and clipping dispersion in mind is the one to choose, since it's intended for use with mulching blades. These decks are designed to disperse fine, mulched clippings in all directions rather than through a single side discharge port. This not only keeps clippings from clumping on one side of the mower, but also disperses them evenly throughout the lawn.

Recent findings suggest that naturally, it's no surprise that the deck of a mulching lawn mower is different from most other models to help achieve its mulching mandate. Compared to a regular side discharge or bag-equipped model, these mowers have a deeper deck intended to keep grass circulating near the blade longer. This allows the mulching blade to chop everything up multiple times over, resulting in the creation of smaller clippings before sending them out into the yard.

Mulching blades are great for cutting grass into small pieces and returning its nutrients to your yard's soil. Depending on your mower setup and lawn condition, though, you may be better off reaching for one of the other lawn mower blade types instead.

Industry observers note that one massive advantage is that I don't have to think too much about organizing or maintaining a separate vault. I create individual documents for different topics and keep everything accessible through Google Drive.

One concern I had about moving away from Obsidian was whether I'd lose the flexibility of working with Markdown files.

If you want to move existing notes into Google Docs, you can also upload Markdown to Drive and open them with Google Docs.

After moving away from Obsidian, I wanted to avoid recreating the same note-taking system in another app.

In 2026, American Honda saw its best results for the month of October since 2020, including a 4.5% increase in passenger car sales. The Civic held steady at 17,960 models sold, a very modest increase over 2025, while Honda also sold about 420 Prelude models in the month.

The CR-V is one of the most popular SUVs in the U.S., and Honda sold more than 34,800 units in October alone. Industry observers note that with gas prices still hovering at an average of more than $4 per gallon nationwide, it would be easy to attribute changing trends to sticker shock. The base LX model of 2026 Honda Accord sees 29 mpg in the city and 37 mpg on the highway. The hybrid Sport model does even better, seeing 46 mpg in the city and 41 mpg on the highway, while the hybrid EX-L gets 51 mpg in the city and 44 mpg on the highway. Honda also saw an increase in hybrid sales, selling more than 7,000 hybrid Accords and 18,500 hybrid CR-Vs in October. Gas prices are certainly a driving factor behind consumer trends — but it's not the only one.

The average price of a upcoming car in America is more than $50,500. Many consumers still buy used, but cost is a bitter pill to swallow for buyers hoping to score a brand new ride. Entry-level sedans like the Accord and Civic are often priced well under $30,000, making them accessible to buyers that may not be able to afford a new SUV. The LX Accord starts at $28,395, while the Civic is priced from $24,995. Hybrid options are more expensive, of course.

Though there's been no official announcement, Honda's U.S. product planning chief disclosed intends to refresh the Accord in 2027, most likely for the 2028 model year. Little is known at the time of this writing, but changes reportedly include more modern styling. With hybrids and EVs in the mix, experts don't predict a massive resurgence of the sedan, but sales indicate the sector is more resilient than some thought.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that operating under European governance, the proposed network would combine large-scale AI computing with sovereign cloud and AI platform services, high-capacity connectivity and decarbonized energy.
  • The planned network would connect facilities in Oulu, Finland; Iru, Estonia; and Valmiera, Latvia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, nokia, Nscale, Skeleton, Telia and Verda have formed AI Gigafactory Northern (AIGF Northern), Nokia unveiled on November 16, 2026. The consortium looks a federated, multi-site AI infrastructure network across the Nordic and Baltic region and intends to bid to build and operate it under a European tender.

It has been revealed that operating under European governance, the proposed network would combine large-scale AI computing with sovereign cloud and AI platform services, high-capacity connectivity and decarbonized energy. It would serve businesses, researchers and public-sector organizations across Europe. The partners strategy to enter the open consortium tender run by the European High Performance Computing Joint Undertaking (EuroHPC JU), making the announcement a proposed bid rather than a tender award.

The planned network would connect facilities in Oulu, Finland; Iru, Estonia; and Valmiera, Latvia. The location of the Swedish site has yet to be determined. Spreading capacity across the four countries is intended to let the consortium draw on multiple sources of decarbonized energy, expand computing where capacity is available and reduce reliance on any single site or supplier.

Nokia provides the secure network infrastructure needed to link sites, move data reliably and support resilient operations. Nscale brings cloud-platform and AI-infrastructure expertise for training and inference, while Verda contributes AI-native infrastructure and cloud expertise for those workloads. Telia and its subsidiary Telia Cygate add connectivity, data transmission, infrastructure operations and cloud capabilities.

Skeleton contributes high-power energy-storage systems intended to improve data-center efficiency and stability while reducing strain on electricity grids. VTT Technical Research Centre of Finland supports the project with quantum computing, semiconductor and photonics capabilities, and KTH Royal Institute of Technology contributes AI research, education and skills development. The research partners are meant to connect the infrastructure with Europe’s research and talent networks.

Mikko Hautala, Nokia’s chief geopolitical and government relations officer, said the consortium unites the connectivity, computing, cloud and energy capabilities needed for trusted, scalable infrastructure. “By linking strengths across borders, we can build a more resilient foundation for European innovation, competitiveness and technological sovereignty,” he said.

On its project site, the consortium describes a technology-agnostic design intended to support startups, researchers and next-generation companies. Distributing capacity across multiple locations is meant to avoid single points of failure and maintain continuity during disruptions. The federated model is also designed to coordinate AI delivery across Europe without dependence on a single provider.

Sources indicate that the consortium’s regional case rests on power and cooling: reliable decarbonized energy, advanced digital networks, a cool climate that reduces cooling demand, heat-recovery potential and competitive energy costs. Those conditions are intended to deliver more computing capacity from existing grid connections, support lower-carbon operations and translate energy efficiency into more cost-competitive AI services.

The announcement’s funding context is the EU-wide InvestAI initiative: Nokia indicates it aims to mobilize €30 billion for AI investment, comprising €20 billion in private-sector funding and €10 billion from EU and national public sources.

EuroHPC JU’s call combines computing scale with operating requirements. Qualifying gigafactories must integrate massive AI computing power, energy-efficient data centers and AI-driven automation to optimize model training, inference and service deployment. The scale test is relative: each facility must integrate at least three to four times the number of the most advanced AI processors currently available in Europe’s most powerful AI factories.

It has been revealed that applicants must also demonstrate adequate power-capacity infrastructure and best practices in energy efficiency, water efficiency and circularity. The call is intended to provide sovereign AI computing for European researchers, public authorities, entrepreneurs, industries and small and medium-sized enterprises.

According to recent reports, the competition has separate lot deadlines. Lot 2 submissions are due December 3, 2026. The Lot 1 deadline is February 4, 2027, following an extension intended to give member states time to complete national budget procedures and submit financial commitments. Those deadlines apply to the tender’s lots, not to a consortium-specific award schedule.

For AIGF Northern, the central task is now to show that a distributed design can satisfy requirements written for very large, energy-efficient facilities. Its cross-border model is intended to improve resilience and use several energy supplies; the tender will test whether those benefits can be delivered together with EuroHPC JU’s processor-scale and efficiency requirements.

#459. Industry News: Are Carbide Chainsaw Chains Worth Paying Extra For?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (510 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Slashgear

Industry News: Are Carbide Chainsaw Chains Worth Paying Extra For?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (510 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashgear

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, whether you regularly use a chainsaw on the job or at home, you may eventually need to replace the chain.
  • Recent findings suggest that carbide chains have cutting teeth with tips made from tungsten carbide, a compound of tungsten and carbon.
  • Sources indicate that however, if you're only occasionally using a chainsaw on your property, a standard model could be the right choice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, whether you regularly use a chainsaw on the job or at home, you may eventually need to replace the chain. This could be a fairly inexpensive purchase, depending on what you buy, as some standard models can range from under $20 up to $30 or more. Carbide chainsaw chains can start under $20 as well, but can go into the hundreds, or even thousands for bulk reels, depending on the model.

Recent findings suggest that carbide chains have cutting teeth with tips made from tungsten carbide, a compound of tungsten and carbon. By combining with carbon, the tungsten becomes nearly as hard as a diamond, and the compound's melting point is a whopping 5,198 degrees Fahrenheit. Along with the ability to stay sharper longer, carbide chains are an ideal option for cutting tree roots, hardwood, and dirty wood. So if you're tackling demanding tasks and need a durable solution that can handle the pressure, a carbide chain may be the right one for you.

Sources indicate that however, if you're only occasionally using a chainsaw on your property, a standard model could be the right choice. Made from hardened steel, a conventional chain can handle everyday tasks like cutting clean firewood. These chains can keep an edge relatively well, and though they might need more sharpening as part of their regular maintenance than a carbide model, standard chains are still a good option. In the end, it's about deciding if what you need the chain for is worth the money you'll spend to get it.

Industry observers note that carbide chainsaw chains can be tougher to sharpen than standard steel chains. In fact, conventional sharpening methods that work on steel chains may not work on carbide. The process is so involved that it might make more sense to just send the chain to a sharpening service to ensure it's done right. That's because carbide chains need specific sharpening equipment, which some pros may not even have.

In a recent development, improper sharpening can have an impact, especially if one side of the chain is sharper than the other. This could result in the chainsaw pulling to one side as you're cutting, which reduces the amount of control you have over the tool. A dull chain, whether it's carbide or steel, also may not move through the material as effectively as it otherwise would. This means that instead of the chain sliding smoothly through the wood, you may have to physically push down harder than usual. You also may not get wood chips when crosscutting, as a dull chain could instead give you sawdust.

Industry observers note that carbide chains may also not cut through clean wood as fast as a standard steel chain can. This might not be a dealbreaker to some consumers, however, since carbide chains typically keep a sharper edge when working in tougher environments. But if you are mostly cutting clean wood and need to maintain a faster pace, you could potentially notice a difference using a carbide chain.

More specifically, there's the matter of their stats and performance levels. Starting with their batteries, they provide the same level of runtime at 2 amp hours, and they're at the same 4-volts voltage level. The batteries also communicate their remaining charge level with the built-in LED system on the tool, and, as mentioned before, charging of both is accomplished with the included USB-to-USB-C cable.

In terms of tool capabilities, their respective product listings spell out exactly what owners can expect from both rotary tool models. According to Ryobi, its battery-powered tool achieves an RPM range between 5,000 and 25,000 across its five different speed settings. With these settings Ryobi recommends it for sanding, carving, engraving, cleaning, polishing, grinding, and sharpening. Meanwhile, Dremel's model ranges in speed between 8,000 and 25,000 RPM with four different speed abilities. Both rotary tools have a ⅛-inch chuck as well to accommodate their selection of bits.

It has been revealed that on the whole, these two rotary tool kits aren't all that different, but which is right for you? For some users, Ryobi may be the better buy, seeing as you get a whole lot more and comparable tool performance at the lower of the two price points. Not to mention, many consider it one of several solid Dremel rotary tool alternatives. With that said, if you're beholden to the Dremel brand, and you're looking to save some money even with the loss of a handful of accessories, perhaps that kit is a better fit for you.

Mercedes Finally Let Us Drive Its Answer To Tesla FSD, But Did San Francisco Defeat It?

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that this week, Mercedes is pushing a number of its newest safety features live to a select group of drivers.
  • According to recent reports, the first of the two systems, Hands-Free Highway Assist, is aptly named.
  • It has been revealed that mercedes' cautious rollout is at odds with the aggressive — some might say reckless — deployment of rivals, like Tesla FSD.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this week, Mercedes is pushing a number of its newest safety features live to a select group of drivers. Part of their MB.Drive suite of driver aids, Hands-Free Highway Driving and MB.Drive Assist Pro will become available soon on U.S. roads. After that, the systems will become available across the country by the end of 2027, according to Mercedes. But first, the systems are going live to their Early Access Program customers in California.

According to recent reports, the first of the two systems, Hands-Free Highway Assist, is aptly named. It allows drivers to remove their hands from the steering wheel while the vehicle navigates highway traffic at speeds up to 85 mph. Point-to-point driving (also referred to as MB.DRIVE Assist Pro) is a step up from the Highway Assist feature. Point-to-point will signal, make turns, stop at stop signs, and get you from your starting point to your destination, so long as a navigation destination is programmed into the car. We've been passenger-seat for a demonstration of these systems before, but now it was time to take control ourselves.

It has been revealed that mercedes' cautious rollout is at odds with the aggressive — some might say reckless — deployment of rivals, like Tesla FSD. The German automaker isn't calling its system self-driving, either, and as Level 2 autonomy the human in the driver's seat remains responsible overall (wise, given parts of my own test experience). Mercedes flew me out to San Francisco, a crowded and difficult-to-navigate city, but one that's pretty tech-forward, and they put me behind the wheel to give both these systems a go.

In one of Mercedes' newest vehicles, the GLC Electric, I drove a short route along SF's crowded Embarcadero boulevard, then north, through some packed-tight residential areas with the steep hills the city is known for. It was one of the last features I tested throughout the day, but it had what was arguably the toughest gauntlet to beat and some of the highest expectations.

According to recent reports, during this drive, it was rush hour in San Francisco, with commuters and pedestrians darting around everywhere, and the system had the task of piloting the GLC through it all. The GLC's point-to-point system did an admirable job of navigating through the controlled chaos. Once I'd given it a destination and engaged the point-to-point hands-free system, the GLC made full stops at all the various stop signs, signaled before turns, and even drifted towards the center line of the road to give parked cars more space when we passed.

Sources indicate that after about 30 minutes of moving through the city, the GLC steered me right back to the hotel where I was staying, safe and sound. It wasn't a completely trouble-free journey, though.

According to recent reports, in what seemed like a pretty ironic moment, along the way, an autonomous Waymo vehicle stopped in front of me while the Mercedes' point-to-point system was engaged. The Waymo, seemingly waiting to pick up a fresh rider, was blocking the road, and the GLC didn't appear to understand what was happening. It stopped, but there was a clear path around the double-parked Waymo, so I took over and drove around the old-fashioned way.

According to recent reports, that was some rightfully conservative driving, but it's a scenario that point-to-point and MB.Drive Assist Pro should've been able to figure out — at least according to Mercedes' presentation on the tech. In other situations, the point-to-point system was too aggressive for my taste. It went over the center line into oncoming lanes more than once, requiring that I take control of the steering. It made a stop, then attempted to turn right at a stop sign, but a pedestrian had already started to cross the intersection from behind me — I took over the braking at that point, too.

Industry observers note that generally, then, the point-to-point system worked admirably, though it still has some growing to do before it's capable of taking you everywhere with zero driver input. That's where the gradual roll out of this system will hopefully pay dividends, as Mercedes tests it in various cities, integrating their learnings along the way.

A step down in difficulty from the point-to-point system was the Hands-Free Highway Assist. A number of other manufacturers have this sort of system at the moment live in their most tech-forward vehicles — GM's Super Cruise and Ford's Bluecruise have been available for years, now — and Mercedes has some of the component features — like lane-keep assist, evasive steering, lane change assist, and even a rim-protection warning — already live on MB.OS-equipped vehicles. This most advanced version of the system, though, will do that while your hands aren't on the steering wheel.

Industry observers note that in a GLS-Class and an S-Class, both of which I drove for a significant time and both of which were equipped with Hands-Free Highway Assist, I drove some of SF's busiest highways. The system maintained speed, kept its distance from cars ahead, and even made a few lane changes when there was space to be taken up.

The Proactive Lane Change Assist portion of the hands-free system moved me over a few lanes as it gradually ensured I was in the right position to change freeways, or even exit the freeway altogether. And in a fast-paced city like San Francisco, being able to do all those tasks at truly highway speeds is valuable for regular commuters.

Knowing the emergency safety features that come with your car is one thing, but you're hardly ever using all of them or testing them out. For instance, if you drive safely and nobody ever runs into you, you're probably not familiar with how airbags work. Or, if you've never had a child dart out in front of your moving vehicle, you may not know how it feels when a car's emergency braking system engages — everyone should be so lucky.

Mercedes made sure I knew how just about every emergency driver aid on their vehicles worked by the end of the day. With remote-controlled manikins in human, motorcycle, and full-SUV forms, Mercedes showed off their braking and evasion systems on a number of closed courses. I wasn't able to pilot the vehicles for these tests, but the driver showed off how the various systems reacted to on-road surprises. A motorcycle cutting across multiple lanes of traffic, a child running into the street after a lost ball, and another vehicle pulling out from a cross street all triggered the car's warning system, and eventually a full panic stop.

Without testing other manufacturer systems back-to-back with the Mercedes tech, it's tough to say that there's a better or worse system out there. But it's worth pointing out that the Mercedes systems presently use both cameras and radar, allowing for redundancy when it's needed most — and that's a system I'd certainly prefer to camera-only tech that some rivals have opted for.

The first test of the day, but the one I'll mention last, was one that involved a bit of tricky parking. The stakes were much lower, but there were a few potentially-smashed pumpkins at stake.

Imagine you're driving to a private beach, one where the road is tight, and the parking spots are scattered. That's the scenario the Mercedes' right-seat instructor had me conjure up in my brain as I drove towards a few parked vehicles and a winding course of pumpkins laid out like traffic cones on the ground. It was one of the more basic activities I took part in during the Mercedes event, but it was still pretty impressive.

After the cameras on the Mercedes SUV I was driving had identified the various available parking spots, I drove down the pumpkin-lined lane towards a dead end. The lane was tight enough to rule out a three-point turn, so the only option was to back up. Thankfully, the Mercedes could retrace its steps via the Automatic Reversing feature. Press a button on the touchscreen, and it'll go back exactly the way it came, controlling its own steering, with the driver simply managing the throttle. If you ever get stuck down a dead-end one-way road while you're searching for untouched sand, it's a pretty cool party trick.

There's quite a bit of combined usability with all of these Mercedes-Benz driver aids. Whether you're sitting in traffic on your way to work and letting the car do your acceleration and braking for you, cruising along the highway on a long road trip and letting the Merc do all the steering, or avoiding injury in a number of different potential accidents and having the car mash the brakes to prevent a collision, it's a desirable set of features.

In a recent development, there are some issues with the tech, though, and like all other hands-free systems that are currently available to the public, the MB.Drive Assist Pro and the Hands-Free Highway Assist aren't yet perfect. But it's worth a test drive. For many current Mercedes owners, the tech will be turned on via over-the-air updates in the next few months. From there, broader availability of the systems will spread across Mercedes' lineup, so you won't have to wait very long.

💡 Key Takeaways
