  • Industry observers note that instead of hours, it takes an average of 18 months for a single F-35 to be built, and no, it's not a 9-to-5 process either.
  • In a recent development, other contractors involved include Collins Elbit Vision Systems, which produces the F-35 Helmet Mounted Display System, which runs the government $400,000 apiece.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When an assembly plant fires up its robotic workers to assemble a modern mass-market car, it takes between 18 and 35 hours. That's incredible when you stop to think about it, because cars are filled with some 30,000 parts and components, each of which has to be fitted and installed so it can safely operate. Fighter jets like the F-35 Lightning II also go through a production line, but it takes quite a bit longer for one to go from parts to finish.

Industry observers note that instead of hours, it takes an average of 18 months for a single F-35 to be built, and no, it's not a 9-to-5 process either. Production runs around the clock, 24/7, ensuring that Lockheed Martin, which produces the F-35, can deliver the aircraft out to customers on time. The F-35 is primarily produced at Lockheed's Fort Worth, Texas, facility, where it works with over 1,600 suppliers to add every small component to the aircraft before it ever leaves the facility. These include Pratt & Whitney, which builds the powerful F135 engine capable of producing over 40,000 lbs. of thrust.

In a recent development, other contractors involved include Collins Elbit Vision Systems, which produces the F-35 Helmet Mounted Display System, which runs the government $400,000 apiece. The facility at Fort Worth assembles all the components into a single platform that is arguably the most complex stealth fighter ever put into service, and Lockheed recently secured an order from the Pentagon for an additional 850 F-35s.

Recent findings suggest that if you thought that cars were complex pieces of machinery, they've got nothing on the F-35. There are three F-35 variants with different models for the U.S. Air Force, U.S. Navy, and U.S. Marine Corps. They boast exponentially more parts than a car, which are all put together at the assembly plant known as Air Force Plant 4. This facility has produced warplanes for the U.S. military and its allies for decades. That stated, there are also smaller assembly plants in Italy and Japan, though the bulk of production is conducted in Texas.

In a recent development, it's there that the F-35 takes shape, as you can see in the above photo, but it takes 18 months before one makes its way out of the plant for testing and delivery. Since the F-35's introduction in 2011, Lockheed has assembled 1,387 for the U.S. and international customers. Thousands of workers assemble various components across a 24-hour day while working alongside all sorts of heavy machinery and specialized tools. It begins with the assembly of the wing section, which is followed by the airframe's primary structure pieces coming together: the tail sections, center fuselage, forward fuselage, and the wings.

Lockheed takes in thousands of parts from partner companies, including some 25% from European suppliers. Once the aircraft is finally completed, it's painted grey, and the paint is specially designed to absorb radar, supporting the F-35's stealth capabilities. They're each flown for testing, and, once this is complete, the F-35 is delivered.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For years, enterprises have approached AI as a series of discrete experiments. Now, as AI agents begin to move into the workflows that run the business, that model is starting to look inadequate. Organizations moving from isolated pilots toward AI agents and autonomous workflows are confronting a deeper challenge: rethinking how data, business processes, governance, and people fit together, turning AI from a collection of tools into part of the enterprise operating model.

Sources indicate that for Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, that shift begins with treating AI as an enterprise platform rather than a collection of disconnected projects. “AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation,” he indicates, arguing that companies need a connected, semantically rich layer that reflects their business before they can reliably deploy AI across processes. The stakes also change as AI moves into mission-critical workflows. For some everyday applications, “80% might be good enough,” he says, but in areas such as supply chains or financial close, that level of accuracy is “a very terrible result.”.

Industry observers note that that foundation also determines which AI applications are worth pursuing. Satinder Pal Singh, associate VP North America for SAP BAIP and SAP AI Strategy at Infosys, frames AI agents as “digital coworkers” and recommends evaluating potential use cases through three lenses: impact, feasibility, and scalability. Companies should identify where an agent can move meaningful business metrics, determine whether their data and talent can support the use case, and then establish whether successful applications can be replicated. “A pilot that can't scale is just an experiment,” he says.

It has been revealed that scaling also brings governance into sharper focus. Clear policies, access controls, monitoring, and oversight are necessary to ensure agents remain trustworthy and aligned with business requirements. “The absence of governance doesn't speed up AI adoption,” Singh says. “It creates a risk backlog” that can ultimately force a more disruptive stop and audit.

Sources indicate that those considerations will become more key as AI agents take on more responsibilities as digital coworkers. Both executives see a future in which agentic systems coordinate work across applications, while customer-specific knowledge graphs and governed data become critical enterprise assets. For Singh, the longer-term opportunity is a shift from AI as a productivity tool to “AI as a decision-making partner,” helping leaders understand what is happening, anticipate what comes next, and determine how to respond.

Sources indicate that NYT Connections is one of several increasingly popular word games made by the Fresh York Times. It challenges you to find groups of four items that share something in common, and each group has a different difficulty level: green is easy, yellow a little harder, blue often quite tough and purple usually very difficult.

On the plus side, you don't technically need to solve the final one, as you'll be able to answer that one by a process of elimination. What's more, you can make up to four mistakes, which gives you a little bit of breathing room.

It's a little more involved than something like Wordle, however, and there are plenty of opportunities for the game to trip you up with tricks. For instance, watch out for homophones and other word games that could disguise the answers.

It's playable for free via the NYT Games site on desktop or mobile.

#448. A major breakthrough has claimed to set a world record for encoding data onto a quantum computer — and, crucially, reading it back again

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Techradar

A major breakthrough has claimed to set a world record for encoding data onto a quantum computer — and, crucially, reading it back again

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (670 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Techradar

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Moth Quantum says its Tessa technique has achieved a new quantum computing record by storing information on a processor and successfully retrieving it.
  • The method placed 1,568 numerical values across IBM’s 120-qubit Phoenix processor, then used the recovered information to recreate an image.
  • This addresses a major challenge in quantum computing: getting ordinary information into quantum machines and retrieving it without significant loss of accuracy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Moth Quantum says its Tessa technique has achieved a new quantum computing record by storing information on a processor and successfully retrieving it.

The method placed 1,568 numerical values across IBM’s 120-qubit Phoenix processor, then used the recovered information to recreate an image.

This addresses a major challenge in quantum computing: getting ordinary information into quantum machines and retrieving it without significant loss of accuracy.

Previous research of this kind recovered 128 numerical values using 12 trapped-ion qubits, making the latest result substantially larger by the study’s definition.

Tessa uses neighboring qubits to control where information is stored, allowing the processor’s existing connections to handle the operation without moving information between distant qubits.

The arrangement avoids extra qubit-moving operations and additional helper qubits, while the tested circuits reached a depth of 19 two-qubit operations.

“Every quantum computer has to get data in before it can do anything useful with it, and that step has been a bottleneck for fields like quantum machine learning,” noted Daniel Bultrini, the Moth researcher who developed Tessa.

“Tessa makes the most of the chip’s capabilities, so the whole processor can be put to work at once.”.

Image tests stored 784 and 441 values, requiring 728 and 428 controlled operations, respectively; each used 8,192 measurement attempts.

However, information recovery was imperfect: the largest color image achieved a correlation of 0.69 with its source, compared with 0.95–0.96 for simpler images.

The average numerical error was 0.130 on Phoenix and 0.131 on IBM’s Fez processor, falling to 0.075 and 0.078 after adjustment.

That adjustment used two statistics taken from the original image, meaning the improved reconstruction relied partly on information already known.

For a separate test combining image brightness and color, Phoenix recorded errors of 0.152 and 0.092, while Fez recorded 0.144 and 0.084.

The Phoenix brightness error was 2.6 times higher than the organization’s noise model predicted, indicating that real hardware introduced additional inaccuracies.

Moth Quantum also tried audio, musical notes, DNA, and protein sequences, using different ways to represent information inside the processor.

A music test containing 347 flute notes recovered 18.7% of pitches correctly before adjustment, improving to 49.3% afterward on the Fez processor.

Biological tests required 32,768 measurement attempts, compared with 8,192 for image experiments, yet accuracy varied substantially between sequences for every measurement basis.

The p53 protein sequence achieved 71.5% correct recovery, while Sonic hedgehog reached 76.2% and mitochondrial protein MT-CO3 recorded 92.3% on IBM’s Phoenix hardware.

Results were weaker for other samples: SUR1 reached 22.6%, while pikachurin achieved 25.8%, showing that longer or more complex sequences remained difficult.

The tests also included a mitochondrial DNA sequence containing 784 building blocks and a POLG2 messenger RNA sequence with 1,582.

The study warns that one incorrect DNA or protein unit can matter biologically, so these recovery percentages do not establish dependable medical applications.

The simulations here do not include all interference between neighboring processor groups, and the hardware experiments used no error-correction techniques.

Tessa also depends on a particular pattern of connections between qubits, while measurement demands rise sharply as those connections become more numerous.

Moth Quantum did not use error mitigation, which the study claims could reduce reconstruction errors significantly in future hardware tests.

“The quantum applications that will have the greatest impact, including those that work closely with AI, will depend on breakthroughs such as Tessa in order to meet the expectations that have been set,” noted Harry Kumar, Moth’s Founder and CCO.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that firefox 151 recently shipped the Document Picture-in-Picture API. This isn’t the same thing as the (regular?) Picture-in-Picture API, which pushes videos into a resizable window that remains visible even after switching browser tabs or OS windows. No, the Document Picture-in-Picture API enables us to put anything into the window.

According to recent reports, I guess we can think of these windows as web widgets. We can use them for floating stock tickers, live chat conversations, playlists, to-do lists, notes, spreadsheets — anything that we’d want to keep on the screen at all times.

Recent findings suggest that the general idea is that we create a Document Picture-in-Picture window (DPIP window), and then we put HTML, CSS, and JavaScript into it. It’s pretty simple when you think about it, but as we explore how the Document Picture-in-Picture API works, we’re going to tackle a slightly more complex scenario that you’ll probably run into.

Recent findings suggest that we’re going to clone a stock ticker from the main document into a DPIP window. This not only gives us an opportunity to talk about some relevant media queries and pseudo-classes, which we’ll use to write targeted CSS for the DPIP window, but it’s also a stark reminder that taking a HTML component out of context can break the CSS, so you’ll need to keep that in mind.

Recent findings suggest that but for it to work, you’ll need to open the demo in debug mode. This is because picture-in-picture doesn’t work in nested browsing contexts such as CodePen s.

In addition, Safari doesn’t support the DPIP API yet, so make sure that you’re using Chrome or Firefox.

First we need to check if the browser supports the Document Picture-in-Picture API. I imagine that it’d be a nice-to-have feature, so why wait for Safari support? Unfortunately though, there’s no way to query whether or not @media (display-mode: picture-in-picture) is supported using feature queries (@supports) because the at-rule() function is only supported by Chrome, and any looks to support preludes (that’s this part: (display-mode: picture-in-picture)) appear to have been dropped anyway.

Note: Safari Technology Preview 251 release notes do mention support for at-rule detection in @supports but it’s unclear when that will rollout. And Firefox 155 revealed support for it just a day after this published.

Instead we have to check browser support using JavaScript, removing the button if DPIP isn’t supported, or making it create a DPIP window if it is supported):

Keep in mind that the Document Picture-in-Picture API is a desktop-only API, so the check above accounts for that too while illustrating exactly why a full-featured at-rule() function would be so useful.

As for creating the DPIP window, there’s one thing that we might want to do first — handle an existing DPIP window. DPIP windows replace existing DPIP windows, so we don’t need to worry about that part of it, but we do need to decide what happens if the button is clicked a second time. The code below closes the DPIP window if it’s already open, effectively making the button a toggle button:

The problem is that focus always switches to the DPIP window, so toggling the DPIP window off might require two button clicks. One solution to that is cloning the button into the DPIP window, but the DPIP window already has a “Close” icon-button, so there’s no point in that. Personally, I wouldn’t do anything, letting subsequent button clicks recreate the DPIP window. In fact, if the user moves or resizes the DPIP window, subsequent button clicks will reset it to its original position and size (with the right options).

On that note, let’s talk about creating DPIP windows and noted options. It’s pretty obvious what the width and height options do, but note that we can’t set one without the other, and if we don’t set either, the browser chooses. The preferInitialWindowPlacement option, if set to true, prevents the browser from saving the position and size of the DPIP window. The disallowReturnToOpener option (not used here), if set to true, hides the “Back to tab” icon-button (which does the same thing as the “Close” icon button, but also takes the user back to the originating tab).

The requestWindow() method of the DocumentPictureInPicture interface returns a promise (hence why we’re using async and await), which means that we can take care of everything else while the window is being prepared.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ever since testing the fantastic Soundpeats H3 (stellar earbuds which have since become favorites among audiophiles on a budget), I'm ready to pay attention to anything the affordable earbud maker puts out. That's especially true of its rivals to the AirPods Pro 3, like the Air4 Pro, because everyone likes to see a brand give the AirPods a run for their money.

Well, next up to the plate is the Soundpeats Air6 Pro (there was an Air5, we just didn't test them). They've been announced by the brand as their latest wireless earbuds, and are available to buy online right now.

These new buds cost $89.99 / £98.99 / AU$113.99 so they're pretty affordable, especially for Aussies who can get these for a steal. For context the AIrPods Pro 3 go for $249 / £219 / AU$429, so these new buds are less than half the price.

Soundpeats sent me the buds to test, and I'll be writing a full review at some point, but only managed to get one short listening session in before writing this news. Early thoughts, then: they look nondescript and are a little fiddly to get into the case, but they sound energetic and sit securely in my ears.

In a recent development, soundpeats has given the Air6 Pro 11mm drivers, which marks an improvement over the 10mm units on the Air5 Pro. They connect via Bluetooth 6.0, and can support Dolby Audio, Snapdragon Sound, Hi-Res AUdio Wireless and various aptX codecs.

Oh, and LDAC, which is a pretty basic high-res codec which the AirPods Pro 3 still somehow don't support.

It has been revealed that talking of ways they beat Apple, the battery life goes up to 12 hours per charge (if you turn ANC off, presumably, though Soundpeats doesn't say that). The AirPods Pro only hit 10 hours. The case offers 52 hours of charge, twice what Apple's case gives.

A key selling point of these buds is Soundpeats Air Series Tuning Gen2, which refers to the refined sound profile it's given the buds. Apparently, this gives mids a more prominent place in the musical mix, to create a natural sound. I'll have to use the buds more to say for sure how it works, but at a first glance (or listen, I suppose), I get what they're saying.

There's ANC here, and it sounds pretty solid from an initial test, and also four microphones per bud to allow for call noise reduction.

Industry observers note that well, that’s a wrap. No, not a flex-wrap, but rather today marks a newly introduced day, week, month, season, aaaand new edition of What’s !important (#18), bringing you the best content that CSS developers have produced over the last couple of weeks or so.

Recent findings suggest that abhishek Jakhar explained why tooltips should be delayed then instant (basically, so that we don’t trigger them accidentally, and then when we don’t want them anymore, so that they disappear immediately). Abhishek highlighted us how to implement all of that, too. One thing that I’d like to point out is that if the hover-able region is too small, the tooltip can be de-triggered unintentionally, so I’d keep the delay in that case.

Chris Coyier then responded to that with a modern implementation that utilizes interest invokers, which come with two key CSS properties: interest-delay-start and interest-delay-end. Only Chrome supports interest invokers at the moment, but progressive enhancement, right?

Speaking of progressive enhancement, the Geolocation API has always been complicated because of all of the external hardware involved (GPS satellites, Wi-Fi networks, cellular towers, etc.) and how frustrating it can be to change the permission status later. fixes a lot of that but introduces a few new quirks. For example, there are some…styling restrictions.

And since only Chrome supports it, I explained how to use alongside the current Geolocation API, which means that you can use it today, essentially.

Sources indicate that dave Rupert made a small syntax highlighter called MicroLighter using the fresh Custom Highlight API. He also showed us how to use MicroLighter, and Geoff talked a bit about it too.

Sources indicate that temani Afif demonstrated how to get CSS grid information into CSS custom properties. Specifically, how to get the number of rows and columns, as well as the coordinates (x/y indexes) of each cell. The only condition is that the columns must have equal widths, but with the way that CSS has been evolving lately, that could definitely change.

Temani also showed us how we can use this to determine hover proximity, which is very cool:.

Lea Verou indicates two-state, but Bramus says tri-state — what do you say? Personally, I like the auto-until-overridden two-state approach, as described by Vale.Rocks:.

Bramus also introduced the class prefix selector, which, even though it isn’t supported anywhere yet, is very simple and very useful (as you can see below), so I’m expecting a quick turnaround on this one.

This is cleaner and more performant than attribute selectors:.

Here’s what Geoff had to say about the class prefix selector.

Bramus (who is kind of on a roll here, to be honest), also introduced the @supports named-feature() function. This one’s supported by Chrome though, and basically queries support for very specific things that would otherwise be impossible to query, such as whether the browser respects transforms when anchor positioning elements, but hopefully it makes @supports more capable all-round.

What’s also fresh to Chrome is flex-wrap: balance, which is basically text-wrap: balance but for flex items. Ahmad Shadeed explained what flex-wrap: balance does and what we can use it for.

Let’s Use the Emergent CSS random() Function in all the Browsers

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The creator of the TV show The Good Place wrote a tie-in book about moral philosophy which includes a chapter called “The Luck of the Draw,” discussing how the myth of meritocracy leads people to “underestimate the role that luck has played in their lives.” Given how God seems to play dice with the universe, there is something compelling in the way art imitates life when websites embrace controlled chaos in their designs.
  • I’m a consultant who often works on short-term, greenfield projects, which provide me with a window into the zeitgeist and the trends companies think are the future.
  • Recent findings suggest that in fact, the requirements became custom enough that we ended up ditching the JavaScript plugin we were using and rolled our own confetti implementation!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The creator of the TV show The Good Place wrote a tie-in book about moral philosophy which includes a chapter called “The Luck of the Draw,” discussing how the myth of meritocracy leads people to “underestimate the role that luck has played in their lives.” Given how God seems to play dice with the universe, there is something compelling in the way art imitates life when websites embrace controlled chaos in their designs. The jury is out on whether extreme versions of this nondeterminism such as generative UI are a helpful usage of unpredictable UX. Indeed, when I see the YouTube comments reacting to Google’s upcoming usage of GenUI in search, maybe it’s taking the idea too far down a bad path. But there is still something about the idea of a webpage that exists in a state of subtle flux each time you land on it, the same way you can’t step into the same river twice.

I’m a consultant who often works on short-term, greenfield projects, which provide me with a window into the zeitgeist and the trends companies think are the future. It’s no coincidence that the idea of randomness permeated one of my recent projects. That’s epitomized by a burst of confetti to give the user a sense of excitement when they run a random draw they configured. And like many a UI feature in the corporate world, the simple idea of confetti was subject to several revisions to make every randomized particle align with the client’s brand.

Recent findings suggest that in fact, the requirements became custom enough that we ended up ditching the JavaScript plugin we were using and rolled our own confetti implementation! This illustrates the tension between the conflicting needs for chaos and control in UX, even in a fun feature like random confetti.

Wouldn’t it be nice if we could wield controlled presentational randomness in the presentation layer without leaving CSS?

Industry observers note that if unpredictable user experiences are having a moment, it follows that CSS will do its part to make randomized layouts easy to implement. The creators of CSS have always been on a mission to harvest common UI patterns into declarative CSS standards. In keeping with that spirit, we see that in late 2025, Safari became the first browser to support the CSS random() spec, as part of an enhancement that emphasized “letting you solve common use cases with HTML and CSS alone, paving the cowpaths, and reducing the need for JavaScript or third-party frameworks.”.

Since then, cool demos and discussions of random() keep popping up. For instance, Schalk Neethling indicated us how CSS random() can give us fine-grained control over the infamous confetti effect, and Alvaro Montoro made a strong argument that CSS turns out to be the most suitable language for such tasks. He points out this approach is in line with the Rule of Least Power, which encourages “solving a problem using the least powerful language capable of expressing and solving it.”.

Sources indicate that now the bad news: half a year after Safari introduced CSS random(), there isn’t clarity on when it will land in the other browsers. At time of writing, there are signs of life that both Chrome and Firefox have been working on it, but no guarantees about when we will be able to use it outside of the Apple world, even behind a browser flag.

So, it seems right now I can only try the online demos of CSS random() on my work MacBook and not on my PC where I do my personal projects. I am tempted to write my own implementation, but the syntax is surprisingly intricate, mostly because of elaborate random caching and keying semantics, combined with the options for base values and intervals. Even if I could manage to get all those details correct, CSS random() is part of an editor’s draft spec that’s in the “early exploration phase” and “major breaking changes are expected.”.

On top of that, from my dive into CSS polyfills in my article on ::nth-letter, we know the whole idea of a CSS polyfill can be a minefield.

With all these obstacles in mind, a person would have to be a special breed of crazy to attempt to polyfill CSS random().

Recent findings suggest that one of the commenters on a neat YouTube demo of the feature marvelled that it’s a “feature that works ONLY IN SAFARI?!? Did the Earth get flipped upside down?” Indeed, I am more accustomed to getting my first opportunity to experience emergent features in Chrome, which means my friends on iPhones often can’t run my experiments.

It has been revealed that and yet, in the case of random(), it’s darkly poetic that a feature based on chance appears in an unexpected place where many of us can’t use it. In fact, even Safari consumers may benefit from my css-random-polyfill package, because Safari updates are tied to the OS, meaning not everyone can upgrade to the latest version of the browser. Besides, we know how much Apple loves it when you hack their stuff to improve compatibility.

Jokes aside, Apple seems serious about the “hackability” and transparency of everything about the open source WebKit engine that powers Safari, and most of the demos I’ve used to test my polyfill are forks of demos from the WebKit blog, in which the Apple Safari team showed off the possibilities for CSS random() back when it was in Safari preview.

Here’s my cross-browser version of the first demo from the Safari team’s article. It’s a randomly scattered field of stars fading in and out at random intervals. The larger, four-pointed stars all tilt at the same randomly selected angle. All stars have subtle, randomly hued shadows around them.

To migrate the Safari-only original to a version that works in Chrome and Firefox, we need to change the HTML to reference my polyfill script and add the randomized marker class to all elements that we want to polyfill.

As for the CSS, unlike my :nth-letter polyfill which uses a nonstandard selector that has to be translated into valid CSS at runtime — and introduces drawbacks in the process — this time we need to support a new function in CSS instead of a new selector. It turns out the CSS we can use in this situation is technically valid, even in browsers that have never heard of CSS random(). More later on why it is valid, but for now, just notice that anywhere we want a random value, we store it in an intermediate custom property, and we always have to follow the convention that the property name starts with the prefix --random.

This starfield demo showcases a few different variations of the supported random() syntax, such as the optional third argument for specifying a step interval which, in this case, is used to randomly select only whole number values within the range:.

…and the element-shared base value, which we use here to tilt every four-pointed star by the same randomly selected angle.

In a recent development, note: In the original starfield demo, most of the random values were used inline, which is admittedly more elegant. The spec that includes random() makes it clear that this kind of function “can be used in place of any part of any property’s value,” just like calc() or min(). So, by requiring extra ceremony and conventions, the polyfill is supporting a subset of what we will get with native random(). To see the glass half-full, it means the CSS stays compatible with the native implementation: we could delete the script reference to the polyfill once native support goes baseline and our code will still work, like it does today when it detects native support in Safari. in this case the polyfill does not process random() calls at all and it lets Safari do all the work. This is a compromise I can live with, especially if the alternative is to press our noses against the glass of Safari-only demos on YouTube and make comments such as one viewer did: “Can’t wait to use this in prod in 4 years.”.

Chris Coyier remarked of the original starfield demo from Apple that he found it “pretty darn compelling!” I agree, and when I was testing my polyfill, that demo was fun to watch randomly twinkling, refresh and see the stars scatter differently using an emergent, declarative CSS standard. By contrast, I can’t say I have ever sat around wishing I could create a 100×100 CSS grid with randomly multicolored cells, so this example from the Safari team feels a bit like a contrived excuse to randomize something. However, it did help me test the polyfill support of a few different variations of the syntax.

Industry observers note that the polyfill allows for some flexible syntax. You can see that references to custom properties passed to the random() function get substituted as expected, and you can see that inlining multiple random() calls in the same value works. For example, we can create a grid-area shorthand property value with randomized row-start and column-start values.

This example is from Tim Nguyen from the Safari team. To continue the themes of chance and synchronicity, I’ll mention that I had the good fortune to meet Tim last year when I spoke at Web Directions 2025. My talk came right after his talk, and now that I’m forking his CSS random() demo to create a cross-browser version, he is once again a tough act to follow.

You can see in this example that the final random position of the wheel uses a different unit for its step interval parameter than for the minimum and maximum parameters.

The mix of types is supported because the specs say the values must be “resolvable to the same data type,” so we are able to mix units as long as they are in the same “overall data type,” such as turn and deg, familiar from the way CSS calc() adds values with different units when it makes sense, using CSS typed arithmetic.

Note: To make the demo work with the polyfill, I had to define the variable in a CSS class that will be applied when the polyfill first loads, in contrast to Tim’s original demo which uses the random() function inside a keyframes animation that was applied based on a checkbox hack. That’s because, for now, the polyfill only processes the computed styles that are applied to elements when the page first loads. Since all my tests pass with this implementation, I am leaving it like that for now in the interest of doing the simplest thing that could possibly work. There are ways we could explore to make the polyfill react to dynamic changes to the computed styles and/or the DOM.

It has been revealed that chris Coyier has a knack for writing code that’s either as tricky or as simple as needed to get his point across, and his CodePen “Very basic random() in CSS” is maybe the simplest demo of CSS random() possible, showing three randomly positioned squares with random colors. Below is my cross-browser version, which I also modified to randomize the size of the squares, as a test that my polyfill supports random value sharing using custom keys.

Here is the code I added to make each square have a random height that is equal to its random width:.

This reassures that we are supporting the correct syntax. Admittedly, custom keys will be more useful in the real native version, which won’t need the intermediate variables. Since we are using intermediate custom properties, we could just have used one custom property named --side and referenced that for both the height and width values.

Many of the above demos include random colors. That’s achieved by passing random numeric values into CSS color functions such as rgb() or lch(). But if we had a list of specific colors we wanted to randomly choose from, we can’t do that easily, which is why the spec for the CSS values and units module mentions the random-item() function, although no browser currently implements it (except for experimental support in safari preview). If we had this function, we could select a random color or anything else from an arbitrary list of values:.

The random-item function takes a mandatory first argument of the type random-caching-options, the same as CSS random(), but then it takes a variable length list of arguments to randomly select from, rather than a minimum and maximum value.

According to recent reports, I don’t feel like complicating the polyfill to support a CSS syntax that isn’t implemented in any browser — evidently I only give myself permission to do that once a year. But now that we have a version of CSS random() in Chromium which also supports CSS custom functions and inline conditionals, it’s hard to resist seeing what happens if we combine all these weird and wonderful things into one experiment. It turns out these features together can get us pretty darn close to the functionality we’d get from random-item().

If you’re using a Chromium-based browser, you can see the code in action in this version of the squares demo which sets all three elements to the same color randomly selected from the list.

The implementation of my generic --item custom CSS function takes an --index argument followed by 10 optional arguments. These could be increased to any number of arguments you think will be the realistic maximum size of a collection you would need. Each of the optional arguments is made optional by defaulting it to an empty value, so the caller of the function only needs to pass in the arguments it needs to index. Lastly, the function maps the --index to the argument at that index, because CSS custom functions do not support variable length collections of arguments the way JavaScript functions do.

Industry observers note that sidenote: This generic helper function is interesting, because Temani Afif has demonstrated cool use cases for being able to choose from a list of colors using an --index variable, but the solution he created was specific to the color data type and he freely admits it’s “more of a hack than a CSS feature. So, use it cautiously.” By contrast, the custom function approach will work with a list of any data type, and I wouldn’t describe it as a hack because it’s using CSS standards as intended, albeit emergent standards that aren’t available in all browsers just yet.

Sources indicate that now we have gained confidence in our random() polyfill, you might be curious how it works. Is this a good time to level with you and say I don’t fully know? That’s a very 2026 predicament, but thankfully it’s not because of AI.

As I hinted at the start, my level of eagerness to use fresh CSS syntax before it’s supported is matched only by my level of laziness to implement and maintain my own version of random(), so I went hunting for an open source JavaScript implementation and was pleasantly surprised it exists!

As you might expect, it’s not designed for the exact purpose I want it for. it’s in an implementation that’s designed to be used at build-time rather than on the client, as a PostCSS plugin. Digging through the source we see that this plugin wraps the MIT-licensed @csstools/css-calc which has no dependencies and isn’t coupled to PostCSS. The Readme for this package says it only implements the older CSS Values and Units Module Level 4, but we see from the commit history that it’s recently had an “update to latest spec” of random() and we see it passing automated tests for the kind of random goodness we have been enjoying in this article.

My main question is how on earth we are going to hook it up to client-side CSS, but it turns out not to be too much custom code:.

Let’s translate this code into natural language steps:.

According to recent reports, point 4 is a big deal. Interpreting arbitrary custom property values using CSS is the closest we have in present day CSS to an honest-to-goodness documented extension point for the language. Since arbitrary expressions in custom variable values are valid and can be read by JavaScript via the computed styles, this approach has the potential to avoid many of the known downsides of polyfilling CSS such as refetching and rewriting stylesheets, doing our own parsing of CSS, and other fun but dangerous pastimes.

Fittingly, it’s only by good luck that an open source project has already done most of the work we need to be able to run CSS random() in any browser while we wait for native support. A lot of people claim they can’t wait for this feature to be available in more browsers, so it will be interesting to see whether people choose to wait now that a polyfill exists. Seeing Chris Coyier’s reaction to the starfield demo, his enthusiasm was contagious! I had a similar moment when I first got the demo working in other browsers. Let me know if having this polyfill available sparks creativity for your own projects. I definitely have ideas for some more advanced use cases for it, which is what prompted me to polyfill it.

Till next time, happy randomizing from your friendly neighbourhood random guy.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Norwegian maritime engineering organization Kongsberg Maritime wants to convert commercial fishing trawlers into autonomous vessels capable of hunting Russian submarines for Britain's Royal Navy.
  • Its Arctic Hunter concept uses an existing 56-meter fishing vessel design, approximately 184 feet long, modified to conduct underwater surveillance without carrying a crew.
  • The proposed conversion would replace fishing equipment with autonomous navigation systems, submarine detection sonar, and secure communications equipment for extended maritime operations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Norwegian maritime engineering organization Kongsberg Maritime wants to convert commercial fishing trawlers into autonomous vessels capable of hunting Russian submarines for Britain's Royal Navy.

Its Arctic Hunter concept uses an existing 56-meter fishing vessel design, approximately 184 feet long, modified to conduct underwater surveillance without carrying a crew.

The proposed conversion would replace fishing equipment with autonomous navigation systems, submarine detection sonar, and secure communications equipment for extended maritime operations.

Kongsberg indicates each vessel would carry sonar equipment supplied by Thales UK alongside protected communications technology.

The ships are expected to operate independently for approximately 60 days, allowing them to undertake extended assignments without requiring onboard personnel.

Kongsberg also intends to modify certain components, including the propulsion system, to minimize unwanted underwater noise that might interfere with acoustic monitoring equipment.

The proposed design falls under Britain's Type 92 program, which seeks relatively affordable autonomous vessels capable of assisting conventional warships with anti-submarine warfare assignments.

The concept draws inspiration from World War II, when Britain converted commercial whaling vessels into naval escorts to protect shipping against German submarines.

Kongsberg Maritime argues that commercial shipbuilding already offers suitable vessel designs for demanding North Atlantic conditions, reducing the need for completely latest military construction.

The organization describes its approach as a maritime engineering exercise rather than conventional weapons development.

Kongsberg's proposed deployment arrangement involves 10 autonomous vessels operating from a support location west of the Bear Gap, between Norway and Svalbard.

That maritime passage connects northern waters with the Atlantic, making it an important geographical reference in discussions about Russian submarine movements.

Establishing the vessels' support facilities closer to their intended operating area would reduce the distance they must travel before beginning assignments.

But Kongsberg Maritime says it would manufacture the proposed Type 92 vessels within Britain if selected to deliver the program.

The Arctic Hunter ships would operate alongside Britain's future Type 26 frigates, which BAE Systems is constructing for several allied naval forces.

Those warships are intended for the United Kingdom, Australia, Canada, and Norway, with autonomous vessels potentially providing additional surveillance support.

The arrangement fits Britain's prepares for a hybrid naval fleet combining conventional warships with remotely operated or independently navigating surface vessels.

However, Kongsberg has only outlined its proposed design, and there is no official confirmation that Britain has awarded it a construction contract.

On the CSS side of things, there are indeed circumstances where CSS Grid is necessary for its intrinsic responsiveness, source order independence, and positioning. That’s why it’s an indispensable tool for layouts. Use that and let HTML tables to do the work of actually displaying tabular data!

What Exactly Is Stiction & What Causes It?

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (425 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Slashgear

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Diesel engines are built for tough jobs, from pulling heavy loads to being ideal for long-haul trucking.
  • This means it isn't technically exclusive to diesel engines, although it's used to describe when a moving part inside the diesel engine gets stuck or moves sluggishly instead of sliding back and forth like it's supposed to.
  • Industry observers note that specifically, when engine oil gets too hot, it breaks down and forms a sticky varnish that clings to metal components, which makes diesel engine parts work less efficiently.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Diesel engines are built for tough jobs, from pulling heavy loads to being ideal for long-haul trucking. And like any engine, diesels have their pros and cons, one particular glitch being stiction. In case the term is unfamiliar, stiction is short for static friction, and it refers to the resistance that must be overcome to get two touching surfaces moving.

This means it isn't technically exclusive to diesel engines, although it's used to describe when a moving part inside the diesel engine gets stuck or moves sluggishly instead of sliding back and forth like it's supposed to. This usually occurs when dirty, degraded oil turns into gunk, preventing engine parts inside from sliding freely.

Industry observers note that specifically, when engine oil gets too hot, it breaks down and forms a sticky varnish that clings to metal components, which makes diesel engine parts work less efficiently. Stiction is often an issue for any engine using HEUI (hydraulically actuated, electronically controlled unit injector) injectors, as they rely on hot, high-pressure engine oil to push fuel into the cylinders. However, stiction is also present in common rail direct fuel injectors, as the engine oil can still break down over time, forming sludge.

A few different things can cause stiction in diesel engines. For starters, oil degradation is likely the most prominent cause, as extreme heat weakens engine oil over time. When that happens, the oil leaves behind a sticky residue that coats internal parts, preventing the engine from operating smoothly. Not surprisingly, skipped oil changes and poor maintenance are another reason, since the longer you go between changes, the more time oil has to break down. Moisture can be an glitch as well, because if the oil never fully warms up, moisture will get in. Frequent short drives can cause this issue to pop up since the engine won't have time to warm up completely.

According to recent reports, cold weather makes the stiction issue even worse because cold oil thickens up. That remarked, if the fuel injectors are affected, common signs of stiction include loss of acceleration and overall pulling power, and a shaky idle or an unevenly running engine. Decreased overall fuel efficiency is another symptom. Luckily, there are ways to combat stiction, from using diesel additives to picking a high-grade synthetic diesel oil. The latter can help keep the injectors clean and give the engine the strongest defense against wear. Additionally, sticking to a regular oil change schedule and using a quality oil filter will go a long way too.

#435. How Do They Build Underwater Tunnels?

How Do They Build Underwater Tunnels?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (845 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashgear

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, tunnels are easy for groundhogs to dig; not so much for humans, even with our persistence.
  • The Thames Tunnel in London began construction in 1825, took 18 years to build, and was the third such attempt at such an under-river crossing.
  • There were a few advancements that improved the tunnel shield during the 1800s: the conversion from a square shield to a circular one; the introduction of compressed air helped keep water away from the dig, and; the injection of a grout lining to reduce impacts from settlement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, tunnels are easy for groundhogs to dig; not so much for humans, even with our persistence. That is especially true when those tunnels are underwater, yet somehow, many of us have daily commutes that take us from one side of a harbor to the other. You might know of those giant tunnel boring machines or TBMs that have made the job of cutting earth easier and safer — Virginia's largest-ever infrastructure project underneath the Chesapeake River was recently helped along by a TBM named Mary — but the origin of underwater tunneling might be a bit more boring (pun intended) than you'd think.

The Thames Tunnel in London began construction in 1825, took 18 years to build, and was the third such attempt at such an under-river crossing. British-French engineer Marc Brunel patented a tunnel shield that he said was inspired by how a naval shipworm ate through wood: boards lined a cap between the dirt and miners who would open each one of them, dig out several inches behind, close the board, and repeat. Once a full section was cleared, workers would auger the shield forward while bricklayers furnished the actual tunnel. At about a quarter of a mile long, the job caused the occasional flood, claimed six workers' lives and the good health of many others. Unlike those earlier attempts, however, this project didn't get washed out. The tunnel opened to pedestrian traffic in 1843.

There were a few advancements that improved the tunnel shield during the 1800s: the conversion from a square shield to a circular one; the introduction of compressed air helped keep water away from the dig, and; the injection of a grout lining to reduce impacts from settlement. Wood and brick gave way to cement and steel. But it would take more than a century before tunnel cutters came into their own.

According to recent reports, in the space between came another technique that was first recorded in the 1890s called immersed tube construction. For modern projects, sections of tunnel are fabricated above ground and then literally floated on-site by tug boats before a catamaran cradling barge aligns it into position. Ballast is loaded onto the tube portion to gently lower them onto a dredged and filled bed. The barge finally drags the tunnel section into its awaiting stub. The interlocking between the two sections is drained and fill material is then dumped to cover the connection. The first transportation tunnel to be built with this general method was the Michigan Central Railway Tunnel in 1906 which connected Detroit with its Canadian neighbor of Windsor, Ontario, just over a mile away.

Not every subaqueous crossing calls for boring machines or pre-cast tubes. For its Substantial Dig, the city of Boston partially drained the once-busy Fort Point shipping channel to construct an approach tube to a larger harbor crossing in the mid 1990s. A mix of somewhat novel techniques were used to keep the soil from collapsing in on the site while protecting the nearby Gilette razor manufacturing facility as well as existing subway tunnels. Engineers injected columns of grout to stabilize the ground before later refrigerating a grid of brine-filled pipes to freeze another section. This allowed MBTA Red Line trains to continue running just five feet below where a fresh underwater highway ramp was to be. Other tunnels in the Big Dig project, including that harbor crossing, also used immersed tube construction and other MBTA services including the commuter rail were not impacted during more than two decades of work.

Attempts at cutting machines in the 19th century were unsuccessful. Belgian engineer Henri-Joseph Maus built a so-called "Mountain Slicer" in 1846 to tunnel through the Alps, but subsequent populist revolutions cut off his Sardinian royal line of credit. At the foot of the Hoosac Range of Massachusetts, the Wilson Patented Stone-Cutting Machine made it through about 10 feet of rock before giving up the goat in 1851.

Sources indicate that fast forward to 1952 when mining engineer James Robbins developed the first successful tunnel-boring machine that was put to use building Oahe Dam in South Dakota. Ahead of the machine's worker shield was a rotating head filled with incisors and cutting discs that worked at the site's soft shale rock. Designs have changed over time as further projects presented grander requirements, tighter constraints, and fresh embedded challenges. For example, in soft soil conditions, a slurry shield may be used where liquidized clay is pumped into the cutter head to maintain pressurized conditions favorable for excavating the soil. This mixed sludge is pumped back through the shield, and the clay is then separated for re-use.

TBMs are used for all sorts of tunnels, including those running underwater. 19 machines were used over the course of a dozen years to build Sydney Metro's network of transit tubes, a good portion of which run underneath harbors, rivers, and bays. Meanwhile, The Boring Company, an Elon Musk venture wants to use a TBM to create a 200-mph tunnel between San Antonio and Austin, Texas.

#432. Should You Buy A 2-Stroke Or 4-Stroke Outboard Motor?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (519 w)

Should You Buy A 2-Stroke Or 4-Stroke Outboard Motor?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (519 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashgear

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that outboards come in different designs and sizes, and picking the right one can make a tangible difference in how a boat runs.
  • For starters, the biggest difference is how each engine burns fuel to create power.
  • Because of their less complex build with fewer internal parts, 2-stroke outboard motors can put out a lot of power without being as heavy as a similar 4-stroke.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that outboards come in different designs and sizes, and picking the right one can make a tangible difference in how a boat runs. So, it's no surprise that boat owners have spent a long time debating between 2-stroke and 4-stroke engines (vocal opinions come with the territory of boat ownership). Both of these outboard motors have disadvantages, but with current technology, those drawbacks are on a much smaller scale than they were in the past. As such, which one to buy will likely depend on personal choice and the boat type.

For starters, the biggest difference is how each engine burns fuel to create power. A 2-stroke motor completes its full power cycle in just two up-and-down movements of the piston, firing every time the crankshaft makes a full turn. On the other hand, a 4-stroke motor needs four piston movements and two full turns of the crankshaft to complete that same single power cycle.

Because of their less complex build with fewer internal parts, 2-stroke outboard motors can put out a lot of power without being as heavy as a similar 4-stroke. In fact, compared to its 4-stroke cousin with the same horsepower, a 2-stroke outboard motor tends to produce more power. Its smaller size also makes it a great fit for smaller boats.

Having remarked that, you might think the choice is obvious. Yet, modern 4-stroke motors generally burn less fuel than 2-stroke models, especially during recreational use. Additionally, 4-stroke outboard motors have reduced emissions and are quieter. That's not to say they aren't capable of producing great power, considering that one of the most powerful outboard boat engines ever built is a 4-stroke.

When it comes to the not-so-great things about these motors, the most noticeable disadvantage of a 4-stroke outboard motor is the size. While technology has made them lighter and more compact compared to older models, 4-stroke motors can still be too bulky for smaller boats. Also, due to their more elaborate design, they typically require more maintenance. A good example is Yamaha outboard motors, for which the company lists extra items needed for the maintenance of 4-stroke models. Having additional components also means there are more parts that could potentially need fixing down the road/waterway. "Potentially" is the key word here because these motors are generally known for their dependability.

As for 2-stroke outboard motors, they're usually categorized as noisier and less fuel-efficient. Older models (especially those with carburetors) have a reputation for rough idling and compromised stability at lower RPMs. In addition, their lubrication system isn't as good at shielding internal parts from wear and tear. Nevertheless, a lot of the above is based on older models, as contemporary 2-strokes have fewer issues with fuel efficiency, for example.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, due to technological advancements, 2-strokes and 4-strokes are considerably more comparable than before. The 4-stroke outboard engines are more common in the market these days, though the choice of which one to buy still comes down to preference. It's best to research individual motors first if a specific one tickles your fancy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jack Wall, the composer for the original Mass Effect, has shared the story of how he landed the job on BioWare's now-iconic sci-fi role-playing game (RPG).

In an interview with TechRadar Gaming, Wall recalled that he was offered a chance to audition for Mass Effect after working on Jade Empire and "had a pretty good time doing that.".

"Of course, then it had a code name: 'SFX'," Wall recalled. "It was a mystery.".

The composer explained that he created some demo music, then got a call shortly after from BioWare producer Shauna Perry, who told Wall they did a blind audition of all the entries to single out their favorite.

It has been revealed that "No one knew whose music was attributed to which composer," he said. "They gravitated to mine and were very happy to find out it was me! I love that story because I had to earn it.".

Wall continued, saying, "I went to BioWare in Edmonton to do our kickoff meeting, and they said there was this one composer, Sam Hulick, who did this one piece that they really liked (the demo that became 'Uncharted Worlds'). I think I said, 'Why did you hire me?' (laughs).".

'Uncharted Worlds' is, of course, one of Mass Effect's most memorable tracks, and Hulick also came on board, too.

Industry observers note that "He was very young in his career at the time, so they were reluctant to hire him outright on his own, but having us both made sense," Wall stated. "I honestly love that piece, and Sam killed it.".

The Mass Effect and Mass Effect 2 scores were a collaborative effort, featuring Wall, Hulick, Richard Jacques, and David Kates, with Jimmy Hinson lending his talent on the sequel. They're two of the best RPG soundtracks of all time, and according to Wall, the other BioWare developers had their favorite tracks.

Namely, 'Vigil', 'Uncharted Worlds', 'The Normandy', and 'The Citadel', Wall stated, adding that game director Casey Hudson called him after he'd completed 'Noveria' and told him, "This was his dream piece fulfilling the brief he had asked for initially.".

It has been revealed that "From ME2, of course, 'Suicide Mission', 'The Illusive Man' and 'Reflections'," Wall added. "I’m going from memory here, so opinions on the dev team may vary!".

Wall also told TechRadar Gaming that 'Suicide Mission' was one of the first things he and Casey Hudson worked on together and is "Probably to date one of the 10 best endings for a video game ever.".

According to recent reports, bharat Semi has about 75 employees across India and the United States, including 10 to 12 in Santa Clara engineering and business-development roles. The leadership team includes Kapoor as CEO and Dalmia as managing director, alongside Chief Technology Officer Boyd Fowler. Fowler previously held the same role at image-sensor maker OmniVision, bringing specialized sensor experience to the tech giant as it works toward production.

Recent findings suggest that bharat Semi intends to remain fabless in its image-sensor business, outsourcing chip manufacturing while focusing on semiconductor design and software. That distinguishes the sensor operation from the Indian fabrication project it revealed aims for in 2024. Kapoor remarked the separate project remains in development while the tech giant seeks domestic partners to build and operate the facility, and that none of the seed money will finance it.

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

With the right funds and the right parts, it's possible to build a computer that rivals some of the more recent consoles. That includes the Nintendo Switch 2. But how much would the total cost actually be, and what would you need to make it happen? With some intuitive shopping, this modern PC build would cost anywhere between $800 and $1,000. You can trim costs in some areas, but ultimately, that's what you're looking at to build a machine capable of matching the Nintendo Switch 2 from scratch.

Before you can dive into any of that, you need to know the Switch 2's internal hardware specifications. According to PCSpecs.io, the Nintendo Switch 2 has an ARM Cortex-A78C 8-core, 8-thread processor, capable of 1.1 GHz clock speeds. It also runs on a custom Nvidia Ampere GPU with 12 GB of LPDDR5 system RAM, with about 9 GB of that memory allocated to games. Altogether, it's capable of 3.07 teraflops of performance and has a memory bandwidth of 102 GB/s in docked mode. For the GPU alone, that's the equivalent of an Nvidia RTX 3050. However, the Switch 2's GPU has fewer CUDA cores, making it less powerful than the desktop graphics card.

Sources indicate that here's where things get a bit hairy. Given that prices can rapidly fluctuate, keep in mind that the total cost can change by the time you're reading this. Right now, you can buy an Nvidia RTX 3050 for between $250 and $300. 16 GB of DDR5 RAM can cost between $240 and $400, though you can get by with half of that or downgrade to something like the Crucial 16GB DDR4 RAM Kit for around $135. With a 4-core, 8-thread processor and a base clock speed of 3.3 GHz, the Intel Core i3-12100F is a comparable CPU that costs around $150. So, for the GPU, CPU, and RAM, you're looking at a base price of at least $640, or $535 if you choose DDR4 RAM.

In a recent development, you'll also need a motherboard, hard drive or solid-state drive, a PC case, power supply, and accessories, whether that's a controller or a mouse and keyboard set. Plus, you'll want speakers and, if you proposal to play online, you'll want a microphone or headset. The motherboard, case, and power supply will add between $50 and $100 for each item. With the hard drive shortage, you're looking at another $100 to $350 for a decent-sized storage drive. Adding all of that together, not including some of the other extras, you're in the $800 to $1,000 range. Granted, these are rough estimates, but that's still quite a bit higher than the Switch 2's current $500 price tag.

At the risk of sounding like an aging tech enthusiast, there was a time when building a PC like this would have cost much less. We are no longer at that point, nor will we be for quite some time, if ever again. RAM shortages and rising PC parts costs are to blame for that. But this also means that the estimated prices listed here will change over time. With some careful planning, and by using retailer promotions and sales, you could build a PC that's equivalent to a Switch 2 for much less. It's no wonder why building a machine to compete with more powerful consoles like the PS5 Pro is prohibitively expensive.

Industry observers note that you can make some concessions and go with a less powerful and more accessible GPU, CPU, or RAM bundle — the suggestion to go with the lower-cost DDR4 RAM is precisely that. Not that this is recommended, but you could also opt for renewed or refurbished parts, specifically the GPU. But this also highlights how the Nintendo Switch 2, which costs $500 all-in, could be an enticing buy for many who don't want to bother putting together their own system.

The Nintendo Switch 2 also has a lot of unique features that even most owners don't know about, which improve the gaming experience. The Joy-Con controllers and their versatility are just one example, as is breaking out the console anywhere for some spur-of-the-moment local multiplayer sessions. Though, you can also connect Joy-Cons to a PC for gaming using Steam. You can also grab one of the other handheld consoles to play anywhere, most of which are cheaper or comparable to the cost of building your own system.

#427. Taming Typography: Building a Modern CSS Reset

Taming Typography: Building a Modern CSS Reset

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1438 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Css-tricks

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that CSS can now make choices about type that used to sit outside a reset.
  • I’ve put together tidy-typography.css, which gathers the useful parts into a default stylesheet: rendering and fallback rules, fluid sizing, vertical rhythm, wrapping, hyphenation, and OpenType detail.
  • In a recent development, use it whole, or take the declaration that solves the particular irritation in front of you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that CSS can now make choices about type that used to sit outside a reset. text-wrap: pretty can prevent a stranded word, container query units can scale a heading to the column it occupies, and text-box can trim the half-leading built into a line box. Some of these features are experimental and browser support is uneven, so they need guardrails rather than blind inclusion.

I’ve put together tidy-typography.css, which gathers the useful parts into a default stylesheet: rendering and fallback rules, fluid sizing, vertical rhythm, wrapping, hyphenation, and OpenType detail.

In a recent development, use it whole, or take the declaration that solves the particular irritation in front of you. I’ll walk you through all the details in this article and give you the full code at the end.

It has been revealed that font-synthesis: none stops a browser from inventing bold or italic when the family lacks that face. The smoothing and text-rendering declarations are rendering hints, mainly for WebKit; results still vary by platform.

In a recent development, text-size-adjust disables mobile font inflation that can make a deliberately sized layout jump on rotation. font-size-adjust: from-font uses font metrics to reduce the apparent size change while a fallback swaps for a webfont.

(As with other snippets in this article, this ⁠:root block is a partial excerpt the final stylesheet combines it with additional custom properties defined later on.).

Sources indicate that viewport-based fluid type does not know how wide its element is. A heading in a narrow sidebar can therefore scale as though it fills the viewport.

Recent findings suggest that container-type: inline-size makes the wrapper a container query, so its children can use cqi: a unit based on the container rather than the viewport. Replacing vw in clamp() lets the same heading scale appropriately in an article column or a 300px sidebar without component-specific media queries.

Sources indicate that line-height includes space above the cap-height and below the baseline: half-leading. It becomes obvious when text must align tightly with another element. text-box-trim removes it, while text-box-edge measures from capital-letter caps to the alphabetic baseline. This is a metrics-aware alternative to font-specific negative-margin nudges.

Industry observers note that selectors Level 5 proposes :heading, matching h1 to h6 and [role="heading"]. It has not landed in browsers, so keep it behind an @supports selector() check.

Default heading wrapping can leave one short final line. text-wrap: balance distributes text across its lines and works best for blocks of up to about six lines. For paragraphs, text-wrap: pretty avoids a stranded final word without balancing the whole block. Both replace JavaScript orphan fixers. Editable text needs text-wrap: stable, which prevents each upcoming word from reshuffling the paragraph.

hyphens: auto relies on the browser’s language dictionaries, so the document needs a correct lang attribute (for example ). Without one the browser has no dictionary to use and won’t be able to hyphenate text. Even with the correct lang, the defaults can leave tiny word fragments or several hyphenated lines in a row.

Industry observers note that hyphenate-limit-chars controls the smallest breakable word and fragments; hyphenate-limit-lines prevents a ladder effect. hyphenate-limit-zone makes breaks less frequent, while hyphenate-limit-last protects the final word. Safari needs the prefixed equivalents, so declare both sets together.

Set code, variables, and headings to hyphens: manual: a broken code word can change meaning, and a hyphenated heading usually reads as an error.

Punctuation marks don’t carry the same visual weight as letters, so a quotation mark sitting at the start of a line can look slightly indented against the text below it. hanging-punctuation lets specified punctuation sit fractionally outside the text block’s edge.

The first value handles opening punctuation, and last handles closing punctuation at the end of a block, while allow-end lets punctuation hang past the right edge rather than force-wrapping. The result is a text block whose edges read as genuinely flush.

In a recent development, underlines have a related problem. Browsers apply flat, one-size-fits-all thickness and position regardless of the font’s actual weight.

Recent findings suggest that text-decoration-thickness: from-font reads the thickness the font’s designer intended. text-underline-offset gives descenders room to breathe, and text-decoration-skip-ink: auto interrupts the underline wherever a descender crosses it rather than drawing straight through the letter.

Variable fonts often include an optical size axis, or opsz. It lets a typeface use thinner strokes at large display sizes and thicker, more legible strokes when set small.

Recent findings suggest that font-optical-sizing: auto lets the font make that adjustment based on its actual rendered size. The @supports block covers the older font-variation-settings syntax some browsers still need, while font-variant-ligatures and font-kerning enable the font’s own ligatures and kerning pairs.

Light text on a dark background genuinely reads heavier than the same weight on a light background. Where a font ships a GRAD, or grade, axis, the dark mode block dials that perceived weight down without changing glyph shape or width the way an actual weight change would. Fonts without a GRAD axis safely ignore the setting.

Mixing a monospace font into running prose often exposes a mismatched x-height at the same declared font-size. The size-adjust keyword, set once at the @font-face level, scales that font’s rendered output specifically, leaving the actual font-size value untouched.

Recent findings suggest that numbers in a table need identical widths so they stack into a clean column on the screen. Conversely, numbers in flowing text don’t need the same treatment and should sit naturally alongside the surrounding words.

Recent findings suggest that the tabular-nums and lining-nums keywords give table digits a fixed width and full cap height. oldstyle-nums and proportional-nums let digits sit alongside lowercase letters without sticking up and disrupting the sentence’s texture.

According to recent reports, font-variant-emoji makes the choice between full-colour and monochrome emoji explicit. Without it, the browser or platform gets to choose a fallback, and the result can vary more than you expect. Apply .emoji-color or .emoji-mono to containers where you want to enforce that choice, rather than setting it globally on the body.

Quote style and character order differ by language and region. English nests single quotes inside double quotes, British English reverses that convention, and French uses guillemets with a thin space.

The quotes property declares the order for each language through :lang(). The native q element then inserts the right pair through open-quote and close-quote. The same markup can render correctly in each locale without hardcoding characters into the content.

Wrapping the rules in :where() keeps them at zero specificity, so a project can override the quote style with one plain class.

Default sub and sup styling is synthesized. The browser just shrinks the text and shifts the baseline, rather than using glyphs actually designed for that position.

Industry observers note that font-variant-position switches to the font’s own purpose-built sub and superscript glyphs where they exist, resetting vertical-align, font-size, and line-height so they don’t fight against the real glyph’s intended size and position. Most typefaces only include proper numerals rather than letters, so check the specific font before applying this broadly.

Sources indicate that :where() always resolves to zero specificity, which is useful for a reset. Every rule here is an opinionated default, and wrapping it in :where() lets a project override a property with a plain class.

It has been revealed that :is() solves a different problem: repetition. The heading selector list appears several times in a typographic stylesheet, and grouping it avoids the risk of forgetting a level.

Unlike :where(), :is() carries the specificity of its most specific argument.

Here’s the complete reset, combining the stable layers. Unsupported declarations are ignored by the browser, so the stylesheet can be adopted gradually.

Much of this CSS removes work that used to leak into other parts of a build. text-wrap can take over orphan handling from JavaScript, container query units keep a component’s type scale tied to its own width, and text-box-trim avoids the negative margins once used to compensate for leading. quotes, font-variant-position, and font-optical-sizing hand several smaller details back to the language and the font instead of a collection of one-off fixes.

According to recent reports, browser support will continue to change, especially for text-wrap and text-box-trim. Unsupported declarations are ignored, but that only helps when the unenhanced typography is acceptable in its own right.

It has been revealed that some of these rules are still too new for a baseline reset. A news article, a marketing page, and an editable product interface do not ask the same things of their text; the set that belongs in yours depends on the font, the content, and the browsers you still need to support.

Enrollment is limited to people aged 21 and older across the United States. Participants need an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone, specifically an iPhone 15 Pro or later, running iOS 26 or later. The study app is free and listed in English for iPhone.

The no-training commitment is separate from the app’s data-collection disclosures. The app’s guardrails are intended to detect certain concerning questions and suggest that participants follow up with a healthcare provider or other resources when needed. Neither the app nor the study provides medical advice, diagnosis or treatment, and participants are directed to consult a medical professional about health concerns or to verify information.

By measuring trust, comprehension and everyday health actions alongside response quality, the study ties the value of conversational health AI to what users understand and do with it. General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Slashgear

10 Of The Best Active Noise Cancelling Headphones You Can Buy In 2026
