#282. Lenovo Googlebook 15 review: Google botched it, yet again

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2032 w)
AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Androidcentral

Lenovo Googlebook 15 review: Google botched it, yet again

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2032 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Androidcentral

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the Lenovo Googlebook 15 is a classic case of a product that shouldn't exist.
  • Lightweight carbon-fiber chassis with a silk-touch finish.
  • Solid port selection with Thunderbolt 4, HDMI & more.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the Lenovo Googlebook 15 is a classic case of a product that shouldn't exist. Not because of the hardware, which is as premium as its $1,099 price tag would indicate, but because of the software. Lenovo paired a 15.3-inch 120Hz OLED display with an array of ports and an understated silk-touch finish, and put it inside a 2.84-pound featherweight body. Google then proved it doesn’t know Android that well by thinking it would suit a desktop OS. The result is a product no one should buy. Not just this one, but all Googlebooks. They’re that useless. Lenovo gets top marks for the hardware, but Google gets none for the software.

Lightweight carbon-fiber chassis with a silk-touch finish.

Gorgeous 15.3-inch 2.8K 120Hz OLED touchscreen.

Solid port selection with Thunderbolt 4, HDMI & more.

Handy Gemini tools like Rambler and Magic Pointer.

Googlebook OS is useless as a desktop OS with stretched phone/tablet apps.

$1,099+ price puts it up against full MacBooks and Windows ultrabooks.

Underwhelming battery life (~5.5 to 7.5 hours depending on workload).

Very little future potential for improvement given Google's track record.

ARM-on-x86 app stutters and broken desktop trackpad/right-click habits.

Why you can trust Android Central Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

It has been revealed that I don’t know why the Lenovo Googlebook 15 exists. More importantly, I don’t think Google can defend why it does, either. Not just this one… but all Googlebooks.

According to recent reports, make no mistake: this isn't on Lenovo. On paper and in the hand, the hardware here is phenomenal. The 15.3-inch 2,8K 120Hz OLED display is vibrant with solid touch response, and Lenovo also packed quad Dolby Atmos speakers, an array of ports, and a Glowbar RGB alert bar into a 2.84-pound featherweight body. This would not be out of place on any true premium laptop.

Which makes what Google did to it even harder to forgive. We’ve been down this road before. We’ve been down this road before. Google created Chromebooks as simple, $200 to $300 browser-first machines, and through sheer determination and low pricing, carved out a real niche. Those early laptops had clear limits, but they were forgivable because they were affordable. Then came Chromebook Plus in 2023, pushing prices from $399 up toward $749 on the theory that better specs and AI perks justified a bigger spend.

Sources indicate that from that trajectory, it’s no surprise Google tried to move even further upmarket with the Googlebook. Given how half-baked many of Google’s hardware and software pivots are, it’s also no surprise that Googlebook OS is the most half-baked of them all. Why? Because running Android apps sounds great in theory until you remember that most of them still lack proper desktop features on foldables and tablets, let alone when you try to use them as your primary computer.

The crazier part is Google’s hubris. The company had enough confidence in this half-finished platform to talk five prominent PC makers (Acer, Asus, Dell, HP, and Lenovo) into launching Googlebooks. The problem is that Google paired their hardware with an operating system that makes Windows Vista look like Windows 11. Seriously: do not buy any Googlebook.

According to recent reports, google wants you to pay a flagship premium for a platform it hasn’t bothered to finish. It’s almost certainly destined for the Killed by Google scrapyard, and that’s where it belongs. Google has yet again proved it doesn’t understand desktop computing, and all five PC makers should rightly think twice before trusting Google with a new category again. It’s time for Google to leave desktop computing to the adults in the room.

Pricing is where the Lenovo Googlebook 15 and all Googlebooks immediately trip over themselves. The cheapest Googlebook from each of the five PC makers ranges from $899 to $1,299, with the base Lenovo Googlebook 15 variant starting at $1,099.99. That gets you an Intel Core Ultra 5 325 processor, 16GB of LPDDR5X RAM, and 256GB of storage. Stepping up to the 512GB configuration pushes the price to $1,149.99 (though Lenovo throws its "AI Mouse" into the box), while European buyers face an eye-watering €1,379 sticker price.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

At $500 or $600, you can forgive rough software edges as the cost of admission. At $1,100, forgiveness evaporates. That price puts the Googlebook 15 directly in the crosshairs of Apple's MacBook Air, Apple's cheaper MacBook Neo, and dozens of capable Windows 11 ultrabooks. All of those machines run mature desktop operating systems with decades of pro-grade software behind them. Crucially, Microsoft and Apple actually know how to build desktop platforms, and Google’s naivety shines right through in Googlebook OS.

Google is asking customers to pay full flagship laptop prices for the privilege of beta-testing a first-generation platform. It’s barely ready for a free beta release, let alone a four-figure price tag. That creates an obvious chicken-and-egg trap: mainstream buyers will not spend over a thousand dollars on a machine that relies on mobile apps, and without a massive install base, major developers have zero incentive to build proper desktop-class apps for Googlebook OS.

Simply put, there’s no reason anyone should root for the Googlebook, from computer makers and developers to retailers and customers.

Strip away Google’s half-baked OS, and Lenovo’s engineering prowess shines. Picking up the Lenovo Googlebook 15 for the first time is a pleasant surprise because a 15.3-inch laptop has no business feeling this light yet premium. Weighing 2.84 pounds and measuring 0.63 inches thick, the magnesium-aluminum and carbon-fiber chassis is lighter than my 14-inch MacBook Pro and feels much better in the hand. This is one of the few Lenovo laptops to feature a textured coating, reminiscent of Asus’ Ceraluminum, and the soft, unglazed-porcelain feel on the off-white Cloud Gray chassis is beautifully designed and made.

In a recent development, the 15.3-inch 2.8K (2880 x 1800) OLED touchscreen is the star of the show. Text looks razor-sharp, blacks are properly inky, and the 120Hz refresh rate keeps scrolling fluid. It is an ideal canvas for running two browser windows side by side or kicking back with HDR movies on a flight. Lenovo also nailed the port layout by placing a 40Gbps Thunderbolt 4 port on both sides of the chassis alongside a full-size HDMI 2.0 port, a 10Gbps USB-A port, and a headphone jack. Being able to charge from either side without carrying a dongle is how every modern laptop should be built.

In a recent development, then there’s biometrics: some people prefer face unlock, others prefer a fingerprint sensor. The Lenovo Googlebook 15 gives you both choices, like any good Android phone, and while it might seem superfluous to some, it’s a pattern I’d like to see on all laptops.

Industry observers note that then there is the Glowbar, an exterior LED strip mounted along the lid near the hinge in a deliberate throwback to the original Chromebook Pixel. When the laptop is closed, it acts as a handy battery fuel gauge and pulses with a Gemini gradient during voice sessions. Across a table, it is a neat visual cue. Once you open the lid to actually use the computer, however, it’s as pointless as much of the OS, since you can’t see a single pixel of it.

The only real problem with the Lenovo Googlebook 15 is a terminal one: Googlebook OS.

Built on a hybrid of Android 17 and ChromeOS windowing, it feels like the big-tech giant equivalent of prompting AI to build this and forgetting the details. It looks pretty, then falls apart in seconds.

This is not new to Android. The chief complaint with Android foldables and tablets is that Android apps are poorly optimized for larger, more varied form factors. It's no surprise, then, that they are incredibly poorly optimized for desktop. The core concern is that Google still thinks scaled-up Android apps are an acceptable substitute for desktop software.

In a recent development, yes, you can resize Play Store apps into floating windows, and Google touts optimized versions of apps like Adobe Photoshop, Lightroom, and Spotify. In practice, most of them still behave like stretched tablet apps. Basic desktop muscle memory breaks constantly: right-click menus are inconsistent, click-and-drag gestures don't always register where you expect, and UI elements feel oversized and awkward when you navigate with a trackpad rather than a fingertip.

Sources indicate that more often than not, running the browser-based web app version of a service works better than installing its native Android counterpart. That begs an uncomfortable question: if web apps are still doing the heavy lifting, what exactly is the $1,100 upgrade over a $450 Chromebook Plus?

It has been revealed that under the hood, running ARM-compiled Android apps on an x86 Intel Core Ultra 5 325 chip causes occasional stutters and compatibility hiccups. Even Google seems painfully aware of how rushed this launch build was. Earlier this month, Google pushed an emergency November software patch specifically to patch NPU memory leaks and browser tab bloat, freeing up between 3GB and 6GB of RAM on 16GB systems. Needing a day-ten rescue patch just to stop a 16GB laptop from choking on its own AI overhead tells you everything you need to know about how ready Googlebook OS was.

Industry observers note that to be fair, Google did get a few ecosystem touches right. If you carry an Android flagship, initial setup links your phone seamlessly. Features like Continue On app handoff and instant access to your phone's local files feel effortless, showing that Google could one day build desktop-mobile integrations as slick as Apple's Continuity suite. Gemini integration is also thoughtfully executed in spots: Rambler does an impressive job turning rambling voice dictation into clean, structured checklists, and Magic Pointer lets you hover over on-screen text for instant contextual actions.

Industry observers note that sounds great, right? Don’t get too excited: these few redeeming software features cannot rescue an OS that lacks real desktop depth, nor can they fix mediocre endurance. Despite a sizable 70Wh battery, real-world stamina hovers around six to eight hours of mixed work with noticeable overnight standby drain, trailing both Apple silicon and modern Windows ultrabooks by a wide margin. Lenovo already knows how to build laptops with excellent battery life, so I’m putting this firmly on how unoptimized Googlebook OS actually is.

No, not at $1,099. In fact, there’s little reason to buy any Googlebook; the OS is that bad.

If you love the idea of a featherweight 15-inch OLED laptop, buy an ultrabook from Lenovo’s Yoga or Slim lineups, or look at the MacBook Air. Either option will cost you roughly the same money (or less), give you vastly better battery life, and run genuine desktop software without forcing you to compromise your workflow. Conversely, if you live entirely inside Google Workspace and Chrome, buy a Chromebook Plus for half the price and keep $600 in your pocket.

The Lenovo Googlebook 15 is a painful reminder of what happens when hardware and software teams operate on completely different wavelengths. Lenovo showed up ready to build a flagship laptop; Google showed up with a half-baked mobile OS and expected consumers to pay a premium. Until Google figures out what a desktop operating system actually needs to be, skip this entirely.

It has been revealed that at this point, I doubt it ever will. So don't buy the Lenovo Googlebook 15. Do not buy any Googlebook. Unless something drastic changes with Google’s approach, I probably wouldn't buy any Google desktop computer, ever.

#280. Researchers allege DeepSeek, Kimi, and other Chinese AI models were trained using banned Nvidia Blackwell GPUs

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (712 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware

Researchers allege DeepSeek, Kimi, and other Chinese AI models were trained using banned Nvidia Blackwell GPUs

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (712 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • trade controls precluding the export of Nvidia and AMD high-end AI accelerator chips to China has taken a few twists lately.
  • The scientists are careful to hedge their findings, noting that while their math checks out, it does not reveal where the chips were, how they were accessed, or prove that export controls were broken.
  • This identification method is limited to models with open weights, and depends on both hardware and software stacks used for model training — and yet it's both clever and simple, like the Egg of Columbus.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The topic of U.S. trade controls precluding the export of Nvidia and AMD high-end AI accelerator chips to China has taken a few twists lately. Jensen Huang's affairs aside, it's an open secret in the industry that Nvidia's Blackwell silicon finds its way into China, whether physically or virtually. UnemploymentLabs, an independent research outfit, has come up with strong evidence that those chips were used for training open-weight Chinese AI models, including DeepSeek V4, Kimi K3.1, MiniMax-M3, and Ling-3.1-Flash.

The scientists are careful to hedge their findings, noting that while their math checks out, it does not reveal where the chips were, how they were accessed, or prove that export controls were broken. As far as we can tell, it's currently not illegal for Chinese companies to rent Blackwell hardware abroad, and even though Nvidia's grip is tightening, U.S. companies aren't strictly prohibited from doing so, as evidenced by the recent Tencent-Oracle deal.

This identification method is limited to models with open weights, and depends on both hardware and software stacks used for model training — and yet it's both clever and simple, like the Egg of Columbus.

Industry observers note that let's establish some base facts. First, different AI accelerator families have unique counts of shader modules (SMs), marginally analogous to CPU cores — Nvidia's Hopper chips have 132, Blackwell B series have 148, and Blackwell GBs come with 152. Second, while there's more than one software stack for training AI models, PyTorch and its CUDA-aware friends are by far the most widely used on the green team's hardware.

Industry observers note that the first step for training a model is initializing its weights, or how strongly the model considers each individual input. In modern LLM architectures, their initialization goes through a randomization step in which their values are adjusted plus/minus pseudo-randomly, using cuRAND — as in, randomly, but a seed starting value results in the same adjustment figures every time.

According to recent reports, as you'd expect, doing this for an entire model is a lot of computational work, so this process is spread out across all the SMs, further subdivided into threads. For large weight sets, the thread count per SM is 2,048 for Blackwell and Hopper silicon, and it's surely carefully chosen and optimized for.

The researchers repeated a facsimile of the initialization process using the same chips, software, and thread counts. Using relatively simple statistical analysis, they spotted that their final statistical distribution of weight values precisely matched that of DeepSeek, Kimi, et al. As a test, they changed the SM and thread counts, and predictably, the correlation completely broke down.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

It has been revealed that this let them pick out each family of Blackwell/Hopper chip used for each model, and eventually they also figured out an approximate count of cards used. They cannot, however, pinpoint which exact variation produced the weights, as this analysis is linked to initialization layout counts alone, thus SM count and usage pattern — not to VRAM capacity, memory bandwidth, or other characteristics that distinguish individual cards.

Industry observers note that what about AMD cards like the MI300X, or other silicon with a high enough SM count, using the same software stack? The scientists say that it's not impossible that an AMD card could be set up to show up as two groups of 152 or 148 shaders, although we imagine there'd be little reason to do so. Nevertheless, for DeepSeek V4, they also ruled out that possibility by analyzing the actual weight values themselves, and found that AMD cards still didn't produce the same weight value pattern.

#277. 'A very well-considered follow-up' — 3 reasons the Honor 700 series could shake up the mid-range Android market

'A very well-considered follow-up' — 3 reasons the Honor 700 series could shake up the mid-range Android market

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1131 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Androidcentral

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Honor has officially lifted the curtain on its next batch of mid-range phones in China, where buyers can now place a deposit for the upcoming Honor 700S, Honor 700, and Honor 700 Pro.
  • If the firm’s previous releases are any indication, the budget-oriented 700S is unlikely to see the light of day in the West, but the more premium 700 and 700 Pro could hit shelves in the coming months.
  • And, honestly, I’m hoping that they do, because both models are set to bring some impressively high-end features to a market segment otherwise dominated by boring-looking slabs like the Oppo Reno 16, Xiaomi 17T, or Google Pixel 10.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Honor has officially lifted the curtain on its next batch of mid-range phones in China, where buyers can now place a deposit for the upcoming Honor 700S, Honor 700, and Honor 700 Pro.

If the firm’s previous releases are any indication, the budget-oriented 700S is unlikely to see the light of day in the West, but the more premium 700 and 700 Pro could hit shelves in the coming months.

And, honestly, I’m hoping that they do, because both models are set to bring some impressively high-end features to a market segment otherwise dominated by boring-looking slabs like the Oppo Reno 16, Xiaomi 17T, or Google Pixel 10.

With that in mind, here are the three reasons the Honor 700 is worth looking forward to — and one reservation that could put a damper on the global launch...

You might think cool rear displays are exclusive to high-end flagships like the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, but Honor is set to bring them to a cheaper price point with the Honor 700 series. All three models come with a small color display on the rear, and the brand has already been showing off what you can do with them in a flurry of posts on the Chinese social media site Weibo.

This includes the ability to play some cute little time-killing mini-games or unwind by tapping it to rotate a virtual wooden meditation bracelet. It also has some more practical applications, like reading your notifications at a glance without having to pick up the phone when it’s face down on your desk, or seeing a live preview of the rear camera when you’re shooting photos for easier posing. These aren’t exactly brand-fresh features in the world of phones with rear screens, but the idea of them being available at a more affordable rate is certainly appealing.

For its part, Honor does seem to have some innovation up its sleeve too. One video reveals how easy it is to change its appearance with your own pictures, emojis, or GIFs. A latest option appears when you hold your finger down to activate the Honor Magic Portal feature. Drag an image to it, and it’ll appear on the rear screen, which seems like a very Gen-Z approach to customization.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

I can already imagine rapidly tweaking it to reflect my mood, or show off the latest TV show I’m watching or game that I’m playing.

It has been revealed that there’s another surprising feature buried here as well, revealed in a recent image post. It appears as though the phone will be able to read your heart rate and blood oxygen level, conveying it with a little graphic on the rear display.

It’s not exactly clear how it will do this, but there’s most likely some kind of sensor hidden somewhere on the exterior of the device that you’ll have to hold for a few seconds in order to get a reading.

Smartwatch users might shrug, but as an analog watch wearer who relies on their phone for step tracking and logging exercise routines, I think it's a pretty cool addition that gives you access to some more health data without the need for a standalone accessory.

Honor hasn't officially revealed the specs of any of the 700 series phones just yet, but the folks over at GSMarena have put together a 700 Pro spec sheet based on the latest leaks from internet tipsters — and it's certainly promising.

It looks like a very well-considered follow-up to the already excellent Honor 600 Pro, maintaining the same glass back and aluminum frame build that made that phone feel impressively premium despite its less-than-flagship price.

The main screen will seemingly be a very similar AMOLED panel, with the same smooth 120Hz refresh rate and incredible 8,000 nits peak brightness to ensure legibility in even the harshest of lighting conditions.

Recent findings suggest that the camera setup appears to be identical too, with a 200MP main shooter, 50MP telephoto lens, and a 12MP ultrawide on the rear, and the same 50MP selfie shooter on the front. I used the Honor 600 Pro as my daily driver for multiple weeks and couldn’t fault its camera performance given its market position. It offered poppy, bright pictures that were perfect for a social media feed, so I can understand Honor not wanting to shake things up this time around.

That said, I am disappointed that the phone will still apparently ship with a USB 2.0 connector, meaning that it will suffer from very slow file transfer speeds if you hook it up to a PC to export all of your pics.

The biggest improvements will likely be to the SoC, with the more recent Qualcomm SM8845 Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 replacing the Qualcomm SM8750-AB Snapdragon 8 Elite for a solid performance boost.

The battery is also getting an upgrade, coming in at 9,000 mAh rather than the 7,000 mAh (or 6,400 mAh in Europe) of the last model for even longer-lasting performance — very promising given I was able to squeeze multiple days of use out of the 600 Pro in my testing. Of course, whether markets outside of China get lower capacities is yet to be seen.

The real elephant in the room here is price, as it could make or break the Honor 700 series as a package.

I’m hoping that Honor will be able to maintain the price point of the 600 line (which would help explain the overall rather similar specs), though this might be tricky given the huge hike in costs of key components like RAM and flash storage.

Recent findings suggest that the Honor 600 Pro retailed for £899.99 in its 12GB of RAM and 512GB storage configuration, though it is almost perpetually discounted to around £599.99, where it represents pretty incredible value. The base Honor 600, meanwhile, retails for £549.99, though, again, it is frequently on sale for £449.99.

If the 700 series is available for the same rates, I could see it being a seriously tempting proposition when put up against major flagships. I'll be following the China launch closely.

He has a particular interest in the Chinese phone market and is devoutly wedded to the latest Honor flagship.
